It holds the section's concept map, an owners table (which note explains which idea, so notes don't overlap), a decision tree where the notes are alternatives, and an at-a-glance table. Read the map before the notes, and check its owners table before writing a new note.

Part A — Foundations (the machinery you reuse in every problem)

Section 0 — Foundations

The ideas the other sections assume. Explained from first principles, with code in Java and Python.

00 · Chapter map — 01-foundations/00-chapter-map.md: reading order, owners, and the tell → principle lookup.

  • F1 · OOP: the four pillars 🔴 — 01-oop-four-pillars.md. Encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism, each as the problem it removes; overloading vs overriding; interface vs abstract class.
  • F2 · SOLID 🔴 — 02-solid-principles.md. Each letter as a violation and its fix on one OrderService. The recognition drill is item 6; the depth notes are items 7, 8, 12, 13.
  • F3 · DRY, KISS, YAGNI 🔴 — 03-dry-kiss-yagni.md. The brakes: when not to add the abstraction SOLID suggests. Pairs with item 26.
  • F4 · The pattern selector 🔴 — 04-pattern-selector.md. From the interviewer's sentence to one pattern; the entry point to Section 3.

Section 1 — Requirements & Scoping

00 · Chapter map — 01-requirements-and-scoping/00-chapter-map.md: the five opening moves and what each produces.

  1. Functional vs non-functional split, out loud 🔴 — 5 minutes of clarification before any class. Candidates who start coding immediately fail on scope, not on code.
  2. Deliberate scope cuts 🔴 — name what you're excluding (payments, auth, persistence) and why; an unasked-for feature costs you the extensible-design points.
  3. Core entities → nouns, core operations → verbs 🔴 — the mechanical first pass: extract nouns as candidate classes, verbs as candidate methods, then prune.
  4. API-first sketch 🟡 — write the 5–8 public method signatures before fields. Forces you to design the contract, not the data.
  5. In-memory-first rule 🟡 — repository interfaces backed by ConcurrentHashMap; persistence is a swappable implementation, never a schema discussion in LLD.

Section 2 — Object-Oriented Design Principles

00 · Chapter map — 02-oo-design-principles/00-chapter-map.md: the diagnosis chain (7 → 10 → 11 → 9 → 8), the mechanics (12 → 13), and the tell → item lookup. Explained from first principles in Section 0.

  1. SOLID, with a concrete violation for each 🔴 — you will be asked "which principle does this violate?"; memorize one 3-line example per letter, especially LSP (square/rectangle) and ISP (fat interface).
  2. Open/Closed as the scoring rubric 🔴 — nearly every LLD follow-up is "now add feature X"; if X requires editing an existing if/else or switch, you designed it wrong. Strategy/polymorphism is the fix.
  3. Composition over inheritance 🔴 — deep hierarchies break on the second requirement change; delegate + inject instead. The classic tell of a mid-level design is a 4-level extends chain.
  4. Law of Demeter / tell-don't-ask 🟡 — a.getB().getC().do() is a design smell; move behavior to the data.
  5. Encapsulation of invariants 🔴 — no public setters on state that must stay consistent (e.g., seat status); expose intent methods (reserve(), release()) that enforce the state machine.
  6. Anemic domain model 🟡 — getters/setters-only classes with logic in a Service is the default failure mode of Spring-trained engineers. Interviewers name it explicitly.
  7. Interface segregation for extension points 🟡 — PricingStrategy, NotificationChannel, AllocationPolicy — each becomes the knob the follow-up question turns.
  8. Dependency injection by constructor 🟡 — no new inside business classes, no static singletons reaching out; makes the design testable, which is a scored dimension.

Section 3 — Design Patterns (only what actually appears)

Don't recite the GoF catalog. Own these ten cold; know the rest by name.

00 · Chapter map — 03-design-patterns/00-chapter-map.md: the families below as a diagram, a "which family?" tree, and each pattern's trigger phrase. Choosing a pattern starts in the pattern selector (from a requirement) or the catalogue decision tree (from a code smell).

Every pattern belongs to a family, and the family says what kind of problem it solves. The item notes carry the LLD-round layer; the catalogue file explains the pattern itself.

Creational — how an object gets made, and who decides which one → catalogue/creational.md

  • 15 · Factory & Abstract Factory 🔴 — object creation by type code; the way you kill a switch on an enum. Know factory-method vs simple-factory vs abstract-factory distinctions.
  • 16 · Singleton, done correctly 🔴 🧵 — enum singleton or holder idiom; be ready to explain why double-checked locking needs volatile (→ Java index #22) and why singletons hurt testability.
  • 21 · Builder 🟡 — objects with many optional fields; pairs with immutability (→ Java index #5a).
  • Catalogue only: prototype, object pool, dependency injection (applied in item 13).

Structural — how objects are wrapped or composed → catalogue/structural.md

  • 20 · Decorator 🟡 — add-ons priced on top of a base (toppings, insurance, seat upgrades) without subclass explosion.
  • 24 · Adapter & Facade 🟢 — third-party integration boundary (payment gateway, SMS provider); the honest answer to "how do you support 3 payment providers?"
  • Catalogue only: proxy, composite, flyweight, bridge.

🎭 Behavioural — how behaviour varies and how objects talk → catalogue/behavioral.md

  • 14 · Strategy 🔴 — the single highest-frequency pattern; pricing, elevator scheduling, parking-fee, matching, eviction policy. The answer to almost every "make it configurable."
  • 17 · Observer / pub-sub 🔴 — notifications, seat-status broadcast, elevator display updates; be explicit about sync vs async dispatch and listener-exception isolation.
  • 18 · State pattern 🔴 — elevator (idle/moving/door-open), booking (created → held → confirmed → expired), order lifecycle. Replaces the nested-if state machine.
  • 19 · Command 🟡 — request as object; undo/redo, elevator request queue, job scheduling.
  • 22 · Template method 🟢 — fixed algorithm skeleton with overridable steps; common in payment/processing flows.
  • 23 · Chain of responsibility 🟡 — middleware, approval chains, request validation pipelines, rate-limit filters.
  • Catalogue only: iterator, mediator, memento, visitor, interpreter, null object.

🗄️ Persistence seam — not a GoF pattern; it keeps storage out of the domain

  • 25 · Repository & Unit of Work 🟡 — the seam that keeps persistence out of your domain; in-memory in the interview, SQL in production.

Judgment — whether to use a pattern at all → catalogue/anti-patterns.md

  • 26 · Pattern overuse 🔴 — applying six patterns to a parking lot is a negative signal. Name a pattern only when it removes a specific future edit.

Section 4 — Concurrency in LLD

00 · Chapter map — 04-concurrency-in-lld/00-chapter-map.md: which tool for which concurrency problem, as a tree.

Where senior candidates separate from mid-level. Assume every LLD problem gets a "now make it thread-safe" follow-up.

  1. Identify the contended resource first 🔴 🧵 — seat, slot, elevator queue, inventory count. Everything else is single-threaded; lock only that.
  2. Optimistic vs pessimistic locking 🔴 🧵 — version/CAS retry vs synchronized/row lock; the double-booking question in BookMyShow is exactly this.
  3. Lock granularity 🔴 🧵 — per-show / per-floor / per-slot locks instead of one global lock; be able to state the throughput consequence.
  4. ConcurrentHashMap.compute / putIfAbsent as the atomic primitive 🔴 🧵 — most interview-scale atomicity is achievable without explicit locks (→ Java index #29).
  5. Deadlock avoidance by lock ordering 🟡 🧵 — two-account transfer, two-seat booking; global ordering by ID is the standard answer.
  6. Idempotency keys 🔴 — retried "book" or "pay" requests must not double-charge; the design answer is a dedupe key, not a lock.
  7. Reservation with TTL / hold-then-confirm 🔴 — seat held 10 min then auto-released; scheduled sweeper vs lazy expiry-on-read — know both and their trade-off.
  8. Background schedulers 🟡 🧵 — ScheduledExecutorService for expiry, elevator step ticks; explain shutdown and missed-tick semantics.

Section 5 — Modeling Craft

00 · Chapter map — 05-modeling-craft/00-chapter-map.md: the slip → the habit.

  1. Enum with behavior 🟡 — enums carrying strategy/fee logic instead of a switch elsewhere; very high signal for small effort.
  2. Value objects vs entities 🟡 — Money, SeatId, TimeSlot as immutable values with equals/hashCode (→ Java index #1); entities have identity and lifecycle.
  3. Never use double for money 🔴 — BigDecimal or long minor units; interviewers notice this in one glance.
  4. Time as an injected dependency 🟡 — Clock/Supplier<Instant> instead of System.currentTimeMillis(); makes expiry logic testable.
  5. Null handling & validation placement 🟡 — validate at the boundary, keep the domain non-null; Optional on return only (→ Java index #42).
  6. Custom exceptions for domain failures 🟢 — SeatAlreadyBookedException beats returning false; but don't build a 12-class hierarchy.
  7. Testability & a couple of unit tests 🟡 — if there's time, write 2 tests for the contended path; it disproportionately raises the score.
  8. UML you actually need 🟢 — class diagram with multiplicity + one sequence diagram for the main flow. Don't draw more.

Part B — The Canonical Problems

Each entry: the discriminating design decision, the classic follow-up, and the failure mode. Practice by implementing, not reading.

Section 6 — State-Machine & Scheduling Problems

00 · Chapter map — not written yet for Sections 6–8; each section's README.md lists per-item status. The mechanisms these problems reuse are owned by the Part A maps: lifecycles by §3 (state), contention and holds by §4.

  1. Elevator system 🔴 🧵 — the canonical LLD.

    • Entities: Building, Elevator, ElevatorController, Request (external: floor + direction; internal: destination floor), Display, Door.
    • Key decision: scheduling policy behind a SchedulingStrategy interface (FCFS → SCAN/LOOK → nearest-car). The whole round is designed to see whether the algorithm is swappable.
    • State pattern for IDLE / MOVING_UP / MOVING_DOWN / DOOR_OPEN / MAINTENANCE.
    • Two request queues per elevator (up-set / down-set, TreeSet) is the standard clean answer.
    • Follow-ups: multiple elevators + dispatcher, express/odd-even elevators, capacity limit, emergency/fire mode, "how does it know when to stop?"
    • Failure mode: modeling a single elevator with a List<Integer> FIFO queue and no direction concept.

  2. Parking lot 🔴 — the warm-up that everyone gets asked eventually.

    • Entities: ParkingLot, Level, ParkingSpot (size-typed), Vehicle hierarchy, Ticket, EntryGate/ExitGate, FeeCalculator.
    • Key decisions: spot-allocation strategy (nearest / first-fit / level-balanced) as a strategy; fee model as a strategy (hourly, slab, day-rate, EV surcharge).
    • Concurrency: two cars, one free spot — atomic spot claim.
    • Follow-ups: multi-floor, reserved/handicapped spots, monthly pass, real-time availability display, payment failure.

  3. Meeting-room / calendar scheduler 🟡 — interval-overlap logic + room allocation.

    • Key decision: interval tree / sorted list for conflict detection; recurring events (RRULE) is the classic hard follow-up.
    • Follow-ups: time zones, attendee availability intersection, double-booking prevention.

  4. Task scheduler / job runner 🟡 🧵 — DelayQueue or PriorityBlockingQueue + worker pool.

    • Follow-ups: cron expressions, retries with backoff, at-least-once vs exactly-once, dependency DAG between jobs.

  5. Vending machine 🟢 — pure state pattern drill (idle → coin-inserted → dispensing → change); good 20-minute warm-up.

  6. ATM 🟢 — state pattern + note-denomination greedy dispense + transaction atomicity; frequently a screening-round problem.

Section 7 — Inventory, Booking & Marketplace Problems

  1. BookMyShow / movie ticket booking 🔴 🧵 — the other canonical, and the concurrency showcase.

    • Entities: City, Theatre, Screen, Movie, Show, Seat, ShowSeat (the join — status per show, not on Seat), Booking, Payment, User.
    • Key decision #1: ShowSeat as a separate entity. Putting isBooked on Seat is the single most common modeling error.
    • Key decision #2: hold → confirm → expire lifecycle with a TTL (typically 5–10 min) and idempotent payment callback.
    • Key decision #3: preventing double-booking — pessimistic lock per (show, seat) vs optimistic version + unique DB constraint on (show_id, seat_id) as the last line of defense. Say the constraint out loud; it's the answer that lands.
    • Pricing as strategy: seat class, weekend/weekday, dynamic, coupons.
    • Follow-ups: seat-lock expiry sweeper vs lazy expiry, group booking atomicity (all-or-nothing across N seats → lock ordering, → #31), payment gateway timeout with unknown outcome (→ Failure-modes index), waitlist, cancellation & refund policy.
    • Failure mode: no distinction between "seat held" and "seat booked."

  2. E-commerce cart & order 🟡 — cart → order → payment → fulfillment state machine; inventory reservation is the same hold/confirm problem as #49.

    • Follow-ups: coupon stacking rules (chain of responsibility), split shipment, partial refund.

  3. Ride-hailing (Uber/Ola) 🔴 — matching + trip state machine.

    • Entities: Rider, Driver, Trip, Location, MatchingService, PricingService.
    • Key decision: driver-matching strategy (nearest, ETA-based, surge-aware) as a strategy; geo-index (quadtree/geohash) mentioned but not implemented in LLD.
    • Follow-ups: driver goes offline mid-trip, concurrent match of the same driver to two riders (→ #28), surge pricing, cancellation.

  4. Food delivery / Swiggy 🟡 — three-party state machine (customer, restaurant, courier); mostly a superset of #51 plus order-prep timing.

  5. Hotel / airline seat booking 🟢 — same skeleton as #49 with date-range inventory instead of per-show inventory; know that the difference is interval availability.

  6. Splitwise / expense sharing 🔴 — clean graph + strategy problem, very common at product companies.

    • Key decision: SplitStrategy (equal / exact / percentage) and a balance sheet as Map<User, Map<User, BigDecimal>>.
    • Follow-up: debt simplification (minimize number of transactions) — the algorithmic twist.

  7. Library management 🟢 — the classic textbook problem; entity modeling + borrowing rules + fines. Low signal but still asked at service companies.

Section 8 — Infrastructure-Flavored LLD

Design-a-component problems: the interviewer wants data-structure judgment plus thread-safety.

  1. LRU cache 🔴 🧵 — HashMap + doubly-linked list, O(1) both ops; know why LinkedHashMap access-order works (→ Java index #35) and why you'd still hand-roll it.

    • Follow-ups: LFU, TTL eviction, thread-safe version (segment locks vs synchronized methods), cache stampede.

  2. Rate limiter 🔴 🧵 — token bucket / leaky bucket / fixed window / sliding-window log / sliding-window counter. Know the memory-vs-accuracy trade-off of each and which one a real API gateway uses (token bucket).

    • Follow-ups: distributed rate limiting (Redis + Lua atomicity), per-user vs per-IP vs per-endpoint, burst allowance.

  3. In-memory key-value store 🟡 🧵 — get/put/delete + TTL + eviction; leads naturally to persistence (WAL) and snapshotting follow-ups.

  4. Logging framework 🟡 — level filtering, appenders (chain of responsibility + strategy), async appender with a ring buffer, formatter. Tests layering instinct.

  5. Notification service 🟡 — channel abstraction (email/SMS/push) + template + retry policy + user preference; observer + strategy + chain.

  6. Message queue (in-process) 🟡 🧵 — topic → subscribers, offset per consumer group, blocking queue, at-least-once delivery. Bridge topic into the Kafka material.

  7. Connection pool 🟢 🧵 — borrow/return semantics, max size, timeout, leak detection (→ Java index #57).

  8. Tic-tac-toe / chess / snake-and-ladders 🟡 — board games test clean abstraction more than algorithms: Board, Piece hierarchy, MoveValidator strategy, GameState, win-detection. Chess adds the piece-movement-rule polymorphism that interviewers actually want to see.

  9. URL shortener (LLD flavor) 🟢 — encoding scheme (base62 of a counter vs hash + collision handling), the ShortCodeGenerator interface, custom aliases. The scaling half belongs in HLD.

  10. File system / directory tree 🟢 — composite pattern; find with predicate filters is the usual follow-up.

  11. Search autocomplete / typeahead 🟡 — trie + top-K per node; ranking as a strategy. Bridges into the RAG index's retrieval material.

The four things LLD interviewers actually score

Most candidates optimize only for #1.

  • 1 — It works: the happy path compiles and runs. Table stakes.
  • 2 — It extends: the named follow-up feature is a new class, not an edit to an existing one (→ #7, #14).
  • 3 — It's safe under concurrency: you identified the contended resource and defended it precisely (→ Section 4).
  • 4 — It communicates: you narrated trade-offs, named what you cut, and your class names read as domain language.

Cross-reference ownership map

  • Strategy (#14) is the answer to nearly every "make X configurable" follow-up — pricing, scheduling, matching, eviction, splitting.
  • State (#18) owns elevator, booking, ATM, vending machine, order, trip. Learn it once.
  • Hold-then-confirm + TTL (#33) is shared by BookMyShow (#49), e-commerce (#50), and hotel booking (#53).
  • Optimistic vs pessimistic locking (#28) is the concurrency question in #44, #49, #50, #51.
  • Java concurrency internals — ConcurrentHashMap (#30), ReentrantLock/AQS, executors — live in the Java index (#26–#30); link, don't re-derive.
  • Anything about replication, partitioning, or QPS belongs to the HLD index — deflect it explicitly ("that's the distributed version; in-process I'd do X").

Suggested study order

  1. Sections 1–2 — scoping and SOLID; cheap, and they set the frame for everything.
  2. Section 3 (patterns) — Strategy, State, Factory, Observer first; the other six after.
  3. #43 Elevator + #49 BookMyShow — implement both end-to-end, from scratch, timed at 60 min. These two cover ~70% of the pattern surface.
  4. Section 4 (concurrency) — then go back and add thread-safety to both implementations.
  5. #44, #54, #56, #57 — parking lot, Splitwise, LRU, rate limiter: the four most common second-round problems.
  6. Section 8 remainder — one pass each; they're variations on data-structure judgment.
  7. Section 7 remainder — skim; they're recombinations of #49 and #51.

The 15 that matter (ranked by interview frequency)

If you only own fifteen, own these. Everything else is recognition-level.

Rank Pattern Group Tier The one-line reason
1 Strategy Behavioral 🔴 The answer to almost every "make X configurable" follow-up
2 Factory Method / Simple Factory Creational 🔴 Kills the switch on a type code
3 Singleton Creational 🔴 Asked to expose your thread-safety and testability instincts
4 Observer Behavioral 🔴 Events, notifications, listeners — the pub/sub ancestor
5 Builder Creational 🔴 Many optional fields + immutability
6 Adapter Structural 🔴 Third-party integration boundary
7 Decorator Structural 🔴 Add behavior without subclass explosion
8 State Behavioral 🔴 Replaces the nested-if state machine
9 Facade Structural 🔴 Simplify a subsystem; the layering instinct
10 Proxy Structural 🔴 Lazy loading, access control, remoting, AOP
11 Command Behavioral 🟡 Request as object → undo, queueing, scheduling
12 Template Method Behavioral 🟡 Fixed skeleton, variable steps
13 Chain of Responsibility Behavioral 🟡 Filters, middleware, approval chains
14 Composite Structural 🟡 Tree structures treated uniformly
15 Flyweight Structural 🟡 Share intrinsic state to cut memory

(You wrote "flywheel" — the pattern is Flyweight, #15. Different thing from the "data flywheel" in AI systems, which is the feedback loop in 06-ai-systems.)

The three questions to answer for every pattern

Make every note in this folder answer these. Anything else is filler.

  1. What varies? Every pattern isolates one axis of change. Name it in one sentence.
  2. What's the cost? Indirection, class count, harder stack traces, runtime overhead. A pattern with no stated cost means you don't understand it yet.
  3. What's the JDK/Spring example? ☕ Citing Collections.unmodifiableList (Decorator) or @Transactional (Proxy) proves you've seen it in the wild, not just in a book.

The comparisons interviewers actually ask

Memorize these six; they're the follow-up to almost any pattern question.

Confusion The distinction
Adapter vs Facade Adapter changes an interface to match a client's expectation; Facade simplifies a subsystem behind a new, smaller interface. Adapter is about compatibility, Facade about complexity.
Decorator vs Proxy Same shape (wrap and delegate), different intent: Decorator adds behavior the client asked for; Proxy controls access to the subject (lazy, remote, security) — often without the client knowing.
Strategy vs State Identical structure. Strategy is chosen by the client and doesn't change itself; State transitions itself based on internal events.
Factory Method vs Abstract Factory Factory Method = one product, subclass decides which. Abstract Factory = a family of related products, kept mutually consistent.
Builder vs Factory Factory: one call, you know the type. Builder: step-by-step construction of a complex object, usually with optional parts and validation at build().
Template Method vs Strategy Template = inheritance, compile-time variation, subclass fills the hooks. Strategy = composition, runtime swap. Prefer Strategy (→ composition over inheritance).

Anti-pattern warnings

(Expanded, with a code-review checklist, in anti-patterns.md.)

  • Pattern-itis. Applying six patterns to a parking lot is a negative signal. Name a pattern only when it removes a specific future edit.
  • Singleton as a global variable. Hidden dependency, untestable, often a hidden concurrency bug. Prefer DI-scoped single instances.
  • Anemic domain model. Getters/setters plus a fat Service — the default failure mode of Spring-trained engineers. Interviewers name it explicitly.
  • Inheritance for reuse. Deep extends chains break on the second requirement change. Delegate instead.
  • Premature abstraction. An interface with exactly one implementation and no foreseeable second one is cost, not design.

Suggested study order

  1. Strategy, Factory, Observer, State — cover ~70% of LLD round usage.
  2. Builder + immutability — pairs with the Java index's immutable-class topic.
  3. Adapter / Facade / Decorator / Proxy — learn as a group, because the exam question is the distinction, not the definition.
  4. The six comparisons above — out loud, one sentence each.
  5. decision-tree.md Gate 0 + the fast-path lookup table — this is what converts recall into judgment. Drill the symptom→pattern table until it's reflexive.
  6. Command, Template, CoR, Composite, Flyweight — one worked example each.

⚡ The fast path — symptom → pattern lookup
🔎 Reverse check — "I already used X. Was it right?"
🎤 The three sentences to say in a design review

docs.html:
Tier: 🔴 CORE · 🟡 SUPPORTING · 🟢 BREADTH · Flags: trap · comparative · ☕ in-JDK

The thesis

Patterns rarely fail because they're wrong. They fail because you reached for one at the wrong moment, for the wrong reason, or as a substitute for naming the real problem.

The hard part was never remembering that Strategy exists. It's deciding whether Strategy is what this code needs right now, or whether a simpler move would do more.

So the tree enforces one step of discipline before you pick anything:

Describe the friction you're trying to remove — in one sentence, out loud, before you name a pattern.

If you can't finish the sentence "right now, changing X forces me to edit Y", you don't have a pattern problem yet. You have a naming problem.

🚦 Gate 0 — Do you need a pattern at all?

Run this before the tree. Most "which pattern?" questions die here, and killing them here is a senior signal, not a lazy one.

Ask If yes →
Has this actually changed, or might it change? Only pattern for change that has happened twice or is on the roadmap. Once is a coincidence.
Would a plain function, a record, or a Map solve it? Do that. A lambda is a Strategy. A Map<K, Supplier<V>> is a Factory. Don't ceremony it up.
Is the "complexity" actually just a bad name? Rename first. Half of perceived design problems are vocabulary problems.
Am I adding this for a hypothetical second implementation? Stop. An interface with one impl and no known second is cost, not design. (→ anti-patterns.md §4)
Can I delete code instead of abstracting it? Always prefer deletion.

The rule of three. Duplicate it once. Duplicate it twice. On the third occurrence, abstract — because now you can see which parts actually vary. Abstracting at the first occurrence means guessing the axis of change, and you will guess wrong.

The root question

Everything branches from one question: where is the pain?

The mnemonic:Creating itCreational. Connecting itStructural. Varying itBehavioral.

🅰️ Branch A — Creation friction

The object exists fine. Getting one is the problem.

Branch A quick table

The friction, in your words Pattern Simpler move to try first The cost you're accepting
"This constructor has 9 args and 6 are optional" Builder 🔴 A record + with* copies; or a parameter object A whole extra class; overkill under ~4 fields
"There's a switch returning new Something()" Factory Method 🔴 Map<Type, Supplier<T>> registry Indirection — harder to see the concrete type
"Mac widgets must never mix with Windows widgets" Abstract Factory 🟡 Two separate factories, no shared abstraction Adding a product type forces edits to every factory
"Opening this connection takes 300ms and we do it per request" Object Pool 🟡 A connection pool library — don't hand-roll Lifecycle bugs, leaked/dirty objects
"We have 10k objects that differ only in position" Flyweight 🟡 Just measure first — usually not the bottleneck Split intrinsic/extrinsic state; genuinely fiddly
"Copying this by hand misses a field every time" Prototype 🟢 A copy constructor or record with Deep vs shallow copy is a permanent trap
"There must be exactly one" Singleton 🔴 A Spring @Bean — same effect, testable Global state, hidden dependency, thread-safety

The Branch A trap. Builder for a 2-field value object, and Factory for a class with one implementation, are the two most common instances of pattern-itis in code review. Both are "I learned a pattern" rather than "I removed a future edit."

🅱️ Branch B — Structure / boundary friction

The objects are fine individually. The seam between them is the problem.

The four wrappers, disambiguated by intent

All four have the same shape — hold a reference, delegate. The exam question is never the shape. It's the intent.

Pattern Intent, one word The client... You reach for it when
Adapter Compatibility ...wanted an interface you don't have Wrapping a vendor SDK, a legacy API, or normalizing N providers
Facade Simplicity ...wanted fewer calls Carving a seam before extracting a service
Decorator Enhancement ...asked for the extra behaviour Logging/retry/caching layered in combinations
Proxy Control ...usually doesn't know you're there Lazy load, access control, remoting, @Transactional

Branch B quick table

The friction, in your words Pattern Simpler move to try first The cost you're accepting
"Stripe's types are showing up in my domain model" Adapter 🔴 One mapper function, if there's only one vendor A class per vendor to maintain
"Callers need 3 of this subsystem's 40 methods" Facade 🔴 A well-named service method Becomes a god-object if it starts deciding
"We have CachedRetryingLoggingRepo and 8 siblings" Decorator 🔴 Just two params on one class, if it's only two flags Deep wrapper stacks are brutal to debug
"I want to add caching without the caller knowing" Proxy 🔴 Put it in the method — if it's one method Invisible behaviour; stack traces get worse
"A folder holds files and folders and I keep type-checking" Composite 🟡 Recursion over a plain tree Leaf ops that don't apply to composites
"{Windows,Mac,Linux} × {Light,Dark} = 6 classes" Bridge 🟢 Accept the 6 classes if it stops at 6 Real indirection for a rarely-real problem

🅲 Branch C — Behaviour friction

The code works. It's the variation that hurts. This branch carries most of the LLD interview and most of real production churn.

Branch C quick table

The friction, in your words Pattern Simpler move to try first The cost you're accepting
"Adding a pricing rule means editing calculate()" Strategy 🔴 A Map<Key, Function<..>> of lambdas Class/lambda proliferation
"if (status == X && prev == Y) five levels deep" State 🔴 An enum with behaviour + a transition table A class per state; transitions get scattered
"Six things must happen after an order is placed" Observer 🔴 Call the three methods directly, if it's three Ordering, failure handling, memory leaks 🧵
"We need undo, or to queue this for later" Command 🟡 A Runnable or a job row in a table Every action becomes a class
"Every importer does the same 5 steps, 2 differ" Template Method 🟡 Strategy — composition beats inheritance Locked to inheritance, compile-time only
"Auth, then rate limit, then validate, then handle" CoR 🟡 An ordered List<Handler> and a for loop Debugging "which link dropped it"
"New report type = edit 12 node classes" Visitor 🟢 switch on a sealed interface (modern Java) Adding a node type breaks every visitor
"Callers do for (int i…) over my internals" Iterator 🟢 Return a Stream or Iterable Rarely worth hand-writing today ☕
"Every component references every other component" Mediator 🟢 An event bus The mediator becomes the god-object

Strategy vs State — the distinction that gets asked. Identical structure. Strategy is chosen by the client and doesn't change itself. State transitions itself based on internal events. If the object decides its own next mode, it's State.

The fast path — symptom → pattern lookup

When you don't want to walk the tree. Find your symptom; the pattern is the answer.

Symptom in the code Reach for
switch / if-else on a type code, returning objects Factory 🔴
switch / if-else on a type code, choosing behaviour Strategy 🔴
switch / if-else on a status field, with transitions State 🔴
Telescoping constructors, or a half-built object window Builder 🔴
new scattered across business logic Factory 🔴 + DI
A third-party type appearing in your domain package Adapter 🔴
ClassNameWithFourAdjectives and its 7 siblings Decorator 🔴
"…and also send an email, and also update search, and also…" Observer 🔴 / domain events
A method that must be called before another to be valid State 🔴 or Builder 🔴
Copy-pasted method with one line different Template Method 🟡 or Strategy 🔴
A growing pipeline of pre-processing steps CoR 🟡
"We need an audit log of what the user did" Command 🟡
Sequence: same 5 steps in 6 places, order matters Template Method 🟡
Expensive object created per call, immutable result Flyweight 🟡 / cache
Type-checking instanceof in a loop over a tree Composite 🟡 or Visitor 🟢

Reverse check — "I already used X. Was it right?"

Run this in code review. Each smell means the pattern is load-bearing for the wrong reason.

Pattern present Smell that it's wrong What to do instead
Strategy Exactly one implementation, no second planned Inline it. Delete the interface.
Factory It returns the same class every time Inline new.
Singleton It holds mutable state, or tests need reset() Make it a DI-scoped bean; pass it in.
Observer Listener order matters for correctness You wanted a pipeline (CoR) or an orchestrator.
Decorator You need to know which layer you're in You wanted parameters, not layers.
Facade It contains business rules and branching It became a god-object. Push logic down.
Builder Fewer than 4 fields, all required Use a record.
Template Method Subclasses override the "fixed" steps too You wanted Strategy.
Inheritance chain 3+ deep Any change breaks a sibling Delegate. Composition over inheritance.
Any pattern You can't name the future edit it prevents Remove it.

💰 The cost ledger

Every pattern buys flexibility on one axis and charges you. Say the cost out loud when you propose the pattern — that's the architect-level move, and it's how you keep a design review from turning into a debate.

You get You pay
Runtime swappability (Strategy, State, Bridge) Indirection — "go to definition" no longer answers "what runs?"
Extension without editing (Factory, Visitor, CoR) Class count, and a registry that must be kept in sync
Decoupling (Observer, Mediator, Adapter) Control flow you can't read from the call site; harder stack traces
Composability (Decorator, Composite) Deep wrapper stacks; unclear ordering semantics
Construction safety (Builder, Prototype) Boilerplate, and a second place a new field must be added
Access control (Proxy) Invisible behaviour; surprising performance and transaction boundaries

The three sentences to say in a design review

  1. Name the friction. "Right now, adding a payment provider means editing PaymentService.charge()."

  2. Name the pattern and the axis. "Strategy isolates the provider-specific call behind one interface, so a new provider is a new class plus a registry entry."

  3. Name the cost, unprompted. "The cost is one more indirection — you can't see from the call site which provider runs, so I'll keep the registry in one file and log the selected strategy."

Volunteering step 3 is what separates "I read the GoF book" from "I've maintained this for two years."

docs.html:
Tier: 🔴 CORE · 🟡 SUPPORTING · 🟢 BREADTH · Flags: trap · comparative · ☕ in-JDK

1. Factory Method / Simple Factory 🔴 ☕

  • What varies: which concrete class is instantiated.
  • Shape: a create(type) method (simple factory) or an overridable createX() hook that subclasses implement (true Factory Method).
  • Use when: you have a switch/if-else on a type code returning new Something(). That switch is the smell; the factory is the fix, and adding a type becomes a new class plus a registry entry.
  • Registry variant: Map<Type, Supplier<Product>> populated at startup — extension without editing the factory (Open/Closed satisfied properly).
  • Cost: one more indirection; over-applied, it hides which class you're actually getting.
  • ☕ JDK: Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getInstance(), LocalDate.of(), Charset.forName().
  • Spring: BeanFactory is the name-brand example; FactoryBean<T> for beans needing custom construction.
  • Trap: "Simple factory" is not a GoF pattern; if the interviewer is pedantic, say which one you mean.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Factory Method design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

2. Abstract Factory 🟡

  • What varies: an entire family of related products that must stay mutually consistent.
  • Shape: GuiFactory → createButton(), createCheckbox(); a MacFactory never returns a Windows button.
  • Use when: cross-platform toolkits, per-cloud provider client sets, per-database dialect object sets.
  • Cost: adding a new product type forces every factory to change — the known weakness. Adding a new family is cheap.
  • vs Factory Method: one product vs a coherent family. Say this sentence and the follow-up is over.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Abstract Factory design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

3. Builder 🔴 ☕

  • What varies: the number and combination of optional construction parameters.
  • Use when: more than ~4 constructor params, several optional; or the object must be immutable and validated as a whole.
  • Shape: fluent .setX().setY().build(), with all validation in build() so an invalid object never exists.
  • Kills: the telescoping-constructor anti-pattern and the setter-based "half-built object" window.
  • Pairs with: immutability — final fields, no setters, defensive copies (→ Java index #5a).
  • ☕ JDK: StringBuilder, Stream.Builder, HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Calendar.Builder, Lombok @Builder.
  • Interview line: "Builder gives me immutability and readability; a 7-arg constructor gives me neither."
  • Trap: a builder for a 2-field value object is pattern-itis. Use a record.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Builder design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

4. Singleton 🔴 ☕

The most-asked and most-misused pattern. The question is a concurrency and testability probe wearing a creational costume.

  • What varies: nothing — it restricts creation to one instance.
  • Correct implementations, in the order you should present them:
    1. Enum singleton — one line, serialization-safe, reflection-safe. The Effective-Java-endorsed answer.
    2. Initialization-on-demand holder — lazy, thread-safe via classloading guarantees, no synchronization cost.
    3. Eager static final — simplest, fine when construction is cheap.
    4. Double-checked locking — only correct with a volatile field; be ready to explain why (partially-constructed object visibility, → Java index #22). Present this as "the one people get wrong," not as your recommendation.
  • ☕ JDK: Runtime.getRuntime(), Desktop.getDesktop().
  • The real answer in modern code: let the DI container manage a single instance (@Component is singleton-scoped by default). You get one instance and constructor injection and testability.
  • Costs to name unprompted: global mutable state, hidden dependency, hard to mock, lifecycle tied to the classloader, and a classic source of test-order flakiness. Interviewers wait for you to volunteer these.
  • Follow-ups to expect: "How do you break it?" (reflection, serialization, cloning, multiple classloaders) and "How does enum defend against each?"

Picture: Singleton UML class diagram, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

5. Prototype 🟢 ☕

  • What varies: creation cost — clone an existing configured instance instead of rebuilding it.
  • Use when: object construction is expensive (heavy parsing, remote fetch) and instances differ only slightly.
  • Trap: Java's Cloneable/clone() is a broken design (shallow by default, no constructor invoked, protected access). Prefer a copy constructor or a static copyOf factory and say so.
  • Modern equivalent: record with-style copying, or a builder seeded from an existing instance.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Prototype design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

6. Object Pool 🟢

  • What varies: instance lifetime — reuse rather than allocate.
  • Use when: the object wraps a scarce external resource: DB connections, threads, HTTP connections, GPU contexts.
  • Trap: pooling plain Java objects is almost always a pessimization on a modern JVM — TLAB allocation is a pointer bump, and pooling defeats generational GC by keeping objects alive into the old gen (→ Java index #49). Say this; it's a strong signal.
  • Real examples: HikariCP, ThreadPoolExecutor, Netty's ByteBuf pool.

7. Dependency Injection 🔴

  • Not GoF, but the pattern that replaces half the creational catalogue in practice.
  • What varies: which collaborator an object receives — decided outside the object.
  • Prefer constructor injection: dependencies become explicit and final, and an object is never in a half-wired state.
  • Why it matters here: DI is why you rarely hand-write Singleton or Abstract Factory in a Spring codebase — the container is both.

Fast comparison table

If the question is... The answer is
"Which concrete type?" Factory Method
"A consistent family of types?" Abstract Factory
"Too many constructor arguments?" Builder
"Exactly one instance?" Singleton — but really, DI-scoped
"Construction is expensive, instances are similar?" Prototype (copy constructor)
"The resource is scarce, not the object?" Object Pool

docs.description: Adapter, decorator, facade, proxy, composite: how objects fit together.
meta: Composing objects and classes into larger structures without rigid coupling.
Parent: README.md · The four wrappers (Adapter/Facade/Decorator/Proxy) are the highest-yield group in this folder — the exam question is the distinction, not the definition.
docs.html:
Tier: 🔴 CORE · 🟡 SUPPORTING · 🟢 BREADTH · Flags: trap · comparative · ☕ in-JDK

1. Adapter 🔴 ☕

  • What varies: the interface of an existing class you cannot change.
  • Intent: compatibility. Make a square peg fit a round hole.
  • Two forms: object adapter (composition — preferred) vs class adapter (multiple inheritance — not available in Java for classes).
  • Use when: wrapping a third-party SDK, a legacy API, or normalizing several vendors behind one interface (payment gateways, SMS providers, LLM providers).
  • ☕ JDK: Arrays.asList(), InputStreamReader (bytes → chars), Collections.enumeration().
  • Interview line: "Adapter is how I keep a vendor's types out of my domain — one class changes when they change."
  • Related: the Anti-Corruption Layer in DDD is Adapter applied at a bounded-context boundary. Name-dropping it lands well at architect level.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Adapter design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

2. Facade 🔴

  • What varies: nothing structural — it reduces the surface area of a complex subsystem.
  • Intent: simplicity. One coarse-grained entry point over many fine-grained calls.
  • Use when: a client needs 3 of the 40 operations a subsystem exposes; or you're carving a seam before extracting a service.
  • Cost: can become a god-object if it accumulates logic; it should orchestrate, not decide.
  • vs Adapter: Adapter fits an existing required interface (compatibility); Facade invents a new simpler one (complexity). A Facade is optional — you can always bypass it. An Adapter is not.
  • Spring: JdbcTemplate over raw JDBC is the canonical example.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Facade design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

3. Decorator 🔴 ☕

  • What varies: responsibilities added to an object at runtime.
  • Intent: add behavior the client explicitly asked for, while preserving the interface. Stackable.
  • Use when: you'd otherwise get a subclass explosion (CoffeeWithMilkAndSugarAndSoy), or you need cross-cutting behavior per instance: buffering, compression, encryption, metrics, retry, rate limiting.
  • ☕ JDK: the whole java.io stack — new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(f))); Collections.unmodifiableList(), synchronizedMap().
  • Trap: deep decorator stacks make stack traces unreadable and ordering matters (compress-then-encrypt ≠ encrypt-then-compress). Name the ordering issue.
  • In LLD rounds: the standard answer to "how do you price add-ons / toppings / seat upgrades?"

Picture: Vanderjoe, Decorator design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

4. Proxy 🔴 ☕

  • What varies: access to the real subject — same interface, controlled path.
  • Four flavors: virtual (lazy init), remote (network stub), protection (authorization), smart reference (ref counting, logging, caching).
  • ☕ JDK: java.lang.reflect.Proxy — JDK dynamic proxies over interfaces.
  • Spring: the pattern behind @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async, @PreAuthorize. JDK proxy when the bean implements an interface, CGLIB subclass proxy otherwise.
  • The self-invocation trap: calling this.someTransactionalMethod() inside the same bean bypasses the proxy and the annotation silently does nothing. One of the highest-frequency Spring interview questions (→ Java index #55).
  • Hibernate: lazy-loaded entities are proxies; touching one outside the session throws LazyInitializationException.
  • vs Decorator: identical structure. Decorator adds behavior and is client-visible and stackable; Proxy controls access and is usually transparent to the client. Both wrap — the intent differs.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Proxy design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

5. Composite 🟡 ☕

  • What varies: whether a node is a leaf or a container — clients shouldn't care.
  • Shape: Component interface, Leaf and Composite implementations, where Composite holds List<Component> and recurses.
  • Use when: file systems, org charts, UI widget trees, nested menus, expression trees, comment threads, or a permission tree.
  • ☕ JDK/real: java.awt.Container, the DOM, Maven POM hierarchies.
  • Trap: the GoF "transparent" variant puts add/remove on the base Component, forcing leaves to throw. Prefer the safe variant (child ops only on Composite) and mention the trade-off — that's the discriminating detail.
  • LLD appearance: the file-system-design question is a pure Composite drill.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Composite design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

6. Flyweight 🟡

The one you called "flywheel." Worth getting the name right because it comes up as a memory question.

  • What varies: nothing behavioral — it shares immutable intrinsic state across many objects, while extrinsic state is passed in per call.
  • Shape: a factory returns cached shared instances keyed by intrinsic value.
  • Use when: millions of similar objects, and memory (not CPU) is the constraint: glyphs in a text editor, tiles/particles in a game, tokens in a parser, string interning.
  • ☕ JDK: Integer.valueOf() caching −128..127 (and therefore the == autoboxing trap, → Java index #48), String.intern() and the constant pool, Boolean.valueOf(), Character cache.
  • Interview line: "It's why Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b is true and 128 == 128 is false." That single sentence proves you understand it.
  • Requirement: the shared state must be immutable — otherwise you've built a shared-mutable-state bug across the whole system.
  • Modern caveat: memory is cheap and this pattern adds indirection; justify it with a number.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Flyweight design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

7. Bridge 🟢

  • What varies: two dimensions independently — abstraction and implementation.
  • Shape: Shape (abstraction) holds a Renderer (implementation); adding a shape and adding a renderer are independent, avoiding an M×N class explosion.
  • Use when: you notice a class hierarchy that would need Circle×{SVG, Canvas, GL} combinations.
  • vs Adapter: Bridge is designed up front to keep two axes separate; Adapter is retrofitted to fix an incompatibility after the fact.
  • Trap: easily confused with Strategy structurally. Bridge separates hierarchies; Strategy swaps an algorithm.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Bridge design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The four wrappers, disambiguated

All four wrap an object and delegate. The distinction is intent — memorize this table, it's the most common structural follow-up.

Pattern Interface vs subject Intent Client aware? Stackable
Adapter Different Compatibility Yes — it asked for the target interface No
Facade New, smaller Simplicity Yes — it's a convenience No
Decorator Same Add behavior Yes — it chose the decoration Yes
Proxy Same Control access Usually no Rarely

docs.description: Strategy, observer, state, command, chain: how objects share work.
meta: How responsibility is assigned and how objects communicate.
Parent: README.md · Strategy, Observer, and State carry most of the LLD round — over-invest in those three.
docs.html:
Tier: 🔴 CORE · 🟡 SUPPORTING · 🟢 BREADTH · Flags: trap · comparative · ☕ in-JDK · 🧵 concurrency follow-up likely

1. Strategy 🔴 ☕

The highest-frequency pattern in the entire catalogue. If you learn one thing in this folder, learn this.

  • What varies: the algorithm, chosen at runtime by the client.
  • Shape: an interface with one method, several implementations, injected into the context.
  • Use when: any "make X configurable" follow-up — pricing, elevator scheduling, parking fees, seat allocation, matching, eviction policy, retry policy, chunking, reranking.
  • Kills: the switch (type) inside a business method. This is the specific edit Open/Closed is trying to prevent.
  • ☕ JDK: Comparator is Strategy; so is any functional interface you pass to Stream operations. In modern Java a Strategy is often just a lambda or a Function<T,R> — say this, it shows you're not cargo-culting 1994 Java.
  • Registry pattern: Map<Key, Strategy> populated by DI (Spring injects List<PricingStrategy> and you index them by a getKey()). This is the production form.
  • Cost: class/lambda proliferation; a strategy with one implementation forever is premature abstraction.
  • Interview line: "Adding a new pricing rule should be a new class and a registry entry — never an edit to an existing method."

Picture: Vanderjoe, Strategy design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

2. Observer 🔴 ☕ 🧵

  • What varies: the set of parties reacting to a state change, and when they attach.
  • Shape: Subject maintains listeners, notifies on change; listeners implement a callback interface.
  • Use when: notifications, UI updates, seat-status broadcast, elevator displays, domain events, cache invalidation fan-out.
  • ☕ JDK: PropertyChangeListener, Swing listeners, Flow.Publisher/Subscriber (reactive streams). java.util.Observable is deprecated — don't cite it as your example.
  • Spring: ApplicationEventPublisher + @EventListener; @TransactionalEventListener for after-commit semantics.
  • Traps to volunteer (this is where the points are):
    • Sync vs async dispatch — synchronous notification means a slow listener blocks the publisher.
    • Listener exception isolation — one throwing listener must not abort the rest.
    • Memory leaks — listeners never unregistered keep the subject alive; weak references or explicit lifecycle.
    • 🧵 Concurrent modification — registering during notification; CopyOnWriteArrayList is the standard fix (→ Java index #37).
    • Ordering — no guarantee unless you impose one.
  • Scaling out: Observer in-process becomes pub/sub across processes → 05-distributed-systems.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Observer design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

3. State 🔴

  • What varies: behavior and allowed transitions, driven by internal state.
  • Shape: a State interface with the operations; each concrete state implements them and returns/sets the next state. The context delegates.
  • Use when: elevator (IDLE / MOVING_UP / MOVING_DOWN / DOOR_OPEN / MAINTENANCE), booking (created → held → confirmed → expired), ATM, vending machine, order lifecycle, trip lifecycle, agent run status.
  • Kills: nested if (status == X && ...) chains that grow with every new status.
  • vs Strategy: structurally identical. Strategy is chosen by the client and doesn't change itself; State transitions itself. That one sentence is the whole answer.
  • Trap: don't build a 12-class hierarchy for a 3-state machine. An enum with abstract methods, or a transition table Map<State, Set<State>>, is often the honest answer — and offering the simpler option is a senior signal.
  • Where it pays: invalid transitions become impossible rather than merely unlikely.

Picture: Vanderjoe, State design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

4. Command 🟡 ☕

  • What varies: the request itself — captured as an object with all its parameters.
  • Unlocks: undo/redo (pair each command with its inverse), queueing, scheduling, retry, logging, replay, macro composition.
  • Use when: elevator request queues, job schedulers, editor undo stacks, transactional outbox entries, agent tool-call records.
  • ☕ JDK: Runnable/Callable submitted to an ExecutorService is Command.
  • Interview link: the CQRS "command" and event-sourcing's stored commands are this pattern at system scale (→ ../../../03-hld).

Picture: Vanderjoe, Command design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

5. Template Method 🟡 ☕

  • What varies: individual steps of a fixed algorithm skeleton.
  • Shape: a final method in the base class calling abstract/protected hook methods.
  • Use when: an invariant process with variable parts — parse → validate → transform → persist; or a request-processing lifecycle.
  • ☕ JDK/Spring: AbstractList, InputStream.read(), JdbcTemplate, HttpServlet.service() dispatching to doGet/doPost.
  • vs Strategy: inheritance and compile-time variation vs composition and runtime swap. Prefer Strategy unless the steps genuinely share a lot of base state.
  • Trap: calling an overridable hook from the constructor — the child override runs before child fields are initialized (→ Java index #4). Classic ordering bug.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Template Method design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

6. Chain of Responsibility 🟡 ☕

  • What varies: which handler processes a request, and how many get a chance.
  • Shape: each handler either handles or passes on; the chain is configurable at runtime.
  • Use when: servlet filters, Spring Security filter chain, middleware, validation pipelines, approval workflows, coupon-rule stacking, LLM guardrail passes.
  • ☕ JDK/Spring: javax.servlet.Filter, HandlerInterceptor, logging framework appender chains, OkHttp interceptors.
  • Trap: a request falling off the end of the chain unhandled — always define the terminal behavior. Also: an ordering-sensitive chain with no explicit ordering is a latent bug.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Chain of Responsibility design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

7. Iterator 🟢 ☕

  • What varies: traversal, decoupled from the collection's internal structure.
  • ☕ JDK: Iterator/Iterable — you use it every time you write a for-each loop.
  • Why it's still asked: fail-fast vs fail-safe semantics. modCount and ConcurrentModificationException for ArrayList; weakly-consistent iterators for ConcurrentHashMap and CopyOnWriteArrayList (→ Java index #37). That's the real question hiding behind "explain Iterator."

Picture: Vanderjoe, Iterator design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

8. Mediator 🟡

  • What varies: how a set of peers coordinate — centralized instead of mesh.
  • Use when: N objects each knowing about the others (N² coupling): a chat room, a form where fields enable/disable each other, an air-traffic controller, an elevator dispatcher coordinating several cars.
  • Trap: the mediator becomes a god object. Cap its scope.
  • At system scale: an orchestrator/supervisor agent, or an API gateway aggregating services, is Mediator.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Mediator design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

9. Memento 🟢

  • What varies: how internal state is captured and restored without breaking encapsulation.
  • Use when: undo, checkpointing, snapshotting, savepoints.
  • At system scale: durable workflow checkpoints and agent-run state snapshots (→ ../../../06-ai-systems).

Picture: Vanderjoe, Memento design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

10. Visitor 🟢

  • What varies: operations over a stable object structure, added without modifying the classes.
  • Use when: AST traversal, compilers, report generation over a fixed node hierarchy.
  • The trade-off to state: easy to add operations, painful to add node types (every visitor must change) — the exact inverse of normal polymorphism. This "expression problem" framing is the impressive answer.
  • Modern Java: sealed interfaces + exhaustive pattern-matching switch largely replace Visitor (→ Java index #44). Saying this dates your knowledge correctly.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Visitor design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

11. Interpreter 🟢

  • Rarely useful, occasionally asked. Grammar as a class hierarchy; in practice you reach for a parser generator or an expression library instead. One-pager only.

Picture: Vanderjoe, Interpreter design pattern UML, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

12. Null Object 🟢

  • A do-nothing implementation instead of a null check. Cheap, underused; pairs with avoiding Optional misuse (→ Java index #42).

Fast comparison table

Confusion The distinction
Strategy vs State Client picks the strategy; the state picks its own successor.
Strategy vs Template Method Composition + runtime swap vs inheritance + compile-time hooks.
Observer vs Mediator Observer is one-to-many broadcast; Mediator is many-to-many coordination through a hub.
Chain of Responsibility vs Decorator CoR may stop the request; Decorator always delegates onward and augments.
Command vs Strategy Command captures a request (with args, for later); Strategy captures an algorithm (to run now).
Visitor vs polymorphism Visitor makes adding operations cheap and adding types expensive; ordinary polymorphism is the reverse.

The framing. A pattern applied without a named friction is not neutral — it's a permanent tax on everyone who reads the code afterwards. Over-engineering costs the same as under-engineering; it just bills you later and in a currency (comprehension) that's harder to notice.

The simpler-move ladder

Before any pattern, walk down this ladder and stop at the first rung that solves it. Most problems stop by rung 4.

# Move When it's enough
1 Delete the code The requirement is gone or was never real. Always the best outcome.
2 Rename things The "complexity" is vocabulary confusion. Costs nothing, fixes a surprising amount.
3 Extract a function One long method doing three things. No new types needed.
4 Add a parameter or a config value The variation is data, not algorithm. Enormously common — most "per-tenant behaviour" lives here.
5 Use a Map or an enum A Map<Key, Function<..>> is a Factory and a Strategy without the class count.
6 Use the language feature record, sealed interfaces + pattern-matching switch, lambdas. Modern Java replaces several GoF patterns outright.
7 Use the framework @Cacheable, @Retryable, @Transactional, Spring's filter chain. These are the patterns, already built and tested.
8 Now apply the pattern Only if 1–7 genuinely don't fit.

The rule of three. Duplicate once, duplicate twice, abstract on the third. Abstracting at the first occurrence means guessing which part varies — and you will guess wrong, then be stuck with an abstraction shaped around the wrong axis.

1. Pattern-itis

The smell: six patterns in a parking-lot exercise. A AbstractVehicleFactoryStrategyProvider. Interfaces named after patterns rather than after domain concepts.

Why it happens: patterns are the most legible thing a mid-level engineer can demonstrate, so they get demonstrated. In interviews it reads as a negative signal — it says "I optimise for looking senior" rather than "I optimise for the next person to touch this."

The test: for every pattern in the diff, finish this sentence: "Without this, adding ____ would require editing ____." If you can't, remove it.

The fix: name patterns in the conversation, not necessarily in the code. "This is Strategy" is a useful thing to say in a review; PricingStrategyFactoryImpl is not a useful thing to name a class. Name types after the domain — PricingRule, not PricingStrategy.

2. Singleton as a global variable 🧵

The smell: Config.getInstance().getDatabase().query(...) buried three layers deep. Tests that need Singleton.reset(). A static field holding mutable state.

Why it's bad: three distinct problems, and people usually name only the first.

  • Hidden dependency — the method signature lies. You cannot tell what a class needs by reading its constructor, so you can't substitute anything in a test.
  • Untestable — test order becomes significant, which produces the worst class of flaky test.
  • Concurrency 🧵 — a lazily-initialised singleton without correct publication is a genuine memory-visibility bug. If you're writing double-checked locking by hand, the field needs volatile, and you should probably be using an enum or a holder class instead.

The fix: you almost always want one instance, not the Singleton pattern. Register it as a DI-scoped bean. Same instance count, zero global state, fully substitutable in tests.

The interview line: "Spring gives me singleton scope with constructor injection — I get one instance and a testable seam. The GoF Singleton gives me one instance and a hidden dependency."

3. Anemic domain model

The smell: entities that are pure getters and setters, and a Service class holding every rule. The default failure mode of Spring-trained engineers, and interviewers name it explicitly.

Why it's bad: invariants have no home. Nothing stops order.setStatus(SHIPPED) on a cancelled order, because the rule lives in a service that this caller didn't go through. Business logic scatters across services and duplicates.

The fix: put behaviour next to the data it protects. order.ship() validates and transitions; there is no public setter for status. Services orchestrate across aggregates; they don't own single-entity rules.

The nuance worth stating: an anemic model is genuinely fine for CRUD-shaped code with no invariants. The anti-pattern is anemia where rules exist — not anemia everywhere.

4. Premature abstraction

The smell: an interface with exactly one implementation, named IThing or ThingImpl. A Strategy with one strategy. A Factory that returns the same class every time. A "plugin architecture" with one plugin.

Why it's bad: you paid the full indirection cost and got no flexibility. Worse, the abstraction was shaped around an imagined second case, so when the real second case arrives it doesn't fit — and now you refactor the abstraction and the two implementations.

The ThingImpl tell: if the only name you can think of for the implementation is the interface name plus "Impl", the interface isn't earning its place. A real abstraction has implementations with meaningful, distinct names.

The fix: write the concrete thing. Extract the interface when the second implementation actually exists — the IDE does this in one keystroke, and by then you know which parts genuinely vary.

5. Inheritance for reuse

The smell: class PremiumInternationalExpressOrder extends InternationalExpressOrder extends ExpressOrder extends Order. Or a BaseService that every service extends for shared helpers.

Why it's bad: inheritance couples subclasses to the implementation of the parent, not just its contract. A change in the base breaks siblings in ways the compiler won't catch, and the hierarchy encodes one classification axis — the second requirement axis (premium × international × express) causes combinatorial explosion.

The fix: delegate. Composition survives requirement changes that inheritance doesn't. Order has an OrderType, has a ShippingPolicy. Use inheritance for genuine "is-a" polymorphism, not for code sharing.

The comparison worth knowing: Template Method (inheritance, compile-time) vs Strategy (composition, runtime). Prefer Strategy unless the skeleton itself is what you're freezing.

6. The god facade

The smell: a Facade that started as five delegating methods and now has branching, validation, and its own state. Everything routes through it; nothing can be tested without it.

Why it happens: a facade is the path of least resistance for "where do I put this?" — and it accumulates.

The rule: a facade orchestrates, never decides. The moment it contains a business rule, that rule belongs one layer down. If you can't find the layer down, that's the real finding.

The same failure with other names: god Mediator (every component talks to it, so it knows everything), god Manager/Helper/Util classes (a name with no domain meaning is a name that will attract anything).

7. Observer spaghetti 🧵

The smell: you can't answer "what happens when an order is placed?" by reading code — you have to grep for listeners. Listener order matters for correctness. A listener throws and silently kills the rest of the chain.

The four specific traps (volunteer these in an interview — this is where the points are):

  • Ordering — if B must run after A, you needed a pipeline (CoR) or an orchestrator. Events are for independent reactions.
  • Failure handling — one listener throwing shouldn't roll back the publisher or skip the others. Decide the semantics explicitly and write them down.
  • Memory leaks 🧵 — listeners that never unsubscribe keep publishers alive. The classic long-lived-cache-holds-short-lived-UI leak.
  • Synchronous fan-out — in-process events run on the caller's thread. Six listeners means the endpoint is as slow as the sum. Go async, and then accept the eventual-consistency semantics that come with it.

The fix: use events where reactions are genuinely independent and optional. Use explicit orchestration where order or failure handling matters.

8. Decorator stack depth

The smell: new TelemetryX(new CachingX(new RetryingX(new RateLimitedX(new RealX())))) and nobody can say whether retry wraps cache or cache wraps retry.

Why it matters concretely: the order changes behaviour, not just style. Retry outside cache re-executes the real call on failure; cache outside retry can cache a failure result. Rate-limit inside retry means a retry consumes a token; outside means it doesn't. These are real production incidents, not theory.

The fix: build the stack in exactly one place, document the order and why, and log which layer produced the response. If you need to know which layer you're in during normal operation, you wanted parameters, not layers.

9. Config-driven everything

The smell: a rules engine, a workflow DSL, or a YAML schema that has grown conditionals, loops, and variables — an accidental programming language with no type checker, no debugger, and no tests.

Why it happens: "so non-engineers can change it." They almost never do. The real users are engineers, editing an untyped language through a worse toolchain.

The test: if your config has branching, it's code. Ship it as code.

The fix: keep configuration to values — thresholds, toggles, endpoints, limits. The moment you need if in config, write a class and deploy it. Deployment is fast now; that was the original argument for config-driven logic and it expired.

10. Interface segregation failure (the fat interface)

The smell: a shared interface where several implementations throw UnsupportedOperationException. The lowest-common-denominator vendor interface from the payments example in industry-problem-playbook.md §1.

Why it's bad: the interface now lies. Callers can't rely on it, so they instanceof-check — which defeats the entire point of having the abstraction.

The fix: split the interface, or model capability explicitly (supports(Feature) / a capability object) so callers can branch honestly. An interface every implementation fully satisfies is worth more than a big one nobody does.

Code-review checklist

Run this against any diff that introduces a pattern.

Check Fail means
Can you name the future edit this prevents? Remove it.
Does the abstraction have ≥2 real implementations today? Premature — inline it.
Is any implementation throwing UnsupportedOperation? Fat interface — split it.
Does a type's name end in Impl? The interface isn't earning its place.
Does a test need a static reset()? Global mutable state.
Do entities have rules, or just getters and setters? Anemic model — push behaviour down.
Does the facade branch on business conditions? God facade — push logic down.
Is the decorator order documented, with reasons? Undocumented order is a latent incident.
Does config contain if? It's code — ship it as code.
Is the inheritance chain deeper than 2? Delegate instead.
Did rungs 1–7 of the ladder get tried? Try them.

The interview framing

The strongest thing you can say about a pattern is often that you didn't use it:

"I considered Strategy here, but there's exactly one rule today and no second one on the roadmap, so I used a plain method. If pricing becomes configurable, extracting the interface is a five-minute refactor — and by then I'll know which parts actually vary, instead of guessing now."

That answer demonstrates you know the pattern, know its cost, and can judge timing. Applying it unprompted demonstrates only the first.
