How to use this file. Find the problem that matches what you're building. Each entry gives you the friction sentence (say this in a design review), the pattern stack, the simpler alternative, and the failure mode you're signing up for. These are stacks, not single patterns — real problems need two or three working together.

🅰️ Integration & vendor boundaries

1. Multiple payment providers (Stripe, Razorpay, PayPal)

  • Friction: "Adding a provider means editing PaymentService.charge() and its switch, and Stripe's Charge type is showing up in our order domain."
  • Stack: Adapter 🔴 per provider (keeps vendor types at the edge) + Strategy 🔴 to select at runtime + Factory/registry 🔴 to resolve provider → adapter + Circuit breaker for the outbound call.
  • Shape: PaymentProvider interface in your domain; StripeAdapter implements PaymentProvider; Spring injects List<PaymentProvider>, indexed by getProviderKey().
  • Simpler first: With exactly one provider, one well-named class. Don't build the registry until provider #2 is funded.
  • Fails when: providers aren't actually substitutable — Stripe supports 3DS flows Razorpay doesn't. The common mistake is a lowest-common-denominator interface that throws UnsupportedOperationException. Model capabilities explicitly instead.
  • Related: the Anti-Corruption Layer (DDD) is this pattern at a bounded-context boundary. Say the name at architect level.

2. Notification fan-out (email, SMS, push, Slack, webhook)

  • Friction: "Every new channel means editing the sendNotification method, and marketing wants a sixth."
  • Stack: Strategy 🔴 per channel + Observer / domain events 🔴 for the fan-out + Template Method 🟡 for the shared render→localize→send skeleton + Chain of Responsibility 🟡 if there's a fallback ladder (push → SMS → email).
  • Simpler first: three direct method calls if it's three channels and they never change.
  • Fails when: the fan-out is synchronous. The moment one channel is slow, the order endpoint is slow. Move to a queue — this is where the OO pattern hands off to ../../../05-distributed-systems/communication.md.
  • Trap: Observer with listener-order-dependent correctness. If channel B must run after channel A, you wanted a pipeline, not events.

3. Multi-vendor LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, self-hosted)

  • Friction: "Provider-specific request shapes and streaming formats are leaking into our orchestration layer, and we need to fail over when one provider is down."
  • Stack: Adapter 🔴 per provider + Strategy 🔴 for routing (by cost, capability, latency) + Decorator 🔴 for cross-cutting layers (retry → cache → rate-limit → telemetry) + Chain of Responsibility 🟡 for the fallback ladder + Proxy 🔴 for the semantic cache.
  • Shape: the decorator stack is the real win here — new TelemetryLLM(new CachingLLM(new RetryingLLM(new AnthropicAdapter()))), each layer independently testable.
  • Simpler first: one provider behind one interface. The routing layer is worth building only when you have a real cost or availability driver.
  • Fails when: you assume providers are interchangeable. Prompts are not portable, token accounting differs, and tool-calling schemas differ. The adapter must normalize semantics, not just HTTP.
  • Cross-ref: ../../../06-ai-systems/ for the gateway design; this file covers only the object-level structure.

🅱️ Configuration & varying behaviour

4. Pricing / discount / fee rules

  • Friction: "calculatePrice() is 300 lines of if (customerType == ...) and every quarter adds a rule."
  • Stack: Strategy 🔴 per rule + Registry (Map<RuleKey, PricingRule>) + Chain of Responsibility 🟡 or a composite if rules stack (base → volume discount → loyalty → tax).
  • Simpler first: a Map<CustomerType, Function<Order, Money>> of lambdas. In modern Java a Strategy often is a lambda — say this, it shows you're not cargo-culting 1994.
  • Fails when: rules interact. Independent strategies compose cleanly; "discount A voids discount B" needs an explicit rules engine or an ordered pipeline with a shared accumulator, not N unaware strategies.
  • This is the single highest-frequency Strategy application in industry. If you own one worked example, own this one.

5. Feature flags & A/B experiments

  • Friction: "if (featureXEnabled) is in 40 files and removing a flag is archaeology."
  • Stack: Strategy 🔴 (old impl vs new impl behind one interface) + Proxy 🔴 or Decorator 🔴 to route at the boundary + Factory 🔴 to pick per request.
  • Simpler first: for a genuinely temporary flag, a single if at the highest level — one place, deleted in two weeks.
  • Fails when: flags become permanent. A flag older than one quarter is a fork in your codebase pretending to be config. Put an expiry date on every flag at creation.

6. Multi-tenant behaviour (per-customer rules, branding, limits)

  • Friction: "Tenant-specific ifs are spreading, and enterprise customers want per-tenant workflow variations."
  • Stack: Strategy 🔴 per tenant-configurable axis + Abstract Factory 🟡 when a family must stay consistent (tenant's storage + auth + branding set) + Template Method 🟡 for the fixed workflow skeleton.
  • Simpler first: a tenant configuration object, not code. Most "per-tenant behaviour" is per-tenant data. Only reach for Strategy when the algorithm genuinely differs, not the parameters.
  • Fails when: you write a class per tenant. That's not extensibility, it's a fork per customer. Cap the axes of variation deliberately and say no to the rest.

🅲 Object construction & lifecycle

7. Complex request/config objects (API clients, search queries, reports)

  • Friction: "The constructor has 11 params, 8 optional, and callers pass null, null, null."
  • Stack: Builder 🔴 with validation in build() so an invalid object never exists + immutability (final fields, no setters).
  • Simpler first: a record plus static named factories (SearchQuery.byKeyword(...), SearchQuery.byVector(...)). Named factories often read better than a builder and are less code.
  • Fails when: the builder allows constructing an invalid combination and only fails at use time. Validate the whole object in build(), not field-by-field in setters.
  • ☕ JDK: HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Stream.Builder, Lombok @Builder.

8. Expensive resources (DB connections, HTTP clients, thread pools, model sessions)

  • Friction: "We're creating an HttpClient per request and burning 100ms on handshakes."
  • Stack: Object Pool 🟡 + Singleton 🔴 (as a DI-scoped bean, not a static) + Proxy 🔴 for lazy initialization.
  • Simpler first: use the library's pool. HikariCP, Apache HttpClient's pool, the JDK's HttpClient — hand-rolling a pool is a reliable source of leak bugs.
  • Fails when: pooled objects carry state between borrowers. A pooled connection with an open transaction is a data-corruption bug that reproduces once a month.
  • Trap: Singleton holding mutable state. If your test needs a reset() method, you built a global variable.

🅳 Workflow, pipelines & state

9. Order / booking / application lifecycle

  • Friction: "if (status == PENDING && previousStatus == DRAFT && !cancelled) five levels deep, and invalid transitions ship to prod."
  • Stack: State 🔴 (each state owns its allowed transitions and rejects the rest) + Command 🟡 if transitions must be audited or undone + Observer 🔴 to notify on transition.
  • Simpler first: an enum with a transition table (Map<State, Set<State>>) checked in one place. This handles most lifecycles and is far less code than a class per state.
  • Fails when: transitions are scattered across state classes and nobody can see the whole machine. Keep a diagram in the file, and consider a table-driven machine so the whole thing is visible at once.
  • Interview: this is where Strategy vs State gets asked. State transitions itself; Strategy is chosen by the client.

10. Request processing pipeline (auth → rate limit → validate → handle)

  • Friction: "Every endpoint repeats the same four pre-checks and someone always forgets one."
  • Stack: Chain of Responsibility 🟡 + Decorator 🔴 (in framework terms: filters, interceptors, middleware).
  • Simpler first: an ordered List<Handler> and a for loop — that is CoR without the ceremony. Or use the framework's filter chain rather than inventing one.
  • Fails when: debugging "which link swallowed my request". Log entry/exit per link with a correlation ID from day one, or you'll add it during an incident.
  • ☕ Where you've already used it: Servlet filters, Spring HandlerInterceptor, Spring Security's filter chain.

11. Long-running multi-step business process (onboarding, KYC, fulfilment)

  • Friction: "Step 4 failed and we have no idea what to roll back, and the flow exists nowhere as readable code."
  • Stack: Command 🟡 (each step an object with execute() and compensate()) + Template Method 🟡 or an orchestrator for the skeleton + State 🔴 for the process status.
  • Escalation: once steps span services, this is a Saga — see ../../../05-distributed-systems/data.md. Prefer orchestration over choreography past three steps.
  • Simpler first: a single transaction, if it fits in one database. That's the strongest argument for keeping related data in one service.
  • Fails when: compensation is assumed to be the inverse of the action. "Refund" is not the inverse of "charge" — fees, windows, and partial states all differ. Compensation is business logic, not a mechanical undo.

12. Import / ETL with per-format variation

  • Friction: "CsvImporter, XlsxImporter and JsonImporter share 80% of their code by copy-paste."
  • Stack: Template Method 🟡 for the fixed skeleton (open → parse → validate → map → persist → report) + Strategy 🔴 for the parse step + Factory 🔴 to pick by file type.
  • Simpler first: one importer taking a Parser function. Composition first — reach for Template Method only when the skeleton itself is the thing worth freezing.
  • Fails when: a format needs a different skeleton, not just a different step. Then inheritance fights you and Strategy would have been right. Prefer Strategy when in doubt — composition survives requirement changes that inheritance doesn't.

🅴 Cross-cutting concerns

13. Retry, caching, logging, metrics around a call

  • Friction: "We have CachedRetryingLoggingUserRepository and three siblings, and adding a combination means a new class."
  • Stack: Decorator 🔴 (composable layers, order is explicit) or Proxy 🔴 (transparent, framework-applied).
  • Simpler first: the framework's annotations — @Cacheable, @Retryable, @Transactional. Those are Proxy; Spring generates it. Don't hand-roll what the container gives you.
  • Fails when: the wrapper stack gets deep enough that a stack trace is unreadable and nobody knows whether retry wraps cache or cache wraps retry. Order matters and must be documented — retry-outside-cache re-executes; cache-outside-retry can cache a failure.
  • ☕ JDK: Collections.unmodifiableList (Decorator), BufferedInputStream (Decorator), dynamic proxies (Proxy).

14. Legacy system strangulation

  • Friction: "We're replacing a 200k-line monolith module and can't do it in one release."
  • Stack: Facade 🔴 over the legacy subsystem (carve the seam) + Adapter 🔴 for the new implementation to fit the old contract + Proxy 🔴 / Strategy 🔴 to route a percentage of traffic to the new path.
  • Shape: this is the Strangler Fig pattern at the architectural level; Facade + Proxy are the object-level mechanics that make it possible.
  • Simpler first: nothing. This one genuinely needs the seam.
  • Fails when: the facade accumulates business logic and becomes the new monolith. It should orchestrate, never decide.

15. Undo / audit / event sourcing

  • Friction: "Compliance wants a full record of what each user changed, and product wants undo."
  • Stack: Command 🟡 (request as object, with undo()) + Memento 🟢 for snapshots + Observer 🔴 to publish the audit event.
  • Simpler first: an append-only audit table written in the same transaction as the change. This gives you ~80% of event-sourcing's value for ~5% of the cost — do not adopt event sourcing just for an audit log.
  • Fails when: undo must reverse side effects that already left the system (emails sent, money moved). Undo works cleanly on state, not on effects.

🅵 Domain modelling

16. Tree / hierarchy structures (org charts, categories, file systems, BOMs)

  • Friction: "if (node instanceof Folder) ... else ... in every traversal."
  • Stack: Composite 🟡 (leaf and container share an interface) + Visitor 🟢 if operations keep being added + Iterator 🟢 for traversal.
  • Simpler first: a plain recursive function over a sealed interface. Modern Java's pattern-matching switch over sealed types gives you Visitor's benefit without Visitor's cost.
  • Fails when: leaf-inappropriate operations exist on the shared interface (add(child) on a file). You either throw at runtime or split the interface — both are compromises. Know which one you chose.

17. Reports / exports over a stable model

  • Friction: "Adding a new export format means editing all 12 domain classes."
  • Stack: Visitor 🟢 + Strategy 🔴 for the format.
  • Simpler first: a switch over a sealed interface — same benefit, far less machinery, and the compiler tells you when a case is missing.
  • Fails when: node types change often. Visitor makes adding operations cheap and adding node types expensive. If your model isn't stable, Visitor is the wrong trade.

The three questions before you commit

Borrowed from README.md, because they apply to every row above:

  1. What varies? Name the single axis in one sentence. If you name two, you probably need two patterns — or you've drawn the boundary wrong.

  2. What's the cost? Indirection, class count, harder stack traces, runtime overhead. A pattern with no stated cost means you don't understand it yet.

  3. What's the simpler move? Every row above has one. Try it first. Being able to say "I considered Strategy and used a Map of lambdas instead, because there's no state and no lifecycle" is a stronger signal than using the pattern.

Tier markers: 🔴 CORE (whiteboard-ready) · 🟡 SUPPORTING (concept + trade-offs) · 🟢 BREADTH (one-pager) Flags: trap = where candidates lose the round · comparative = interviewer probes the alternatives · numbers = have the back-of-envelope figures memorized

Part A — The Building Blocks

Section 1 — Framing the Round

  1. The 6-step frame 🔴 — requirements → estimation → API → data model → high-level diagram → deep dive + bottlenecks. Announce it in the first minute; it buys you the interviewer's cooperation.
  2. Functional vs non-functional requirements 🔴 — the NFRs (latency target, availability tier, consistency need, read:write ratio) determine the architecture. Candidates who skip them design a generic CRUD app.
  3. Scope negotiation 🔴 — "I'll design feed generation and skip auth, ads, and moderation — agree?" Cutting scope is a senior signal, not a weakness.
  4. Read-heavy vs write-heavy classification 🔴 — the single most architecture-determining fact. 100:1 read ratio → caching + read replicas + denormalization; write-heavy → LSM store, partitioning, async ingestion.
  5. Latency budget decomposition 🟡 — a 200 ms p99 API budget split across gateway/service/cache/DB/network; forces concrete choices instead of hand-waving.
  6. Driving the round yourself 🟡 — silence is scored as inability. Narrate the decision and the alternative you rejected.

Section 2 — Estimation & Numbers

  1. Back-of-envelope method 🔴 — DAU → requests/user/day → QPS → peak QPS (×2–3) → storage/day → storage/5yr → bandwidth. Round aggressively; precision is not the point.
  2. Latency numbers every engineer should know 🔴 — L1 ~1 ns, memory ~100 ns, SSD random read ~100 µs, network round-trip within DC ~0.5 ms, cross-continent ~150 ms, disk seek ~10 ms. Used to justify cache tiers.
  3. Capacity constants 🟡 — a single commodity box: ~10–50 K QPS for a cache, ~1–5 K QPS for an RDBMS with indexes, ~10 K writes/s per Kafka partition, ~1 TB usable per node before ops pain.
  4. Storage sizing 🟡 — bytes/record × records/day × retention × replication factor (×3) × index overhead (~1.3). The number determines shard count.
  5. The availability ladder 🟡 — 99.9% = 43 min/month, 99.99% = 4.3 min/month, 99.999% = 26 s/month. Ties directly to how much redundancy you can justify.

Section 3 — Networking & Entry Layer

  1. DNS, anycast & GSLB 🟢 — how a request reaches the nearest region; TTL as the failover lever.
  2. Load balancing 🔴 — L4 vs L7, round-robin / least-connections / consistent-hash; health checks, connection draining, and why sticky sessions are a design smell.
  3. API gateway responsibilities 🔴 — authn/z, rate limiting, request routing, aggregation, protocol translation; the difference between a gateway and a service mesh sidecar.
  4. CDN & edge caching 🔴 — static assets, cache-control/ETag, origin shield, cache invalidation strategy; the answer to most read-heavy media problems.
  5. Protocol choice 🟡 — REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL vs WebSocket vs SSE vs long-polling; know which real-time transport you'd pick for chat (WebSocket) vs notifications (SSE/push).
  6. Backpressure & load shedding 🔴 — bounded queues, 429/503 with Retry-After, admission control; a system with no shedding plan fails the reliability follow-up.
  7. Idempotency at the API layer 🔴 — idempotency keys on POST, exactly-once effects over at-least-once delivery. Comes up in every payments/booking question.

Section 4 — Data Storage

  1. SQL vs NoSQL decision framework 🔴 — driven by access pattern + consistency need + scale, never by preference. Be able to defend Postgres at 10 K QPS instead of reflexively reaching for a NoSQL store.
  2. The NoSQL families 🔴 — key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), wide-column (Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable), document (MongoDB), graph (Neo4j), time-series (Timescale, InfluxDB), search (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch). One canonical use case each.
  3. B-tree vs LSM-tree 🔴 — read-optimized in-place update vs write-optimized append + compaction; explains why Cassandra/RocksDB win on writes and pay in read amplification and compaction stalls.
  4. Indexing 🔴 — primary/secondary, composite index column order, covering indexes, why an index costs writes; global vs local secondary indexes in a partitioned store.
  5. Normalization vs denormalization 🔴 — denormalize for read-heavy at scale; the price is fan-out writes and eventual inconsistency you must name.
  6. Partitioning / sharding 🔴 — range vs hash vs directory-based; the hot-shard / celebrity problem and its mitigations (salting, dedicated shard, request coalescing).
  7. Consistent hashing & virtual nodes 🔴 — how you add/remove nodes without a full reshuffle; the standard follow-up on any cache or partitioned store.
  8. Replication 🔴 — leader-follower, multi-leader, leaderless (quorum, R+W>N); replication lag and read-your-own-writes as the user-visible symptom.
  9. Resharding / rebalancing 🟡 — the operationally hardest thing in the design; double-write + backfill + cutover is the standard playbook.
  10. Transactions & isolation levels 🔴 — read-committed vs repeatable-read vs snapshot vs serializable; lost update, write skew, phantom reads.
  11. Distributed transactions 🔴 — 2PC and its coordinator-blocking failure, Saga with compensating transactions, TCC. Saga is the expected answer in microservice designs.
  12. Outbox pattern & CDC 🔴 — the only correct way to atomically update the DB and publish an event; Debezium as the concrete tool. Extremely high signal.
  13. Object/blob storage 🟡 — S3-class store for media with a metadata DB pointer; presigned URLs for direct upload/download (never proxy bytes through your service).
  14. Data lake / warehouse split 🟢 — OLTP vs OLAP separation, columnar formats (Parquet), why analytics never runs on the production DB.

Section 5 — Caching

  1. Cache topologies 🔴 — client → CDN → API-gateway → application (local/Caffeine) → distributed (Redis/Memcached) → DB buffer pool. Name the layer you mean.
  2. Cache patterns 🔴 — cache-aside (default), read-through, write-through, write-behind, refresh-ahead; know the consistency and durability cost of each.
  3. Invalidation strategies 🔴 — TTL, explicit invalidation on write, versioned keys. "Cache invalidation is hard" is not an answer; pick one and state the staleness window.
  4. Stampede / thundering herd 🔴 — many misses on one hot key at expiry; mitigations: request coalescing (single-flight), probabilistic early expiry, stale-while-revalidate, lock-on-miss.
  5. Hot key & large key problems 🟡 — one key exceeding a node's capacity; local-cache fronting, key splitting, replication of the hot key.
  6. Eviction policies 🟡 — LRU / LFU / FIFO / ARC / TTL-only; ties to LLD #56.
  7. Redis beyond get/set 🟡 — sorted sets for leaderboards and rate limiting, streams, pub/sub, Lua for atomic multi-op, cluster mode and its multi-key limits.
  8. Bloom filters & sketches 🟡 — negative-lookup avoidance, HyperLogLog for cardinality, count-min sketch for heavy hitters; cheap way to look experienced. (Note written 24 Oct 2026: sizing math, Python run, overfill Break it.)

Section 6 — Messaging & Async

  1. Queue vs log 🔴 — SQS/RabbitMQ (delete-on-ack, per-message) vs Kafka/Pulsar (append-only log, offsets, replay). Picking wrong here undermines the whole design.
  2. Kafka architecture 🔴 — topics/partitions/offsets, partition key → ordering guarantee, consumer groups, ISR and acks=all, retention vs compaction. See the Failure-Modes index for the operational half.
  3. Delivery semantics 🔴 — at-most-once / at-least-once / effectively-once; there is no free exactly-once across a network — you get idempotent consumers or transactional producers.
  4. Ordering guarantees 🔴 — per-partition only; ordering requires a partition key, which creates the hot-partition trade-off (→ #24).
  5. Consumer lag & scaling 🔴 — lag as the primary health metric; consumers ≤ partitions, rebalance storms, why over-partitioning is the cheap insurance.
  6. DLQ, retry topics & poison messages 🔴 — bounded retries with backoff into a retry topic, then DLQ with replay tooling; unbounded in-place retry blocks the partition.
  7. Event-driven architecture patterns 🟡 — event notification vs event-carried state transfer vs event sourcing; CQRS and when the read-model complexity is worth it.
  8. Stream processing 🟡 — windowing (tumbling/sliding/session), watermarks, late data, stateful operators; Flink / Kafka Streams / Spark Structured Streaming as the concrete options.
  9. Change data capture 🟡 — DB log tailing as an event source; the twin of #30.
  10. Batch vs streaming vs micro-batch 🟢 — lambda vs kappa architecture; the honest answer is usually "streaming for freshness, batch for correctness/reprocessing."

Section 7 — Consistency, Coordination & Correctness

  1. CAP and its correct statement 🔴 — the choice only applies during a partition; "we chose AP" without naming the partition scenario is the classic shallow answer. Prefer PACELC (else: latency vs consistency).
  2. Consistency models 🔴 — strong / linearizable, sequential, causal, read-your-writes, monotonic reads, eventual. Map each to a user-visible symptom.
  3. Quorum arithmetic 🟡 — R + W > N for overlap; tunable consistency in Cassandra/Dynamo.
  4. Consensus 🟡 — Raft/Paxos at the level of leader election + replicated log; you should know what you'd use it for (metadata, leader election, config) not how to implement it.
  5. Distributed locks & leases 🔴 — Redlock's contested safety, fencing tokens as the correct fix, ZooKeeper/etcd ephemeral nodes; a lock without a fencing token is unsafe under GC pause.
  6. Clocks & ordering 🟡 — clock skew, NTP limits, logical clocks (Lamport), vector clocks, hybrid logical clocks, TrueTime; why "just use timestamps" breaks.
  7. Conflict resolution 🟡 — last-write-wins and what it silently loses, CRDTs, application-level merge; relevant to any multi-region write design.
  8. Uniqueness & ID generation 🔴 — UUIDv4 vs UUIDv7 vs Snowflake vs DB sequence vs ticket server; monotonicity and index-locality trade-offs. Frequent standalone question.
  9. Multi-region / geo-distribution 🟡 — active-passive vs active-active, data residency, cross-region replication lag, conflict handling, failover runbook.
  10. Idempotency & dedupe at scale 🔴 — dedupe key store with TTL, Bloom filter pre-check, exactly-once effects. Recurs in payments, notifications, and ingestion.

Section 8 — Reliability & Operations

  1. Availability patterns 🔴 — redundancy, failover, health checks, graceful degradation, static fallback; know active-active vs active-passive cost.
  2. Resilience patterns 🔴 — timeouts (always), retries with jitter and budget, circuit breakers, bulkheads, fallbacks (→ Java index #59).
  3. Retry storms & metastable failure 🔴 — naive retries amplify load and turn a blip into an outage; retry budgets and exponential backoff with full jitter are the fix. Very high senior signal.
  4. Cascading failure & isolation 🔴 — thread-pool/connection-pool exhaustion propagating across services; bulkheads and per-dependency pools.
  5. Observability three pillars + one 🔴 — metrics (RED/USE), structured logs, distributed traces, and SLO/error budget as the decision framework. Name the specific dashboard you'd open.
  6. Health checks & readiness 🟡 — liveness vs readiness vs startup; the deep-health-check cascade anti-pattern.
  7. Deployment safety 🟡 — blue-green, canary, feature flags, expand/contract DB migrations, rollback triggers.
  8. Capacity planning & autoscaling 🟡 — scale on the right signal (queue depth/lag, not CPU), warm-up time, scaling floor for spiky traffic.
  9. Chaos & failure testing 🟢 — game days, fault injection; a credible senior-level mention.
  10. Cost as a design constraint 🟡 — $/request, storage tiering, egress cost, the cost of ×3 replication; architects are expected to raise this unprompted.

Section 9 — Security & Governance

  1. AuthN vs AuthZ 🟡 — OAuth2/OIDC flows, JWT vs opaque tokens, refresh/rotation, token revocation as the JWT weak spot.
  2. Service-to-service trust 🟡 — mTLS, workload identity, short-lived credentials, secret management.
  3. Multi-tenancy isolation 🟡 — shared vs siloed data, per-tenant rate limiting and noisy-neighbor control, row-level security.
  4. PII, encryption & compliance 🟡 — at-rest/in-transit, envelope encryption + KMS, tokenization, GDPR delete/right-to-erasure and how it conflicts with append-only logs and backups.
  5. Audit logging & lineage 🟢 — immutable audit trail; increasingly asked in fintech/health and AI-governance contexts.

Part B — The Canonical Problems

Each entry: the discriminating decision the round is really testing.

Section 10 — Read-Heavy / Feed & Content

  1. URL shortener 🔴 — ID generation (#58), read-heavy caching, custom aliases, analytics pipeline. The standard warm-up; the real test is estimation discipline.
  2. Pastebin / file-sharing 🟢 — blob store + metadata DB + presigned URLs + expiry.
  3. Twitter/X timeline 🔴 — fan-out on write vs fan-out on read, and the hybrid for celebrities. The single most-asked HLD trade-off; know the hybrid answer, not just the two extremes.
  4. Instagram / news feed ranking 🔴 — #78 plus media pipeline (upload → transcode → CDN) and a ranking service; bridges naturally into the RAG/ML index.
  5. YouTube / Netflix video 🔴 — upload → chunked transcode (adaptive bitrate) → CDN; the "how do you serve 4K to 100M users" question is a CDN + pre-positioning answer.
  6. Search / typeahead 🔴 — inverted index, sharding by term vs document, trie + top-K for autocomplete, ranking layer, index freshness lag.
  7. Web crawler 🟡 — frontier queue, politeness/robots, dedupe (Bloom + content hash), distributed scheduling, trap detection.
  8. Google Docs / collaborative editor 🟡 — OT vs CRDT, WebSocket session layer, presence, persistence and snapshotting.

Section 11 — Write-Heavy / Real-Time

  1. WhatsApp / chat system 🔴 — connection layer (WebSocket + gateway with session registry), message store (per-conversation partitioning), delivery receipts, offline queue, group fan-out, ordering per conversation.
  2. Notification system 🔴 — multi-channel fan-out, template service, user preferences, per-user rate limiting, provider failover, dedupe (#60). Very common at product companies.
  3. Rate limiter (distributed) 🔴 — Redis + Lua sliding window, local token bucket with periodic sync, the accuracy-vs-latency trade-off; the distributed twin of LLD #57.
  4. Uber / ride-matching 🔴 — geospatial index (geohash/S2/quadtree), driver-location ingestion at high write rate, matching service, trip state machine, surge pricing. Location updates are the write-scale problem.
  5. Live streaming 🟡 — ingest → transcode ladder → HLS/DASH segments → CDN; latency vs quality trade-off, and why low-latency streaming (LL-HLS/WebRTC) costs more.
  6. Metrics/monitoring system 🟡 — high-cardinality time-series ingestion, downsampling/rollups, retention tiers, push vs pull (Prometheus) trade-off.
  7. Log aggregation & analytics 🟡 — agent → Kafka → stream processor → hot (ES/OpenSearch) and cold (object store) tiers; the archetypal Kafka pipeline.
  8. Distributed job scheduler / cron 🟡 — leader election, at-least-once execution + idempotency, time-wheel or DB-backed queue, missed-window handling.

Section 12 — Transactional & Money

  1. Payment system 🔴 — idempotency keys, ledger with double-entry, saga across authorize/capture/settle, reconciliation job, the unknown-outcome gateway timeout (→ Failure-Modes index). Never say "eventual consistency" about money without naming reconciliation.
  2. Ticket booking (BookMyShow at scale) 🔴 — the distributed version of LLD #49: seat-hold in Redis with TTL, DB unique constraint as the source of truth, queue/waiting-room for flash sales, inventory partitioning per show.
  3. E-commerce / Amazon 🔴 — catalog (search + read replicas), inventory reservation, cart, order saga, payment, fulfillment; flash-sale hot-key handling is the standard curveball.
  4. Food delivery / Swiggy at scale 🟡 — #87 plus restaurant capacity and multi-party state; ETA prediction is the ML hook.
  5. Ad serving / bidding 🟡 — sub-100 ms budget for the whole auction, candidate retrieval → ranking → pacing/budget enforcement, click/impression event pipeline with dedupe.
  6. Stock exchange / order matching 🟢 — single-threaded matching engine per symbol, sequencer, deterministic replay for recovery; a good place to demonstrate that not everything should be distributed.

Section 13 — Storage & Platform Systems

  1. Dropbox / file sync 🟡 — chunking + content-addressed dedupe, delta sync, metadata service, conflict resolution across devices.
  2. Distributed cache 🟡 — consistent hashing (#25), replication, eviction, hot-key handling; often the follow-up to any read-heavy design.
  3. S3-like object store 🟢 — metadata service + placement + erasure coding vs replication, durability math.
  4. Key-value store (Dynamo-style) 🟡 — consistent hashing + quorum + vector clocks + hinted handoff + Merkle-tree anti-entropy; the classic "design a database" question.
  5. Feature store / ML platform 🟡 — offline (training) and online (serving) stores, point-in-time correctness and training-serving skew, materialization pipeline. The clearest bridge from HLD into AI-architect rounds → RAG index.

The four dimensions HLD interviewers score

  • 1 — Requirements & estimation discipline: did the NFRs and numbers actually drive the design (→ Sections 1–2)?
  • 2 — Correct primitive selection: right storage engine, right messaging semantics, right consistency model (→ Sections 4–7).
  • 3 — Failure thinking: what breaks, how it's detected, how it degrades, how it recovers (→ Section 8, and the Failure-Modes index).
  • 4 — Trade-off articulation: every choice paired with the alternative rejected and the cost accepted. This is the only dimension that separates Staff from Senior.

Cross-reference ownership map

  • Fan-out on write vs read (#78) recurs in feeds, notifications (#85), and chat groups (#84).
  • Hot key / hot partition (#24, #37, #44) is the same problem in the shard, the cache, and the Kafka topic — one mental model.
  • Idempotency (#18, #43, #60) is the spine of payments (#92), booking (#93), and any at-least-once pipeline.
  • Outbox/CDC (#30, #49) is the answer whenever a design writes to a DB and a queue in the same operation.
  • Retry storms (#63) connects resilience patterns, backpressure (#17), and every incident question.
  • LLD counterparts: rate limiter, LRU cache, URL shortener, and ticket booking all have an in-process version in the LLD index — know which round you're in.
  • Java runtime specifics (GC pauses causing p99 spikes, thread-pool sizing, connection pools) live in the Java index (#17–#20, #28, #57) — a JVM-backed answer to a latency question is a differentiator.

Suggested study order

  1. Sections 1–2 — the frame and the numbers; without these every answer sounds junior.
  2. Sections 4–5 (storage + caching) — the majority of design surface area.
  3. Section 6 (messaging) — Kafka semantics specifically; it appears in nearly every modern design.
  4. Section 7 (consistency) — CAP stated correctly, saga, idempotency, ID generation.
  5. #78 Twitter feed + #84 chat + #92 payments — implement the diagrams end-to-end; they cover read-heavy, real-time, and transactional archetypes.
  6. Section 8 (reliability) — then revisit all three designs and add the failure story.
  7. Sections 10–13 remainder — one pass each; they recombine the archetypes.
  8. Section 9 (security) — last, unless the role is fintech/health/platform.

How to read this note. The 28 concepts follow one request's lifecycle: it leaves a client, gets routed, gets served, hits storage, and then the system has to stay consistent and alive while doing it a million more times. Each concept is written as:

  • 💥 The failure it prevents — the concrete production symptom you see when it is missing.

  • Mechanism — how it actually works, one level below the buzzword.

  • 💸 The trade-off — what it costs. If you cannot name this, you do not understand the concept.

  • Numbers to quote — the figures to have on your tongue in an interview.

  • When NOT to use it — the misapplication that makes you look junior.

  • One-liner — the verbal-delivery compression.

Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What does a load balancer NOT protect you from? Correlated failure — bad deploy, poisoned cache, shared DB saturation. It spreads load, not blast radius.
Why is cache invalidation the hard part? Two writers of truth. Any TTL > 0 is a deliberate staleness budget you must name and defend.
CAP in one sentence? On a network partition you choose availability or linearizability. You never "choose CP over CA" — CA is not on the menu.
Cost of adding a secondary index? Reads get faster, every write gets slower and the table gets bigger. Indexes are a write tax paid for read speed.
Retries without which two things are an outage amplifier? Exponential backoff with jitter, and a circuit breaker. Naive retries turn a blip into a retry storm.
What breaks first when you shard? Cross-shard queries, joins, and transactions. Your shard key freezes your access patterns.
Rough latency ladder? Memory ~100ns, SSD ~100µs, same-DC RTT ~0.5ms, cross-continent RTT ~150ms. Each step is ~1000×.
Why is statelessness the precondition for horizontal scaling? If any server holds unique state, you cannot add, kill, or replace instances freely.

If you cannot answer six of these cold, read the note top to bottom before touching any HLD design.

Part I — Sending the Request

Everything in this part happens before your code runs. It is also where the cheapest wins live: a request served at the edge costs you nothing in origin capacity.

1. Client–Server Model

💥 The failure it prevents. Teams that never make the client/server boundary explicit end up enforcing rules on the client — price calculation in JavaScript, "admin" flags in a cookie, validation only in the mobile app. The failure is a user with curl bypassing all of it. The second failure mode is a fat client that makes 40 sequential calls to render one screen, so every 50ms of network latency multiplies into a 2-second page.

Mechanism. The client initiates, the server owns state and authority. The boundary is a trust boundary: anything on the client side is attacker-controlled input, full stop. The server's contract is the only enforcement point. This also defines who owns retry, timeout, and caching semantics — usually the client for retries, the server for state.

💸 The trade-off. Centralising authority on the server means the server is now a scalability and availability bottleneck for every decision. Thin clients are secure but latency-sensitive and useless offline; thick clients are fast and offline-capable but must be treated as untrusted and require conflict resolution when they sync.

Numbers to quote. A page that needs 40 sequential round trips at 50ms RTT is 2s of pure network. Reducing to 4 batched calls gets you to 200ms. The single highest-leverage frontend performance fix is almost always fewer round trips, not faster code.

When NOT to use it. Peer-to-peer and CRDT-based collaborative systems (Figma-style multiplayer, local-first apps) deliberately break the model — the "server" becomes a relay and merge referee, not the authority. Also, edge compute blurs the boundary: code runs on infrastructure you control, physically near the client.

One-liner. "The client is a rendering surface and an untrusted input source. Every rule that matters is enforced server-side, and my first design question is which round trips I can eliminate."

2. IP Addressing, DNS & Anycast

💥 The failure it prevents. A region goes down and traffic keeps flowing to dead IPs for the full TTL — 300 seconds of a total outage you cannot shorten because clients cached the record. Or worse: you hard-coded an IP somewhere, and now failover requires a deploy. DNS is the layer that turns "our infrastructure moved" into "nobody noticed."

Mechanism. DNS resolves a name to an address through a recursive walk: resolver → root → TLD → authoritative nameserver. Each answer carries a TTL that every layer caches. Beyond plain A records, DNS is your first routing tier:

  • Weighted round-robin — split traffic across regions or shift 5% to a canary.

  • Latency-based / geo routing — send the user to the nearest healthy region.

  • Health-checked failover — pull a region out of rotation automatically.

  • Anycast — one IP advertised via BGP from many PoPs; the network itself routes the packet to the topologically nearest one. This is how CDNs and public resolvers (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8) work, and it gives failover in seconds at the routing layer rather than TTL-bound minutes.

💸 The trade-off. Low TTL = fast failover but far more DNS queries and dependence on resolver behaviour. High TTL = cheap and resilient but slow to change. Worse, TTL is advisory: some resolvers, OSes, and JVMs cache far longer than you asked. Anycast avoids the TTL problem entirely but requires BGP-capable infrastructure and makes stateful TCP sessions fragile if routes flap.

Numbers to quote. Typical production TTL: 30–60s for records you may need to fail over, 3600s+ for stable ones. Cold DNS resolution adds 20–120ms to a first request. Java's networkaddress.cache.ttl historically defaulted to caching forever with a security manager — a classic failover bug.

When NOT to use it. DNS is a poor load balancer for fine-grained decisions — it has no visibility into per-server load or request cost, and caching means your weights are approximate. Use it for coarse geographic and regional routing; use L4/L7 balancers for anything precise.

One-liner. "DNS is my coarsest routing tier. I keep TTLs low on anything I might need to fail over, and I assume some clients will ignore the TTL anyway — so real failover happens at anycast or the load balancer, not DNS alone."

3. HTTP/HTTPS & Connection Reuse

💥 The failure it prevents. Without TLS: credentials and session tokens readable by anyone on the path, and content injectable by any intermediary. Without connection reuse: every request pays a TCP handshake (1 RTT) plus TLS handshake (1–2 RTT), so a 20ms API call becomes 100ms of handshake plus 20ms of work. Under load this shows up as CPU burn on TLS setup and port exhaustion on the client.

Mechanism. HTTP is a stateless request/response protocol over TCP (or QUIC/UDP for HTTP/3). The pieces that matter architecturally:

  • Keep-alive / connection pooling — amortise handshakes across many requests. Always size and reuse pools; never create a new HTTP client per request.

  • HTTP/2 multiplexing — many concurrent streams over one connection, eliminating head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer (though not at TCP). HTTP/3 over QUIC removes the TCP-level HOL blocking too.

  • TLS termination — usually at the load balancer or CDN, so backend hops are cheaper. Session resumption and TLS 1.3's 1-RTT (or 0-RTT) handshake cut setup cost further.

  • Cache-control semantics — Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified. These are what make CDN and browser caching correct rather than a guess.

  • Status codes as a contract — 4xx means "don't retry as-is", 5xx and 429 mean "retry with backoff". Getting this wrong makes every downstream client misbehave.

💸 The trade-off. TLS costs CPU and a handshake; termination at the edge means the internal hop is plaintext unless you also run mTLS internally (which costs operational complexity in certificate rotation). HTTP/2's single connection means one lost packet stalls all streams on that connection at the TCP layer — on lossy mobile networks HTTP/1.1 with multiple connections sometimes wins.

Numbers to quote. TCP handshake = 1 RTT. TLS 1.3 = 1 additional RTT (0 on resumption); TLS 1.2 = 2. At 50ms RTT that is 100–150ms per fresh connection. Connection reuse is typically the single largest latency win in a chatty service-to-service mesh.

When NOT to use it. HTTP is a poor fit for low-latency bidirectional streams (use WebSocket or gRPC streaming) and for high-throughput internal RPC where binary framing and no header overhead matter (use gRPC).

One-liner. "TLS everywhere, terminated at the edge, mTLS internally if the threat model demands it — and connection pooling on every client, because handshakes are usually a bigger share of my latency budget than my actual work."

4. API Styles — REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket

💥 The failure it prevents. The wrong API style produces one of three recognisable pathologies: over-fetching (mobile downloads a 40-field object to show two fields, burning battery and data), chattiness (N+1 round trips to build one screen), or polling storms (10k clients polling every 2s for a notification that arrives once an hour — 300k wasted requests per event).

Mechanism. Four styles, four fits:

  • REST/JSON — resource-oriented, cache-friendly (leans on HTTP semantics), universally supported. Default for public APIs. Weakness: the server fixes the response shape, so clients over- or under-fetch.

  • GraphQL — client specifies the shape; one round trip for a composite screen. Weakness: HTTP caching mostly stops working (everything is a POST to one endpoint), and an unbounded query is a self-inflicted DoS. Requires query depth/complexity limits and persisted queries, plus DataLoader-style batching to avoid N+1 at the resolver layer.

  • gRPC / Protobuf — binary, schema-first, code-generated, HTTP/2 streaming. Default for internal service-to-service: 3–10× smaller payloads and strong contract evolution. Weakness: not natively browser-callable (needs grpc-web/a proxy), harder to debug by eye, and schema management becomes a real workflow.

  • WebSocket / SSE — server-initiated push. WebSocket is bidirectional and stateful; SSE is unidirectional, simpler, and rides plain HTTP. Weakness: both hold long-lived connections, which reintroduces state to your "stateless" tier and caps instances by file-descriptor and memory limits.

💸 The trade-off. Each style trades flexibility against cacheability and predictability. REST is the most cacheable and least flexible. GraphQL is the most flexible and least cacheable. gRPC is the fastest and least accessible. Push protocols are the most responsive and the most stateful.

Numbers to quote. Protobuf payloads are typically 3–10× smaller than equivalent JSON and considerably cheaper to parse. A single server can hold roughly 10k–100k idle WebSocket connections depending on per-connection memory; plan ~10–50KB per connection and size accordingly.

When NOT to use it. Do not put GraphQL in front of a system whose main win was CDN caching — you just deleted it. Do not use WebSocket where SSE or long-polling suffices; bidirectional state is expensive to operate. Do not use gRPC for a public partner API unless you enjoy support tickets.

One-liner. "REST at the edge for cacheability and reach, gRPC internally for efficiency and contracts, SSE or WebSocket only when the server genuinely needs to initiate — and GraphQL only when composite client-driven reads are the actual bottleneck, with complexity limits from day one."

5. CDN & Edge Caching

💥 The failure it prevents. Origin meltdown. A product launch, a viral post, or a marketing email drops and 500k people request the same 2MB hero image from your origin in ten minutes. Without a CDN your origin bandwidth and connection count are the constraint, and static assets take down dynamic requests sharing the same servers. The second failure is the latency floor: a user in Sydney hitting an origin in Virginia pays ~200ms RTT on every asset, and no amount of backend optimisation fixes physics.

Mechanism. Geographically distributed PoPs cache origin responses close to users, usually reached via anycast. Key mechanics:

  • Cache key — URL plus whatever you vary on (Vary header, cookies, device class). Every extra dimension multiplies cache entries and lowers hit rate.

  • TTL and revalidation — Cache-Control: max-age for freshness, stale-while-revalidate to serve slightly-stale content while refreshing in the background, ETag for cheap 304s.

  • Cache-busting via content hash — app.9f3c2a.js with a one-year TTL is strictly better than a short TTL on app.js. Immutable URLs make invalidation a non-problem.

  • Origin shield — a mid-tier cache so that N PoP misses collapse into one origin request instead of N.

  • Edge compute — run auth checks, A/B assignment, or personalisation at the PoP so dynamic content stays cacheable.

💸 The trade-off. You have introduced a second copy of the truth that you do not control the eviction of. Purges are eventually consistent and can take seconds to minutes globally. Any bug in cache-key configuration is a security bug — caching a personalised response under a shared key serves user A's data to user B, which is one of the most common serious CDN incidents.

Numbers to quote. A healthy static-asset hit rate is 90–99%; that means the origin sees 1–10% of traffic. Cross-continent RTT is 100–200ms versus 5–20ms to a nearby PoP. CDN egress is typically cheaper than cloud egress, so a CDN often reduces bill as well as latency.

When NOT to use it. Highly personalised, low-reuse responses (a user's dashboard) gain nothing — the hit rate is zero and you have added a hop. Strictly-real-time data (live prices, seat availability) either bypasses the CDN or uses very short TTLs with explicit staleness communicated to the user.

One-liner. "CDN for anything with reuse — static assets, public API reads, media. Content-hashed immutable URLs so I never fight invalidation, an origin shield so a global purge does not stampede my origin, and a paranoid review of the cache key because cache-key bugs are data-leak bugs."

Part II — Routing the Request

6. Load Balancing

💥 The failure it prevents. One instance dies at 3am and the product is down. Or one instance is fine but saturated while three others idle, because traffic was pinned by DNS. A load balancer is the component that makes "a server" plural and therefore makes single-instance failure a non-event.

Mechanism. A balancer sits in front of a pool, runs health checks, and distributes requests. The dimensions that matter:

  • Layer 4 (transport) — routes by IP/port, cannot see the request. Extremely fast, connection-level, no TLS termination needed. Good for raw throughput and non-HTTP protocols.

  • Layer 7 (application) — parses HTTP, so it can route by path or header, terminate TLS, retry idempotent requests, and inject headers. This is where path-based microservice routing and canary splits live.

  • Algorithms — round robin (naive, assumes equal request cost), least connections (much better when request cost varies), least response time, weighted (for heterogeneous instance sizes), consistent hashing (for cache affinity — see concept 13). Power-of-two-choices is the pragmatic default in modern proxies: sample two backends, pick the less loaded.

  • Health checks — shallow (is the port open) versus deep (can it reach its DB). Deep checks are more accurate but can cascade: if the shared DB blips, every instance fails its check simultaneously and the balancer removes the entire pool. Guard with a minimum-healthy-hosts floor (a.k.a. panic threshold).

💸 The trade-off. The balancer itself becomes a critical component, so it needs redundancy (usually anycast VIPs or an active-active pair). L7 gives you power at the cost of latency and CPU. Least-connections needs shared state or per-balancer approximation. And the balancer spreads load, not blast radius — it does nothing against a bad deploy or poisoned shared cache, which is what deployment strategies and cells are for.

Numbers to quote. Health check interval 5–10s with 2–3 consecutive failures before ejection: 10–30s to notice a dead node. That window is your failover budget. A modern L7 proxy adds roughly 1–5ms of latency.

When NOT to use it. For internal service-to-service traffic, a client-side balancer or service mesh sidecar often beats a central one — it removes a hop and a shared failure domain. And a balancer cannot fix an undersized backend: if the pool is at capacity, it just distributes the pain evenly.

One-liner. "L4 for throughput, L7 where I need routing and retries. Least-connections over round-robin because request cost is never uniform, deep health checks with a healthy-host floor so a DB blip cannot eject the whole fleet — and I remember a balancer spreads load, not correlated failure."

7. Forward Proxy vs Reverse Proxy

💥 The failure it prevents. Without a reverse proxy, every service independently implements TLS, compression, request logging, header sanitisation, and connection buffering — inconsistently. Backends are directly exposed to slow clients, so a slowloris-style trickle ties up application threads that should be serving real work.

Mechanism. The direction of the arrow is the whole distinction:

  • Forward proxy — sits in front of clients, on their behalf. Corporate egress filtering, outbound IP allowlisting, caching for a fleet of internal machines, and the standard way to give services a stable outbound IP for partner allowlists.

  • Reverse proxy — sits in front of servers, on their behalf. Clients think they are talking to the proxy. Responsibilities: TLS termination, request buffering (absorb slow clients so backends see fast complete requests), compression, static file serving, header normalisation and X-Forwarded-For handling, path-based routing, and WAF integration.

Every L7 load balancer is a reverse proxy; not every reverse proxy balances load. Nginx, Envoy, HAProxy, and Traefik all occupy this space.

Pictures: H2g2bob, Forward proxy and Reverse proxy, Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

💸 The trade-off. Another hop, another config surface, another thing that can be misconfigured in a security-relevant way — header spoofing via unsanitised X-Forwarded-For, request smuggling from proxy/backend parsing disagreements, or accidentally caching authenticated responses. Buffering also adds latency for streaming responses unless explicitly disabled.

Numbers to quote. Request buffering means a backend worker is held for the service time rather than the client time — with slow mobile clients that can be the difference between a 20ms and a 2000ms thread occupancy, i.e. a 100× effective capacity change on a thread-per-request server.

When NOT to use it. Do not proxy long-lived streaming responses through a buffering proxy without turning buffering off. And for a single small service with TLS handled by the cloud LB, a separate reverse proxy is a hop with no payoff.

One-liner. "Forward proxy protects the network from the clients; reverse proxy protects the servers from the clients. I put TLS, buffering, compression and header hygiene in the reverse proxy so no service has to reimplement them."

8. API Gateway

💥 The failure it prevents. In a 30-service estate without a gateway, every service ships its own authentication, its own rate limiter, its own logging format, and its own CORS config. The failure is not dramatic — it is slow: an auth bug fixed in 27 of 30 services, inconsistent 401 versus 403 semantics, and no single place to see who is calling what. Meanwhile the mobile client is calling 8 services directly and cannot ship a change without coordinating with all of them.

Mechanism. A single managed entry point that owns cross-cutting concerns:

  • Authentication and token validation — verify JWT/OAuth once at the edge; pass a trusted identity header inward.

  • Authorisation coarse checks — scope and tenant validation before traffic reaches a service.

  • Rate limiting and quota — per key, per tenant, per route.

  • Routing and versioning — map public paths to internal services; keep /v1 stable while services are refactored behind it.

  • Request/response transformation and aggregation — the Backend-for-Frontend pattern: one gateway shape per client type (web, mobile, partner) so mobile is not forced into the web's chattiness.

  • Observability — one place where every request is logged with a correlation ID.

💸 The trade-off. It is a central point of failure and, more insidiously, a central point of coupling — if every team must file a ticket to change a gateway route, the gateway becomes the bottleneck the microservices were supposed to remove. Business logic creeping into the gateway ("just this one field mapping") is the classic slide back toward an ESB.

Numbers to quote. Budget 2–10ms of added latency for a gateway doing token validation and rate limiting. Cache JWKS keys aggressively — a per-request fetch of the signing key is a common self-inflicted latency and availability bug.

When NOT to use it. A single service or a small monolith does not need one; a reverse proxy is enough. Internal east-west traffic is usually better served by a service mesh than by forcing calls back out through the gateway. And a gateway should not do request-level business logic — that belongs in a service.

One-liner. "The gateway owns authentication, quota, routing and correlation IDs so no service reimplements them — and nothing else. The moment business logic appears in gateway config, I've rebuilt an ESB."

9. Rate Limiting & Throttling

💥 The failure it prevents. One misbehaving client — a partner's retry loop, a scraper, a bug in your own mobile app — sends 50k req/s and saturates the pool. Everyone else sees timeouts. Without rate limiting, your availability is a function of your worst-behaved caller. It is also the primary defence against credential-stuffing and enumeration attacks, and the primary control on cost in any usage-billed backend (very much including LLM APIs).

Mechanism. Four common algorithms:

  • Token bucket — tokens refill at a steady rate up to a burst capacity; each request consumes one. Allows controlled bursts. The pragmatic default.

  • Leaky bucket — requests drain at a fixed rate; smooths output completely. Good for protecting a downstream with a hard throughput ceiling.

  • Fixed window — simple counter per interval. Cheap, but permits a 2× burst across a window boundary.

  • Sliding window log / counter — accurate, more expensive in memory or arithmetic. Sliding-window-counter is the usual compromise.

Distributed enforcement is the hard part: with N gateway instances, either each enforces limit/N (simple, wastes headroom, breaks on uneven routing) or they share state in Redis (accurate, adds a hop and a dependency). A common production shape is a local token bucket synced periodically against a central counter.

Always respond with 429 plus Retry-After and X-RateLimit-* headers. A limit the client cannot discover produces retry storms.

💸 The trade-off. Legitimate traffic gets rejected at spikes, and tuning thresholds is a permanent chore. Distributed accuracy costs latency; local approximation costs precision. Too aggressive and you break customers; too lax and you have decoration, not protection.

Numbers to quote. Public API tiers typically land at 100–1000 req/min per key. Redis-backed distributed limiting adds ~1ms. Note that rate limiting (a business/fairness control) is distinct from load shedding (an availability control that drops low-priority work when the system is already in trouble) — a good design has both.

When NOT to use it. Internal trusted service-to-service calls usually want concurrency limits, bulkheads and backpressure rather than request-rate caps. And never rate-limit health checks or your own control plane out of existence.

One-liner. "Token bucket per API key at the gateway, Redis-backed for accuracy, always returning 429 with Retry-After. Rate limiting is fairness and cost control; load shedding is the separate availability control for when I'm already overloaded."

10. Statelessness & Session Management

💥 The failure it prevents. In-memory sessions mean a user is logged out every time you deploy, autoscale down, or lose an instance. It forces sticky sessions, which in turn means uneven load, a stampede when a hot instance dies, and rolling deploys that are user-visible. Statelessness is the precondition that makes concepts 6 and 11 actually work.

Mechanism. No request depends on which instance served the previous one. Session state moves somewhere shared:

  • Server-side session store (Redis/Memcached) — opaque session ID in a cookie, state in Redis. Revocation is instant, payload is small, but you have added a hard dependency on the store and a network hop per request.

  • Client-side signed token (JWT) — claims travel with the request; no lookup needed. Cheap and fully stateless, but revocation is the problem: a token is valid until it expires. Mitigations are short TTLs with refresh tokens, a denylist for compromised tokens (which reintroduces state), or a token-version claim checked against the user record.

  • Sticky sessions — the fallback when neither is feasible. Treat as technical debt with a date on it.

💸 The trade-off. Statelessness moves state, it does not delete it — and now that store is a critical dependency whose outage logs everyone out. JWTs trade revocation latency for lookup-free auth. Bigger tokens also mean bigger headers on every request; a fat JWT is a per-request bandwidth tax.

Numbers to quote. Access token TTL 5–15 minutes with refresh tokens of days is a common shape — it bounds the revocation window to the access TTL. Keep JWTs under ~1KB; some proxies cap header size around 8KB.

When NOT to use it. Genuinely stateful workloads — WebSocket connections, in-progress uploads, streaming LLM responses, game servers — have to hold state somewhere. The right answer is to isolate that state deliberately (a connection-manager tier with its own routing) rather than pretend the whole system is stateless.

One-liner. "Stateless app tier is the precondition for horizontal scaling. Short-lived JWTs for auth, Redis for anything needing instant revocation — and where state is unavoidable, like WebSockets, I isolate it in a tier designed for it rather than letting it leak into the general fleet."

11. Horizontal vs Vertical Scaling

💥 The failure it prevents. Vertical-only scaling has a ceiling and you discover it during your biggest traffic event. You are on the largest instance type available, and the only remaining options are a risky emergency re-architecture or an outage. Horizontal scaling converts a hard ceiling into a cost curve.

Mechanism.

  • Vertical (scale up) — bigger machine. Zero architectural change, works for anything, including things that cannot be distributed (a single-writer RDBMS primary). Bounded by the largest instance available; scaling usually requires a restart/failover.

  • Horizontal (scale out) — more machines behind a balancer. Effectively unbounded, gives redundancy for free, but demands statelessness (concept 10), and pushes you into distributed-systems problems: coordination, consistency, partial failure, and distributed debugging.

  • Autoscaling — reactive (CPU/latency/queue-depth thresholds) or predictive (schedule-based). Queue depth or request concurrency is usually a better signal than CPU for I/O-bound services.

Cells / shuffle sharding is the mature extension: run many independent copies of the whole stack and partition customers across them, so a bad deploy or poison-pill request damages one cell rather than everything.

💸 The trade-off. Vertical is simple and expensive at the top end (price is superlinear near the largest sizes) and gives you no redundancy — one machine is still one failure. Horizontal is cheaper per unit but buys you coordination overhead, eventual consistency, and a much harder operational story. Amdahl's law is the ceiling: the serialised fraction of your workload (usually the database, or a lock) caps the benefit of adding instances.

Numbers to quote. Autoscaling reaction time is realistically 1–5 minutes end to end (metric window + scaling decision + instance boot + warm-up). If your traffic spikes faster than that — a marketing email, a live event — you must pre-warm or over-provision; autoscaling is not a spike defence. Keep steady-state utilisation around 40–60% so you have headroom to absorb the reaction delay.

When NOT to use it. Scale vertically first when you are small: one bigger box is dramatically cheaper in engineering time than a distributed system, and most companies never outgrow it. Scale the database vertically for as long as you possibly can — sharding (concept 22) is the most expensive irreversible decision in this note.

One-liner. "Vertical until it hurts, then horizontal — because horizontal buys unlimited headroom and redundancy at the price of distributed-systems complexity. And I remember autoscaling takes minutes, so it handles growth, not spikes."

Part III — Serving the Request

12. Caching

💥 The failure it prevents. The same expensive work, repeated. A product page that runs 12 queries and 200ms of rendering, requested 5000 times a second by users who all see identical output. Without caching the database is the bottleneck at a fraction of the traffic you need, and every optimisation you make is swamped by volume. Caching is the highest-leverage performance lever in most systems and simultaneously the largest source of correctness bugs.

Mechanism. Caching happens at every layer, and naming the layer is half the skill:

  • Browser cache → CDN (concept 5) → reverse proxy cache → application/distributed cache (Redis, Memcached) → database buffer pool → materialised views.

Patterns, in order of how often you will use them:

  • Cache-aside (lazy loading) — app checks cache, on miss reads DB and populates. Simple, resilient (cache down ≠ app down), but the first request after a miss is slow and there is a stampede risk.

  • Read-through — the cache library owns the fetch. Cleaner code, tighter coupling.

  • Write-through — write to cache and DB together. Cache is always fresh; writes are slower.

  • Write-behind — write to cache, flush to DB asynchronously. Fastest writes, real durability risk on cache loss.

Eviction: LRU is the default; LFU suits skewed popularity; TTL is your explicit staleness budget; W-TinyLFU is what modern caches (Caffeine) use.

The two failure modes with names worth knowing:

  • Thundering herd / cache stampede — a hot key expires and 5000 concurrent requests all miss and hit the DB simultaneously. Fixes: request coalescing (single-flight), probabilistic early expiry, or a short lock on repopulate.

  • Hot key — one key takes a disproportionate share of traffic and saturates a single cache node. Fixes: local in-process cache in front of the distributed cache, or key replication across nodes.

💸 The trade-off. You now have two sources of truth and no transactional link between them. Every cache is a deliberate decision to serve stale data, and the design question is not "should it be fresh" but "how stale, for how long, and what breaks at that staleness?" Cache invalidation is genuinely hard because correctness now depends on cross-system ordering. Debugging also gets worse: "works on my machine" often means "your cache is warm."

Numbers to quote. Redis GET: ~0.1–1ms versus a typical indexed DB query at 1–10ms and a complex aggregate at 100ms+. At a 90% hit rate you have cut DB load 10×; at 99% you have cut it 100×. Rule of thumb: caching is worth it when read:write ratio exceeds roughly 10:1 and the data tolerates staleness.

When NOT to use it. Write-heavy data with low read reuse (you pay invalidation cost and get no hits). Data where staleness is a correctness or compliance problem — account balances at the moment of a transaction, permission checks, inventory at checkout. And never cache before you have measured: caching an already-fast query adds a dependency for nothing.

Wrong instinct: "Add Redis in front of the database and we'll be fine."

Better: Name the cache key, the TTL, the invalidation trigger, the expected hit rate, and what the user sees during the staleness window. Then add the stampede protection before launch, not after the first incident.

One-liner. "Cache-aside with an explicit TTL that I can defend as a staleness budget, single-flight to prevent stampedes, and a local L1 in front of Redis for hot keys. Every cache is a second source of truth, so I decide the invalidation strategy before I add it."

13. Consistent Hashing

💥 The failure it prevents. You have 10 cache nodes and route keys with hash(key) % 10. You add one node. Now it is % 11, and roughly 90% of keys map to a different node — the entire cache is effectively cold at once, every request misses, and the database takes full traffic at the exact moment you were trying to add capacity. The same problem applies to database shards, where it means a full data migration for every topology change.

Mechanism. Map both nodes and keys onto a hash ring (say 0 to 2³²−1). A key belongs to the first node found walking clockwise from the key's position. Adding or removing a node only affects the keys in the arc between it and its predecessor — on average K/N keys move rather than nearly all of them.

Two refinements you must mention or the answer is incomplete:

  • Virtual nodes (vnodes) — each physical node is placed at many points on the ring (typically 100–500). Without them, ring positions are uneven and load is lumpy; with them, distribution smooths out and you can weight heterogeneous machines by giving bigger ones more vnodes. Vnodes also make rebalancing parallel: a departing node's data is pulled from many peers rather than one.

  • Bounded loads — plain consistent hashing still lets one node run hot under skewed keys. "Consistent hashing with bounded loads" caps any node at a factor of the mean and overflows to the next node on the ring.

💸 The trade-off. More complex than modulo, and it requires all clients to agree on the ring — a membership/gossip problem. Distribution is statistically even, not perfectly even, so you still need hot-key handling. Range queries are impossible: hashing deliberately destroys key locality, so WHERE id BETWEEN x AND y becomes a scatter-gather across all nodes.

Numbers to quote. Modulo hashing with N→N+1: roughly N/(N+1) of keys remap — 90% at 10 nodes. Consistent hashing: 1/(N+1) — about 9%. With 150 vnodes per node, load variance typically sits within about 5% of the mean.

When NOT to use it. When you need range scans or ordered access — use range partitioning instead (concept 22). When node membership is fixed and never changes, modulo is simpler and fine. And when a coordinator or directory service can track key→node mapping explicitly, an explicit lookup table gives you finer control (this is what many managed shard routers do).

One-liner. "Consistent hashing so scaling the cache or shard set moves 1/N of keys instead of nearly all of them, with 100–500 virtual nodes per physical node for even distribution and weighted capacity. The cost is that I give up range queries entirely."

14. Idempotency

💥 The failure it prevents. The customer is charged twice. A client submits a payment, the response is lost to a network timeout, the client retries, and the server processes a second charge. This is not a rare edge case — it is the guaranteed outcome of combining retries (concept 28) with non-idempotent operations at any meaningful scale. The same failure produces duplicate orders, double-sent emails, and double-applied inventory decrements.

Mechanism. An operation is idempotent when performing it N times has the same effect as performing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics; POST is not, which is why POST needs help:

  • Idempotency key — the client generates a unique key (UUID) per logical operation and sends it in a header. The server stores key → (status, response) atomically with the business write. On a repeat key: if complete, return the stored response; if in-flight, return 409 or wait; if new, process.

  • Natural idempotency — design the operation so repetition is harmless: SET balance = 100 instead of INCREMENT balance BY 10; upsert on a unique business key instead of blind insert.

  • Deduplication window — consumers of at-least-once queues (concept 15) keep a seen-message-ID set for a bounded window.

  • Optimistic concurrency / fencing tokens — include an expected version; reject if it does not match. This also protects against the stale-actor problem where a paused process wakes up and writes old data.

The subtle requirement: the key record and the business effect must be written in the same transaction, or you get a crash window where the effect happened but the key was not recorded.

💸 The trade-off. You need durable storage for keys and a retention policy (24h is common), which is extra state and extra writes on the hot path. Clients must be disciplined about generating and reusing keys correctly — a client that generates a fresh key per retry has gained nothing. And the semantics of a concurrent in-flight duplicate are genuinely awkward to specify.

Numbers to quote. Typical idempotency key retention: 24 hours (Stripe's window). Key storage adds roughly 1ms and one row per mutating request. If you are doing 1k writes/s that is 86M rows/day to expire — TTL indexes or partitioned tables, not a nightly DELETE.

When NOT to use it. Pure reads do not need it. Genuinely append-only event logging where duplicates are acceptable or filtered downstream does not need it. But be honest — the set of operations where a duplicate is actually harmless is much smaller than teams assume.

One-liner. "Every mutating endpoint takes an idempotency key, stored in the same transaction as the business write, with a 24-hour retention window. Retries are inevitable in a distributed system, so exactly-once effects have to be built at the application layer — the network will never give them to me."

15. Message Queues & Pub/Sub

💥 The failure it prevents. Synchronous coupling. Your checkout endpoint calls payment, then inventory, then email, then analytics — synchronously. The email service is slow, so checkout is slow. The analytics service is down, so checkout returns 500 for a non-essential step. And a traffic spike hits every downstream simultaneously with no buffer, so the weakest one collapses and takes checkout with it.

Mechanism. A durable intermediary decouples producer from consumer in time, throughput and availability.

  • Queue (point-to-point) — one message, one consumer from a competing group. Work distribution. SQS, RabbitMQ.

  • Pub/Sub (fan-out) — one message, every subscriber gets a copy. Event notification. SNS, Kafka consumer groups, Pub/Sub.

  • Log-based (Kafka, Kinesis, Pulsar) — an ordered, replayable, retained partition log. Consumers track their own offset, so you can add a new consumer that reprocesses history, or replay after a bug. This is the meaningful architectural difference from a classic queue, where a consumed message is gone.

Mechanics that decide your design: partition key (ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, so pick a key like user_id when per-entity order matters), consumer groups (parallelism capped by partition count), acks and visibility timeout, dead-letter queues for poison messages, and backpressure when consumers fall behind.

Delivery semantics: at-most-once (fire and forget), at-least-once (the practical default — hence concept 14), exactly-once (only within a closed transactional system such as Kafka's transactions; across arbitrary systems it does not exist).

💸 The trade-off. You have converted a synchronous call into an eventually-consistent flow, and the user-visible contract changes: "your order is placed" now means "queued". Debugging becomes distributed tracing rather than a stack trace. You gain a new operational surface: consumer lag, DLQ depth, partition skew, rebalance storms. And ordering guarantees are weaker than most people assume.

Numbers to quote. Kafka handles millions of messages/sec per cluster with single-digit-ms produce latency; retention is typically 7 days but is a config, not a law. SQS standard gives at-least-once with best-effort ordering; FIFO gives ordering at ~3000 msg/s per message group with batching. Consumer parallelism is hard-capped by partition count — 10 partitions means at most 10 useful consumers in a group.

When NOT to use it. When the caller genuinely needs the result to respond (an auth check, a price quote). When strict global ordering across all entities is required — that is a single partition, i.e. a single-threaded system. And for tiny systems, a queue is often premature: a background thread and a retry table go a long way.

One-liner. "Queue anything the user doesn't need to wait for — email, analytics, indexing, webhooks. Log-based like Kafka when I want replay and multiple independent consumers, partitioned by entity ID where ordering matters, at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers and a dead-letter queue."

16. Event-Driven Architecture & CQRS

💥 The failure it prevents. A write model contorted to serve read patterns. Your normalised orders schema is correct for transactions but the "customer order history with product details and shipping status" screen needs a seven-table join that takes 800ms, so you start denormalising into the transactional schema and now writes are slow and the model is confusing. Separately: services calling each other synchronously in a web produce a dependency graph where any one outage cascades.

Mechanism. Two related but distinct ideas — do not conflate them in an interview.

Event-driven architecture: services publish facts about what happened (OrderPlaced, PaymentCaptured) and interested services react. Key distinction:

  • Event notification — thin event ("order 123 changed"), consumer calls back for details. Low coupling to schema, more chatter.

  • Event-carried state transfer — fat event containing the data, so consumers need no callback. More autonomy, more duplication and staleness.

  • Event sourcing — the event log is the source of truth; current state is a fold over events. Gives perfect audit and time-travel, but schema evolution, GDPR deletion, and rebuild time become real engineering problems. Powerful and expensive; do not adopt it casually.

CQRS: separate the write model from the read model. Commands go to a normalised store optimised for consistency; a projection process consumes the change stream and materialises denormalised read models (Elasticsearch for search, a wide row per screen, a cache). Reads never touch the write store.

💸 The trade-off. Eventual consistency becomes user-visible: a user updates their profile and does not see it on the next screen because the projection lags. You must handle this explicitly (read-your-writes via the write model, optimistic UI, or a version token). Operationally you now own projection lag, projection rebuilds, and schema versioning of events. There is no single place to read "the truth" — a huge cognitive cost.

Numbers to quote. Projection lag is typically 10ms–1s in a healthy system and is the number you must monitor and alert on. A full projection rebuild for 100M events is hours, so plan for it before you need it at 2am.

When NOT to use it. CRUD applications where reads and writes have similar shapes gain nothing but complexity. Small teams — the operational burden is real. And never adopt event sourcing purely because you want an audit log; an append-only audit table gives you 80% of the value for 5% of the cost.

Wrong instinct: "We'll do CQRS across the whole system for scalability."

Better: Apply CQRS to the specific bounded context where read and write shapes genuinely diverge — usually search, feeds, or reporting. Keep the rest CRUD. Architecture is applied per-context, not per-company.

One-liner. "Events for decoupling, CQRS where the read shape genuinely differs from the write shape — search and feeds, typically. The price is user-visible eventual consistency, so I decide up front how the UI handles a stale read, and I monitor projection lag as a first-class SLI."

17. Batch vs Stream Processing

💥 The failure it prevents. Two symmetric failures. Batch-only: your fraud model scores transactions in a nightly job, so fraud is detected 14 hours after the money left — the analytics are correct and useless. Stream-only: you have no way to recompute six months of history after fixing a bug in the aggregation, because the data was never retained in a reprocessable form.

Mechanism.

  • Batch — bounded data, scheduled, high throughput, easy to reason about and re-run. Spark, dbt, warehouse SQL. Correctness is easy because you see all the data at once.

  • Stream — unbounded data, continuous, low latency. Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming. Correctness is hard because of the fundamental problem: event time versus processing time. Events arrive late and out of order, so you need windowing (tumbling, sliding, session) and watermarks to decide when a window is "done" and how late is too late.

  • Lambda architecture — run both: a stream layer for fresh approximate results and a batch layer that recomputes the accurate truth, merged at query time. Correct but you maintain two implementations of the same logic, which drift.

  • Kappa architecture — stream only, with a retained replayable log. Reprocess by replaying from offset zero into a new job and swapping. One codebase; requires long retention and cheap replay.

💸 The trade-off. Batch buys simplicity and correctness at the cost of freshness.
