Stream buys freshness at the cost of substantially harder correctness (late data, exactly-once state, checkpointing), harder testing, and much harder operations — a stateful streaming job with a corrupted checkpoint at 3am is a bad night. Lambda doubles your code; Kappa demands storage and replay discipline.

Numbers to quote. Batch: minutes to hours of latency, unbeatable cost per record. Micro-batch (Spark Structured Streaming): seconds. True streaming (Flink): tens to hundreds of milliseconds. Watermark allowed-lateness is typically minutes to hours depending on how bad your mobile clients are.

When NOT to use it. Do not stream what nobody consumes in real time — a daily report does not need Flink, and you will pay for that decision in ops time forever. Do not batch anything where the decision is time-critical: fraud, alerting, rate limiting, personalisation. Ask "what decision does this power, and how fast must it be made?" and let the answer choose.

One-liner. "Freshness requirement drives the choice. Batch for reporting and model training, stream for anything that drives a real-time decision. I lean Kappa — one streaming codebase over a retained log — because maintaining two implementations of the same aggregation in Lambda always drifts."

Part IV — Storing the Data

18. SQL vs NoSQL

💥 The failure it prevents. Choosing storage by fashion rather than access pattern, then discovering the mismatch after you have 500M rows. Two classic outcomes: a document store chosen for "scale" that now needs multi-entity transactions and cross-collection joins it cannot do; or a relational database chosen by default that is now doing 200k writes/s of time-series data it was never designed for.

Mechanism. The real axis is not "SQL vs NoSQL" — it is which access patterns the storage engine makes cheap.

  • Relational (Postgres, MySQL) — normalised, strong ACID, flexible ad-hoc queries via a query planner, joins. You do not have to know your queries in advance. Scales vertically extremely far; scales horizontally with real effort. Default choice, and modern Postgres with JSONB, arrays and full-text search covers a startling fraction of "we need NoSQL" cases.

  • Document (MongoDB, DynamoDB) — a record per aggregate, schema-flexible, horizontally scalable, single-item operations are fast. You must design around known access patterns; DynamoDB in particular demands you enumerate every query before you pick a key schema. Cross-document consistency is limited.

  • Key-value (Redis, Memcached, DynamoDB) — O(1) lookup by key. Caches, sessions, counters, rate-limit buckets, feature flags.

  • Wide-column (Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB) — massive write throughput, tunable consistency, partition-key-driven. Time-series, event history, IoT. Query flexibility is near zero.

  • Graph (Neo4j) — relationship traversal where a relational multi-hop join explodes. Social graphs, fraud rings, recommendations.

  • Search (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch) — inverted index, relevance ranking, faceting. Never the source of truth; always a projection.

  • Time-series (TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, Prometheus) — timestamp-partitioned, compressed, downsampling built in.

  • Vector (pgvector, Pinecone, Qdrant, Weaviate) — ANN search over embeddings. The AI-era addition; the same rules apply — it is a projection, not truth.

💸 The trade-off. Relational buys query flexibility and consistency at the price of horizontal-scaling difficulty. NoSQL buys scale and write throughput by making you commit to your access patterns at schema-design time — flexibility you lose is not recoverable without a migration. And polyglot persistence (using several) buys the right tool per job at the price of N operational surfaces, N backup strategies, and a synchronisation problem between them.

Numbers to quote. A well-tuned Postgres on modern hardware comfortably handles tens of thousands of writes/s and terabytes of data — far beyond where most teams assume they need to switch. Cassandra scales to millions of writes/s across a cluster. If your justification for NoSQL is "we might get big", you are almost certainly wrong about the timeline.

When NOT to use it. Do not reach for NoSQL for scale you do not have. Do not use a document store when your data is genuinely relational and you need transactions across entities. Do not make Elasticsearch or a vector DB your system of record — they are rebuildable projections, and treating them as truth means an index corruption is data loss.

One-liner. "Postgres by default — it covers relational, JSON, full-text and now vectors, and it scales further than most teams will ever need. I move to a specialised store when a specific access pattern proves expensive: wide-column for write-heavy time-series, search for relevance, key-value for hot lookups — always as a projection, never as truth."

19. Indexing

💥 The failure it prevents. A query that is instant on 10k dev rows and takes 40 seconds on 50M production rows, because it is a sequential scan. This is the single most common cause of "the site got slow as we grew" — the code did not change, the data did. The inverse failure is over-indexing: a table with 15 indexes where every insert has to update 15 B-trees, so writes crawl and the indexes consume more disk than the data.

Mechanism. An index is a separate ordered structure mapping column values to row locations — trading write cost and storage for read speed.

  • B-tree — the default. O(log n) point lookups, and crucially supports range scans and ordered retrieval. Handles =, <, >, BETWEEN, ORDER BY, and prefix LIKE 'abc%'.

  • Hash — O(1) equality only, no ranges.

  • Composite index — order matters, and this is where most people go wrong. An index on (a, b, c) serves queries filtering on a, a+b, or a+b+c — the leftmost prefix rule. It does not efficiently serve a query filtering only on b.

  • Covering index / index-only scan — if the index contains every column the query needs, the engine never touches the table. Often a 10× win.

  • Partial index — index only rows matching a predicate (WHERE status = 'active'), much smaller and cheaper.

  • Specialised — GIN/GiST for JSONB, arrays and full-text; inverted index for search; LSM-trees (Cassandra, RocksDB) which optimise for write throughput at the cost of read amplification and compaction work; HNSW/IVF for vector ANN.

The skill is reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE: sequential scan versus index scan, estimated versus actual rows (a big gap means stale statistics), and whether the planner chose the index you expected.

Picture: CyHawk, B-tree, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

💸 The trade-off. Every index is a write tax paid for read speed. Each insert, update and delete must maintain every affected index; each index consumes disk and buffer-pool memory that would otherwise hold data. Indexes also increase lock contention on write-heavy tables, and creating one on a large table can lock it unless you use a concurrent build.

Numbers to quote. Sequential scan of 10M rows: seconds. Index lookup: sub-millisecond. Rule of thumb: an index earns its place if it lets a query skip 90%+ of rows — below roughly 10–20% selectivity the planner will often prefer a scan anyway. Watch for low-cardinality indexes (a boolean column) which rarely help.

When NOT to use it. Small tables (the planner will scan them anyway and be right). Columns with very low cardinality. Write-heavy tables where the query is rare — sometimes a slow analytical query is better run against a replica or the warehouse than paid for on every write forever.

One-liner. "Index to match access patterns, composite indexes ordered by the leftmost-prefix rule, covering indexes where the query is hot enough to justify it. Every index is a write tax, so I audit for unused indexes as carefully as I add missing ones — and I read EXPLAIN ANALYZE rather than guessing."

20. Normalization vs Denormalization

💥 The failure it prevents. Fully normalised: your feed query joins eight tables and the fan-out makes it unservable at scale. Fully denormalised: a user changes their display name and you now have to update it in 40 million cached rows, and you will miss some, so the same user appears under two names in different parts of the product. Both failures are real; the question is which one you would rather manage.

Mechanism.

  • Normalization (3NF) — each fact stored exactly once, relationships by foreign key. Updates touch one row. No possibility of internal contradiction. Cost: reads require joins, and join cost compounds with data volume and join count.

  • Denormalization — duplicate data where it is read. Precompute the join. Reads become a single lookup. Cost: writes must fan out to every copy, and the copies can drift.

The mature answer is that you normalise the write model and denormalise the read model — which is exactly CQRS (concept 16). The write store stays 3NF and authoritative; projections carry the duplicated, read-optimised shape and are rebuildable from the truth. That reframes duplication from "risk of corruption" to "derived data with a rebuild procedure."

Middle grounds worth naming: materialised views (denormalisation the database maintains for you), computed/cached columns (a comment_count on the post row), and summary tables refreshed on a schedule.

💸 The trade-off. Normalization optimises write correctness and storage; denormalization optimises read latency. You are choosing where to pay: at write time (fan-out, consistency management) or at read time (joins, latency). The critical corollary: denormalised data must have a rebuild path. If you cannot regenerate a denormalised copy from the normalised source, it is not a cache — it is a second, unreconcilable source of truth.

Numbers to quote. An 8-table join at scale can be 100ms–1s; the denormalised equivalent is a 1–5ms single-row read. Storage is the cheap side of this trade: duplicating a display name across 40M rows costs a few GB, which is nothing. The expensive side is the update fan-out and the consistency reasoning.

When NOT to use it. Do not denormalise before you have measured the join cost — premature denormalisation buys you consistency bugs in exchange for latency you did not need. Do not denormalise data that changes frequently relative to how often it is read; the fan-out cost will exceed the read saving.

One-liner. "Normalise the write model so there's exactly one place to change a fact; denormalise into read projections where the join cost is proven and the data is rebuildable. Storage is cheap, so the real cost of denormalisation is the update fan-out and the drift I have to detect."

21. Replication

💥 The failure it prevents. A disk dies and the data is gone. Or: your read traffic is 100× your write traffic and a single primary is saturated serving reads that any copy could have served. Or: an entire availability zone goes offline and there is no second copy in another one. Replication is the foundation of both durability and read scalability, and it is what makes availability targets above ~99% possible at all.

Mechanism. Maintain copies of the same data on multiple nodes.

  • Single-leader (primary-replica) — all writes to the primary, replicated to read replicas. Simple, no write conflicts, the default for relational databases. Failover requires promoting a replica.

  • Multi-leader — multiple accepting writes, typically one per region. Low write latency everywhere, but write conflicts are now your problem and need resolution (last-write-wins, which loses data; CRDTs; or application-level merge).

  • Leaderless (Dynamo-style, Cassandra) — write to any N nodes, read from several, use quorums. W + R > N gives strong-ish consistency; tune W and R to trade latency against consistency. Read repair and anti-entropy reconcile divergence.

Synchronous vs asynchronous is the decision that matters most:

  • Sync — the primary waits for a replica to acknowledge. Zero data loss on primary failure (RPO = 0), but write latency now includes the replica round trip, and a slow replica stalls all writes.

  • Async — primary acknowledges immediately. Fast, but a primary crash loses everything not yet shipped.

  • Semi-sync — wait for at least one of N replicas. The usual production compromise.

Replication lag is the practical consequence: a user writes, is routed to a replica for the next read, and does not see their own change. Fixes: read-your-writes routing (send a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after a write), monotonic-read session pinning, or a version token the client passes so the replica can wait or redirect.

💸 The trade-off. Async replication trades durability for latency. Sync trades latency and availability (a stalled replica blocks writes) for durability. Every replica also multiplies your storage cost and your write amplification. And multi-leader trades write locality for the genuinely hard problem of conflict resolution.

Numbers to quote. Same-region async replication lag: typically 1–100ms, but seconds to minutes under write bursts or long transactions. Cross-region: add the RTT, so 50–200ms minimum. Automated failover detection and promotion is realistically 10–60 seconds. Quote RPO (how much data you can lose) and RTO (how long you can be down) — those two numbers are the replication design.

When NOT to use it. Read replicas do not help a write-bottlenecked system at all — that is sharding (concept 22). Replicas also do not protect you from logical corruption: a bad DELETE replicates perfectly to every copy in milliseconds. Replication is not backup. You need point-in-time recovery as a separate control.

Wrong instinct: "We have three replicas, so we're safe."

Better: Replicas protect against node and zone failure. They replicate your bugs faithfully. Backups with point-in-time recovery, tested restores, and a documented RPO/RTO are a separate requirement.

One-liner. "Single-leader with semi-sync replicas for durability plus async read replicas for scale, with read-your-writes routing so users don't see stale data after their own writes. I state RPO and RTO explicitly — and I never confuse replication with backup, because a bad DELETE replicates in milliseconds."

22. Sharding & Partitioning

💥 The failure it prevents. A single database node has finite disk, finite IOPS, and finite write throughput. When your write volume or dataset exceeds what the largest available machine can handle, replication does not help — every replica must accept the same write volume. Sharding is the only answer to a write or dataset size ceiling. The failure it prevents is the hard wall; the failure it causes if done badly is the hot shard, where 80% of traffic lands on one partition and you have all the complexity with none of the benefit.

Mechanism. Split data across independent nodes, each owning a subset.

  • Vertical partitioning — different tables or columns on different nodes. Simple first step; splits by feature, not volume.

  • Horizontal sharding (the real thing) — rows split by a shard key:

    • Range-based — users a–h, i–p, q–z. Supports range scans, but hotspots badly on skewed or sequential keys (timestamps are the classic disaster: all writes hit the newest shard).

    • Hash-based — hash(key) % N, or better, consistent hashing (concept 13). Even distribution, no range queries.

    • Directory/lookup-based — an explicit key→shard mapping service. Maximum flexibility for rebalancing, but the directory becomes a critical dependency.

    • Geo-based — shard by region for locality and data residency.

Choosing the shard key is the highest-stakes decision in the system. It must give even distribution, keep related data that is queried together on the same shard, and match your dominant access pattern. For a multi-tenant SaaS, tenant_id is usually right — until one tenant is 40% of your data, at which point you need a composite key or a dedicated shard for whales.

💸 The trade-off. You lose things that were free: cross-shard joins become scatter-gather in application code, cross-shard transactions become distributed transactions (concept 26), ORDER BY ... LIMIT across shards requires fetching from all and merging, and globally unique IDs need a scheme (Snowflake IDs, UUIDv7). Rebalancing is a data migration. Operations multiply: N schema migrations, N backups, N failovers. And the shard key freezes your access patterns — changing it later is one of the most expensive migrations in software.

Numbers to quote. Rules of thumb before sharding: exhaust vertical scaling, add read replicas, add caching, archive cold data, and consider table partitioning within a single node. Most teams shard 2–3 years earlier than necessary. Once sharded, expect hot shards to be your recurring operational problem; monitor per-shard load as a first-class metric.

When NOT to use it. Almost always, at first. Sharding is the most expensive and least reversible decision in this note. Managed distributed SQL (Vitess, Citus, CockroachDB, Spanner, Aurora Limitless) can hide much of the mechanics — consider those before hand-rolling. And if your problem is read volume, not writes or data size, replicas and caching solve it far more cheaply.

One-liner. "Shard only when writes or dataset size exceed one node — replicas and caching solve read problems more cheaply. The shard key is the decision: even distribution, co-located related data, matching the dominant access pattern. And I plan for the whale tenant before it exists, because rebalancing a hot shard under load is genuinely painful."

23. Object Storage, OLTP vs OLAP

💥 The failure it prevents. Two distinct mistakes with the same root cause — using one store for jobs with opposite access patterns.

First: storing 5MB images as BLOBs in Postgres. Your backups take hours, your buffer pool is full of image bytes instead of hot rows, replication lag balloons, and every schema migration is terrifying. Second: the analyst who runs SELECT ... GROUP BY over 200M rows against the production primary at 9am and takes the checkout flow down with it.

Mechanism.

Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) — flat namespace of immutable-ish blobs with HTTP access, effectively unlimited capacity, 11-nines durability, and lifecycle policies to tier cold data to cheap classes. The architectural pattern: store the bytes in object storage, store the metadata and the URL in your database. Uploads go direct from client to object storage via presigned URLs so the bytes never touch your application servers, and downloads go through the CDN.

OLTP vs OLAP — the same data, opposite shapes:

  • OLTP — row-oriented, many small indexed reads and writes, normalised, strict consistency, milliseconds. Your production database.

  • OLAP — column-oriented (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, ClickHouse, DuckDB), few enormous scans aggregating a handful of columns across billions of rows, denormalised star schemas, seconds to minutes. Columnar layout means an aggregate over one column reads only that column's compressed data — often 10–100× less I/O than row storage.

The bridge between them is CDC (change data capture) — stream the database's write-ahead log (Debezium et al.) into the warehouse or lakehouse, giving near-real-time analytics without polling the production database. The lakehouse pattern (Iceberg, Delta Lake, Hudi over object storage) is the current default: cheap object storage for the bytes, table formats providing schema, ACID and time travel on top.

💸 The trade-off. Object storage gives you cheap unlimited capacity but only eventual listing consistency in some operations, per-request cost, higher latency than a local disk (tens of ms), and no query capability — you cannot WHERE an S3 bucket without a query engine over it. Separating OLTP from OLAP means maintaining a pipeline, tolerating its lag, and reconciling two models of the same business entities that inevitably drift in definition ("what counts as an active user?").

Numbers to quote. S3 durability is 99.999999999% (11 nines); availability ~99.99%. S3 GET latency is roughly 20–100ms first byte — fine behind a CDN, wrong for a hot read path. Storage cost is roughly an order of magnitude below block storage, and cold tiers another order below that. Columnar compression on analytical data commonly hits 5–10×. Typical CDC lag into a warehouse: seconds to minutes.

When NOT to use it. Object storage is wrong for small, frequently-mutated records — per-request cost and latency dominate. It is not a filesystem: no partial updates, no append-in-place, no rename (that is a copy plus delete). And a warehouse is wrong for point lookups by primary key — that is what OLTP is for.

One-liner. "Bytes in object storage with presigned direct upload and CDN delivery, metadata in the database. Analytics never touch the production primary — CDC into a columnar warehouse, accepting seconds of lag, because OLTP and OLAP have opposite access patterns and one store cannot be good at both."

Part V — Keeping It Consistent

24. CAP & PACELC

💥 The failure it prevents. Promising, in the same design review, that the system is always available and always returns the latest write and survives a network partition. CAP is the formal proof that you cannot have all three, and it exists to force the conversation about which one you are actually giving up — before an incident makes the choice for you.

Mechanism. In the presence of a network Partition, a distributed system must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write — formally, linearizability) and Availability (every request gets a non-error response).

The framing most people get wrong: you do not "choose CA." Network partitions are not optional — they happen, whether as a cut cable, a saturated link, or a GC pause long enough to look like one. So the real choice is:

  • CP — on partition, refuse requests on the minority side rather than serve stale or divergent data. Consensus systems: etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner, HBase, MongoDB (with majority concerns).

  • AP — on partition, keep serving from all sides and reconcile afterwards. Dynamo-lineage: Cassandra, DynamoDB (eventually consistent reads), Riak.

PACELC is the more useful extension, because partitions are rare and the trade-off exists all the time: if Partition, then A or C; Else (normal operation), Latency or Consistency. Spanner is PC/EC — it pays latency (TrueTime commit-wait) to keep consistency always. Cassandra is PA/EL — available under partition, low-latency the rest of the time, consistency tunable per query. DynamoDB is PA/EL by default with an opt-in strongly-consistent read.

The other essential nuance: CAP is per-operation, not per-system. In one product, "add to cart" can be AP (never block a user from adding an item) while "confirm payment" is CP (never double-charge). Designing the whole system at one consistency level is the amateur move.

Picture: JamieMcCarthy, CAP Theorem Euler Diagram, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0. Read it with care: the CA region is the popular picture, but partitions aren't optional, so a real system picks CP or AP when one happens, as the diagram above shows.

💸 The trade-off. CP systems have lower availability by construction — the minority partition is down by design, and every write costs a consensus round trip. AP systems have higher availability and lower latency but hand you conflict resolution, and the user-visible artifacts of eventual consistency (a deleted item reappearing, a counter going backwards).

Numbers to quote. Consensus write with a majority quorum: 1 RTT to a majority — sub-millisecond same-rack, 1–10ms same-region, 50–150ms cross-region. Spanner's commit-wait is bounded by TrueTime uncertainty, historically single-digit milliseconds. That is the concrete price of "C" in the E half of PACELC.

When NOT to use it. Do not use CAP as an argument-ender ("it's a CAP trade-off") without saying which operations and which failure mode. And do not let CAP push you into eventual consistency for a system that comfortably fits on one node — CAP only binds you once the data is distributed.

One-liner. "Partitions aren't optional, so the choice is availability or linearizability when one happens — and PACELC reminds me I'm also paying latency for consistency the other 99.9% of the time. I make that choice per operation: cart operations AP, payment CP."

25. ACID, BASE & Isolation Levels

💥 The failure it prevents. Two users click "book the last seat" simultaneously and both succeed. A balance transfer debits one account and the credit is lost to a crash. A report reads half of a transaction's changes and produces a number that never existed. These are not exotic — they are the default behaviour of concurrent access without the right isolation, and they are silent: no error, just wrong data.

Mechanism.

ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (invariants preserved — the weakest and most-misunderstood letter, it really means "the DB enforces your declared constraints"), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not corrupt each other), Durability (committed means survives a crash).

Isolation levels are the dial, and knowing the anomalies each one permits is the senior signal:

Level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom read Write skew
Read Uncommitted possible possible possible possible
Read Committed prevented possible possible possible
Repeatable Read prevented prevented possible* possible
Serializable prevented prevented prevented prevented

* Postgres's Repeatable Read (snapshot isolation) actually prevents phantoms but still allows write skew — two transactions each read a consistent snapshot, each individually valid, and together violate an invariant (the classic: two doctors both go off-call because each sees the other still on). This is the anomaly that bites real systems and the one worth being able to describe.

Defaults matter and differ: Postgres and Oracle default to Read Committed; MySQL/InnoDB defaults to Repeatable Read. Most teams never check.

BASE is the counterpoint for AP systems: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency. Not a weaker ACID — a different contract. It says the system converges given no new writes, and it hands you the responsibility for conflict resolution and for designing operations that are commutative or idempotent so ordering matters less.

💸 The trade-off. Higher isolation costs concurrency: Serializable in Postgres uses SSI, which aborts conflicting transactions, so your application must handle serialization failures and retry. Lock-based serializable (2PL) instead costs throughput and deadlocks. Lower isolation costs correctness, but silently. BASE buys availability and latency and charges you in application complexity — every consumer must tolerate stale and out-of-order data.

Numbers to quote. Serializable typically costs 10–30% throughput versus Read Committed and introduces retry-on-abort logic. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (pessimistic) versus a version column (optimistic): optimistic wins when contention is low, pessimistic wins when contention is high and retries would thrash.

When NOT to use it. Full ACID across services is usually the wrong goal — see concept 26. And do not run everything at Serializable "to be safe"; identify the specific invariants that need it (booking the last seat, moving money) and use explicit locking or constraints for those, keeping the rest at Read Committed.

One-liner. "Read Committed by default, Serializable or an explicit lock for the specific invariants that can't tolerate write skew — booking, inventory, money movement. And I check the engine's default, because Postgres and MySQL disagree and most teams never look."

26. Distributed Transactions — 2PC, Saga & Outbox

💥 The failure it prevents. The order service records an order, the payment service crashes before capturing, and now you have an order nobody paid for. Or the reverse: money taken, no order. Once a business operation spans two services or two databases, a single database transaction cannot cover it, and the gap between "committed here" and "committed there" is where money and trust leak.

Mechanism. Three approaches, in increasing order of how often you should reach for them.

Two-Phase Commit (2PC) — a coordinator asks all participants to prepare (durably promise they can commit), then tells everyone to commit. Gives atomicity across systems. The fatal flaw: it is a blocking protocol. If the coordinator dies between phases, participants hold locks indefinitely, waiting. Under distributed load, locks held across a network round trip destroy throughput. Use it inside a single trusted boundary (an XA transaction across two databases in one datacentre) if at all; do not use it across microservices.

Saga — decompose into a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action that semantically undoes it. Reserve inventory → charge card → create shipment; if shipment fails, refund the card and release inventory. Two flavours:

  • Choreography — each service listens for events and reacts. No central coordinator, minimal coupling, but the overall flow exists nowhere in code and is very hard to reason about beyond a few steps.

  • Orchestration — a saga coordinator (Temporal, Step Functions, or a state machine you own) drives the steps explicitly. The flow is visible and debuggable; the coordinator is another component to run. Prefer orchestration for anything over three steps.

Critically, sagas provide ACD, not ACID — there is no isolation. Intermediate states are visible to other transactions, so you need countermeasures: semantic locks (an PENDING status), commutative updates, or reordering steps so the riskiest is last.

Transactional Outbox — the pattern that fixes the most common bug in event-driven systems: writing to the database and publishing to Kafka are two separate systems, so a crash between them loses the event (or publishes an event for a write that rolled back). Instead, write the business row and an outbox row in the same local transaction, then a separate relay (polling or CDC on the WAL) publishes from the outbox. Atomicity restored, using only a local transaction. Pair with Inbox/dedup on the consumer side for at-least-once safety.

Picture: Jayaprabhakar, Two phase commit sequence diagram, Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

💸 The trade-off. 2PC buys atomicity and charges availability and throughput. Saga buys availability and charges you isolation, compensation logic (which is business logic — "refund" is not the inverse of "charge", there are fees and windows), and eventual consistency the user may see. Outbox buys atomicity cheaply and charges you a relay process, table growth, and duplicate delivery you must dedupe.

Numbers to quote. Outbox relay lag is typically 100ms–1s polling, or tens of ms with CDC. A saga's end-to-end completion is seconds to minutes, and you must design the UX for the pending state. Budget for compensations failing too — every compensating action needs its own retry and a dead-letter path to a human.

When NOT to use it. If the operation fits in one database, use one transaction — this is the strongest argument for keeping related data in one service. Do not build a saga for a two-step flow where an idempotent retry would do. And be suspicious of a design that needs many sagas: that is usually a sign the service boundaries are wrong, and the right fix is to move the boundary, not to add a coordinator.

Wrong instinct: "We'll use 2PC to keep the services consistent."

Better: 2PC blocks on coordinator failure and holds locks across the network. Saga with an orchestrator plus transactional outbox is the production answer — and if you find yourself needing many sagas, redraw the service boundaries so the transaction fits inside one.

One-liner. "No 2PC across services — it's blocking. Orchestrated sagas with explicit compensating actions, transactional outbox so the DB write and the event publish are atomic, and idempotent consumers. Sagas give me ACD, not ACID, so I handle the missing isolation with semantic locks and pending states in the UI."

27. Consensus & Leader Election

💥 The failure it prevents. Split brain. The network partitions, both sides believe they are the primary, both accept writes, and when the partition heals you have two divergent histories and no correct way to merge them. This is among the worst failures in distributed systems because it is silent, it corrupts data rather than stopping service, and recovery is manual. Consensus is the mechanism that makes "exactly one leader" true rather than aspirational.

Mechanism. Consensus lets a group of nodes agree on a single value (or an ordered log of values) despite failures.

  • Raft — designed for understandability and the practical default. Terms, leader election by timeout with randomised jitter, log replication where the leader commits an entry once a majority has persisted it. Used by etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiKV.

  • Paxos / Multi-Paxos — the original, correct, and famously hard to implement. Chubby and Spanner descend from it.

  • ZAB — ZooKeeper's protocol, similar guarantees.

The load-bearing idea is quorum: with 2f+1 nodes you tolerate f failures, because any two majorities must overlap in at least one node, so a new leader is guaranteed to see the previous leader's committed writes. This is also why an even cluster size is pointless — 4 nodes tolerate the same single failure as 3, while adding a node that must be available for a majority.

Other essentials:

  • Fencing tokens — a monotonically increasing number issued with leadership. A resource rejects requests carrying an old token, protecting against a paused-then-resumed old leader that still thinks it is in charge. Leases alone are not sufficient because clocks and GC pauses lie.

  • Where it is used — leader election for a primary database, distributed locks, cluster membership, service discovery, config distribution, and ordered log replication.

  • What you should usually do — not implement it. Use etcd, ZooKeeper, or your platform's primitives. Hand-rolled leader election is a reliable source of split-brain incidents.

💸 The trade-off. Every consensus write costs a round trip to a majority, so latency is bounded by your slowest majority member — brutal across regions. Throughput is capped by the leader, since all writes funnel through it. Availability requires a majority: a 3-node cluster losing 2 nodes is unavailable, not degraded, and that is the correct behaviour. And the cluster must be sized and geographically placed deliberately — 3 nodes in one AZ survives node failure but not AZ failure.

Numbers to quote. Cluster sizes: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2. Beyond 5–7, write latency degrades faster than the extra fault tolerance is worth. Raft election timeout is typically 150–300ms randomised, so leader failover is sub-second in-region. Cross-region consensus writes: 50–150ms, which is why global strongly-consistent databases are expensive in latency terms.

When NOT to use it. Do not put consensus on a high-throughput data path — use it for metadata and coordination, and let the data path be leaderless or leader-replicated. Do not use a distributed lock where an idempotent operation or an optimistic version check would do; distributed locks are correctness-critical and easy to get wrong (a lock without a fencing token is not safe).

One-liner. "Raft via etcd for leader election and cluster metadata, never hand-rolled. Odd-numbered clusters of 3 or 5 sized for the failure domain I care about, fencing tokens so a resumed old leader can't write — and consensus on the coordination path only, because every write costs a majority round trip."

Part VI — Keeping It Alive

28. Failure Handling & Observability

💥 The failure it prevents. Cascading failure — the mechanism behind most large outages. One dependency slows from 20ms to 2s. Callers have no timeout, so their threads block. Their thread pools exhaust. Now they are slow, so their callers block. Within minutes an entire system is down because of one degraded component. Naive retries make it strictly worse: a struggling service receives 3× traffic exactly when it is least able to handle it, guaranteeing it never recovers — the retry storm.

The parallel failure is blindness: an incident where you know the site is slow but not which of 40 services is responsible, and you spend 45 minutes of a 60-minute outage finding out.

Mechanism. Layered defences, all of which must be present:

  • Timeouts on every remote call. The single most-skipped control. An unbounded call is an unbounded outage. Set the timeout from the dependency's P99, not from hope. Budget them so the total across a chain fits inside the caller's timeout, and propagate the remaining deadline downstream so nobody does work whose result is already discarded.

  • Retries with exponential backoff and jitter. Backoff spreads load in time; jitter is what prevents synchronised retry waves — without it, all clients retry at the same instant forever. Cap total attempts (3 is typical), and only retry idempotent operations (concept 14) and retryable statuses (5xx, 429, timeouts — never 4xx).

  • Circuit breaker. Track failure rate over a window. On threshold, trip OPEN and fail fast without calling the dependency, giving it room to recover. After a cooldown go HALF_OPEN and let a probe through; on success close, on failure reopen. This converts a slow cascading failure into a fast, contained one.

  • Bulkheads. Separate thread pools / connection pools / instance groups per dependency or per tenant, so exhaustion in one cannot starve the others. This is the pattern that turns "one bad dependency" into "one degraded feature."

  • Load shedding and backpressure. When overloaded, reject cheaply and early (with priority — shed background before interactive) rather than accepting work you cannot finish. Accepting everything at overload is how a system goes from degraded to dead.

  • Graceful degradation. Every non-critical dependency needs a defined fallback: stale cache, default ranking, feature hidden. Decide these at design time — "what does the page look like when recommendations are down?" — not during the incident.

  • Redundancy and blast-radius control. Multi-AZ by default; multi-region if the RTO justifies the cost. Cells / shuffle sharding so a poison input or bad deploy hits a fraction of customers. Progressive delivery — canary, then percentage rollout — with automated rollback on SLO burn.

Observability is what makes all of the above operable, and it is three signals plus one discipline:

  • Metrics — cheap, aggregated, high-cardinality-unfriendly. Alert on these. Track the RED method for services (Rate, Errors, Duration) and USE for resources (Utilisation, Saturation, Errors). Always P50/P95/P99, never averages — an average hides the tail where your users live.

  • Logs — structured (JSON), sampled at volume, always carrying the trace ID.

  • Traces — distributed request tracing (OpenTelemetry) is the only practical way to answer "which of the 40 services caused this". Propagate context across every hop, including through queues.

  • SLOs and error budgets — the discipline. Define what "working" means numerically, alert on burn rate rather than raw thresholds, and use the remaining budget to arbitrate between shipping features and paying down reliability work. Alerts should be symptom-based and actionable; if a page has no runbook action, it should not page.

💸 The trade-off. Every one of these adds latency, code, and configuration surface. Timeouts too aggressive cause spurious failures on healthy-but-slow calls; too loose and they do nothing. Circuit breakers can trip on a transient blip and turn a partial degradation into a full one for the cooldown window. Bulkheads waste capacity by reserving it. Observability itself costs real money — tracing and high-cardinality metrics at scale can rival your compute bill, which is why sampling strategy is an actual design decision.

Numbers to quote. Availability: 99.9% = 43 min/month down; 99.99% = 4.3 min/month; 99.999% = 26 sec/month. Serial dependencies multiply — ten components at 99.9% each gives 99% overall, i.e. 7 hours a month. That arithmetic is the argument for graceful degradation: make dependencies optional and you stop multiplying. Circuit breaker typicals: trip at ~50% failure rate over a 10s window, cooldown 30s. Retries: 3 attempts, base 100ms, full jitter. Trace sampling: 1–10% of normal traffic plus 100% of errors.

When NOT to use it. Do not retry non-idempotent operations without an idempotency key — you will duplicate side effects. Do not circuit-break a dependency you cannot degrade around; failing fast into a hard error is not obviously better than waiting. And do not build a five-layer resilience stack for an internal tool with ten users — resilience engineering is proportional to what an outage costs.

Wrong instinct: "We added retries, so we're resilient."

Better: Retries without backoff, jitter, a cap, and a circuit breaker are an outage amplifier. Resilience is timeouts first, then bounded jittered retries, then breakers, then bulkheads, then a defined degraded mode — and observability good enough to tell you which one fired.

One-liner. "Timeouts on every call with propagated deadlines, bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter on idempotent operations only, circuit breakers to fail fast, bulkheads so one dependency can't starve the pool, and a defined degraded mode per non-critical dependency. Observability is RED metrics on P99, structured logs with trace IDs, and SLO burn-rate alerts — because I need to know which of forty services is the problem in two minutes, not forty-five."

Appendix A — Numbers Every Architect Should Have Memorised

Latency ladder (order of magnitude — each step is roughly 1000×):

Operation Latency
L1 cache reference ~1 ns
Main memory reference ~100 ns
SSD random read ~100 µs
Redis GET (same DC, over network) ~0.1–1 ms
Indexed DB query ~1–10 ms
Disk (HDD) seek ~10 ms
Same-datacentre round trip ~0.5 ms
Cross-region round trip (US east–west) ~60–80 ms
Cross-continent round trip ~150–200 ms

Availability arithmetic:

SLO Downtime per month Downtime per year
99% ~7.3 hours ~3.65 days
99.9% ~43 minutes ~8.8 hours
99.95% ~22 minutes ~4.4 hours
99.99% ~4.3 minutes ~53 minutes
99.999% ~26 seconds ~5.3 minutes

Serial dependency multiplication — N components in series at availability a gives aᴺ. Ten 99.9% components in series = 99.0%. This is why optional dependencies with fallbacks matter more than making each dependency slightly better.

Capacity estimation shortcuts:

  • 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 req/s average. Peak is typically 2–5× average, and a launch spike can be 20×.

  • 1 billion rows at 1KB each = 1 TB. Comfortable on one machine.

  • 86,400 seconds in a day. 2.5M seconds in a month. 31.5M seconds in a year.

  • A modern server handles ~10k concurrent connections comfortably; 100k+ needs deliberate tuning (event loop, file descriptors, memory per connection).

Appendix B — The Decision Ladder

When someone says "make it scale", this is the order. Each step is roughly 10× cheaper than the one after it.

🤖 Appendix C — How Each Concept Reappears in AI Systems

These primitives do not go away when the workload becomes LLM inference — they get sharper, because inference is 100–1000× slower and more expensive per unit of work than a database query. The mapping below is the bridge from this note into the 06-ai-systems designs.

Concept AI-system manifestation
CDN / edge caching (5) Semantic caching — cache by embedding similarity, not exact string. A 30% hit rate on a $0.01 call is direct margin.
Rate limiting (9) Token-based, not request-based. Provider TPM/RPM limits are a hard external constraint; you need per-tenant token quotas and a queue in front of the model.
Statelessness (10) Conversation state must live in Redis or a DB, never in process — but streaming responses reintroduce sticky connections you must design for.
Caching (12) Three distinct layers: exact-match response cache, semantic cache, and provider-side prompt/KV cache (put the stable system prompt and context first to maximise prefix hits).
Idempotency (14) Essential — an LLM call is expensive and non-deterministic, so a retry without an idempotency key costs money and returns different output.
Queues (15) The default shape for anything over ~10s: submit job, return job ID, stream or poll. Also the buffer that absorbs provider rate limits.
CQRS / projections (16) The vector index and the document store are projections of source documents. Reindexing is a projection rebuild, and it takes hours — plan it.
Batch vs stream (17) Batch embedding jobs (often ~50% cheaper via batch APIs) versus real-time ingestion for freshly-uploaded documents.
Storage choice (18) Vector DB for ANN, plus a relational store for metadata and filters, plus object storage for source documents. Vector store is never the system of record.
Indexing (19) HNSW vs IVF-PQ: recall/latency/memory trade-off, exactly analogous to a B-tree's read/write trade-off. Hybrid dense-plus-BM25 because dense misses IDs and exact keywords.
Sharding (22) Namespace or index per tenant for isolation; the whale-tenant problem is identical and arrives faster.
CAP / consistency (24) "Document uploaded" versus "document searchable" is a genuine eventual-consistency window users notice. Surface it in the UI.
Saga / outbox (26) Multi-step agent workflows are sagas — each tool call is a local transaction needing a compensating action. Durable execution (Temporal) is the orchestration answer.
Circuit breakers / degradation (28) Model provider outages are frequent. Fallback ladder: primary model → secondary provider → smaller model → cached answer → honest error. Route by cost and capability, not just availability.
Observability (28) RED metrics plus AI-specific SLIs: tokens/request, cost/request, time-to-first-token, groundedness and eval scores. Cost per request is a first-class SLI in a way it never was for CRUD.

Self-Test Before Moving On

Answer these out loud. If you hesitate on more than two, re-read the relevant concept before starting an HLD design note.

  1. Your P99 latency tripled but P50 is unchanged. What are your first three hypotheses?

  2. You add a cache and the hit rate is 12%. Name three plausible causes.

  3. A user updates their profile and the next page shows the old value. Give three possible causes at three different layers.

  4. Your service calls five dependencies, each 99.9% available, all synchronous and required. What is your ceiling, and what would you change?

  5. You must shard a users table. Name your shard key, and name the query it makes expensive.

  6. Payment succeeded but the order was not created. Describe the mechanism that should have prevented this.

  7. A dependency's latency goes from 20ms to 2s. Walk through what happens in your service, in order, with and without a circuit breaker.

  8. When would you deliberately choose availability over consistency, and when would you refuse to?

This note has one job: know when an exact answer is too expensive and a nearly exact one is enough. A Bloom filter answers "have I seen this?" with no false negatives. A count-min sketch answers "how often?" and only ever over-counts. HyperLogLog answers "how many distinct?" within about 1–2%. Each uses kilobytes where an exact structure would use gigabytes. This is HLD index item 40, and it recurs in item 60 (dedupe), item 82 (web crawler) and the LSM read path.

REVISION BLOCK

1. Recall Check (Cover the answers — test before you read)

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What can a Bloom filter get wrong? It can say "maybe present" for an absent key (a false positive). It never says "absent" for a present key.
Bits per item at a 1% false-positive rate? About 9.6 bits with 7 hash functions. Every 10× lower rate costs about 4.8 more bits.
Why can't you delete from a plain Bloom filter? Bits are shared between keys, so clearing one key's bits can erase another key. Use a counting Bloom filter or a cuckoo filter.
Which way does count-min err? It only over-counts, by at most about ε·N with probability 1 − δ.
HyperLogLog's error with m registers? A standard error of about 1.04/√m: 1.6% at 4,096 registers. Redis quotes 0.81% in 12 KB.
Draw by hand: a Bloom lookup key → k hashes → k bit positions → any 0? "definitely absent" : "maybe present, check the real store".

2. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

When an exact set or counter would cost gigabytes, I accept a small, one-sided error. A Bloom filter keeps about ten bits per key and tells me "definitely not here" or "maybe here". It sits in front of an expensive lookup (a disk read, a database, a remote call) so most misses never pay for it. Count-min gives over-estimated frequencies for heavy hitters. HyperLogLog counts distinct items in kilobytes. Each is sized from a target error, and each breaks when it fills past that size.

3. At a glance

Answers Error, and its direction Memory The tell that you need it
Bloom filter "seen this key?" false positives only, rate p ~1.44·log₂(1/p) bits per key most lookups are for keys that don't exist
Counting Bloom / cuckoo filter the same, with delete false positives only ~4× a Bloom filter (counting); about the same (cuckoo) keys expire or get removed
Count-min sketch "how often has x occurred?" over-counts by ≤ ε·N ⌈e/ε⌉ × ⌈ln(1/δ)⌉ counters top-K or rate limits over millions of keys
HyperLogLog "how many distinct?" ±1.04/√m, either way m small registers (Redis: ≤ 12 KB) unique visitors, distinct IPs, per-key cardinality

The Bloom filter sits in front of the expensive store. It only removes work; it never answers on its own that a key is present.

4. Bloom filter — "have I seen this?" in ten bits a key

The question it answers: how do I skip an expensive lookup for keys that aren't there?

A real violation. A web crawler keeps a HashSet<String> of every URL it has fetched, to avoid fetching one twice. At 5 billion URLs and an assumed ~80 bytes per entry (string plus set overhead), the set needs about 400 GB of RAM. The other version of the same mistake skips the set and asks the database "seen this URL?" for every link found, which puts a round trip on the crawler's hottest path.

The fix. Use a bit array of m bits and k hash functions. Adding a key sets its k bits. A lookup checks those bits: any 0 means the key was never added; all 1s means the key may have been added. Two hashes are enough: position i is h1 + i·h2 (mod m).

The sizing math:

m  = −n · ln p / (ln 2)²       bits for n keys at false-positive rate p
k  = (m / n) · ln 2            hash functions (round to an integer)
p' ≈ (1 − e^(−k·n'/m))^k       the real rate once n' keys are in

p = 10%  → 4.79 bits/key, k ≈ 3
p = 1%   → 9.59 bits/key, k ≈ 7
p = 0.1% → 14.38 bits/key, k ≈ 10

At 1%, the crawler's 5 billion URLs fit in about 6.0 GB instead of about 400 GB. Fewer than one URL in 100 falsely reported as seen is then skipped, which a crawler can afford.

Python (run on Python 3, standard library):

import math

M64 = (1 << 64) - 1
def h64(s: str) -> int:                       # FNV-1a, then a splitmix64 finaliser
    h = 0xcbf29ce484222325
    for b in s.encode():
        h = ((h ^ b) * 0x100000001b3) & M64
    h ^= h >> 30; h = (h * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9) & M64
    h ^= h >> 27; h = (h * 0x94d049bb133111eb) & M64
    return h ^ (h >> 31)

class Bloom:
    def __init__(self, n, p):
        self.m = math.ceil(-n * math.log(p) / math.log(2) ** 2)   # bits
        self.k = round(self.m / n * math.log(2))                   # hash functions
        self.bits = bytearray((self.m + 7) // 8)
    def _idx(self, key):
        h = h64(key); h1, h2 = h & 0xffffffff, h >> 32
        return [(h1 + i * h2) % self.m for i in range(self.k)]     # double hashing
    def add(self, key):
        for i in self._idx(key): self.bits[i >> 3] |= 1 << (i & 7)
    def might_contain(self, key):
        return all(self.bits[i >> 3] >> (i & 7) & 1 for i in self._idx(key))

bf = Bloom(n=10_000, p=0.01)
for i in range(10_000): bf.add(f"user{i}")
fp = sum(bf.might_contain(f"other{i}") for i in range(100_000))
print(f"m={bf.m} bits ({len(bf.bits)} bytes), k={bf.k}")
print("false negatives:", sum(not bf.might_contain(f"user{i}") for i in range(10_000)))
print(f"false positives: {fp} of 100000 = {fp/1000:.2f}%")

It prints:

m=95851 bits (11982 bytes), k=7
false negatives: 0
false positives: 976 of 100000 = 0.98%

Break it: fill it past its size. Add 20,000 keys to the filter sized for 10,000, and the false-positive rate measured the same way is 15.77%. The formula predicts 15.75%. At 40,000 keys it predicts 67.9%. A Bloom filter doesn't fail loudly; it slowly starts saying "maybe" to everything. Size it for the expected peak, and rebuild it or add a new layer (a scalable Bloom filter) before it reaches that peak.

Deleting and expiring. A plain filter can't delete, because bits are shared between keys.

Need Use Cost
Delete individual keys counting Bloom filter (a small counter per slot) ~4× the memory
Delete, at Bloom-like size cuckoo filter (stores short fingerprints) inserts can fail when it's nearly full
Keys expire by time one filter per time window, rotated a lookup checks each live window
Unknown final size scalable Bloom filter (new layers with tighter p) a lookup checks each layer

Verdict: a Bloom filter is a "definitely not" oracle in front of an expensive store; size it from the peak key count and an error budget, and never let it answer "yes" by itself.

5. Count-min sketch — "how often?" without a counter per key

The question it answers: which keys are hot, among millions, in fixed memory?

A real violation. A rate limiter or trending-topics job keeps a HashMap<String, Long> of counts per IP or hashtag. Under an attack or a viral event, the number of distinct keys explodes, the map grows without bound, and the process runs out of memory at the worst possible moment.

The fix. Use d rows of w counters. Each key increments one counter per row, chosen by that row's hash. Its estimate is the minimum across the rows. Collisions only ever add to a counter, so the estimate is never too low. Size it with w = ⌈e/ε⌉ and d = ⌈ln(1/δ)⌉. The over-count is then at most ε·N (N = total events), with probability 1 − δ.

Python (count-min and HyperLogLog together, the same hash as §4):

import math
M64 = (1 << 64) - 1
def h64(s: str) -> int:                       # same hash as the Bloom filter
    h = 0xcbf29ce484222325
    for b in s.encode():
        h = ((h ^ b) * 0x100000001b3) & M64
    h ^= h >> 30; h = (h * 0xbf58476d1ce4e5b9) & M64
    h ^= h >> 27; h = (h * 0x94d049bb133111eb) & M64
    return h ^ (h >> 31)

class CountMin:                               # over-counts, never under-counts
    def __init__(self, eps, delta):
        self.w, self.d = math.ceil(math.e / eps), math.ceil(math.log(1 / delta))
        self.t = [[0] * self.w for _ in range(self.d)]
    def add(self, key):
        for r in range(self.d): self.t[r][h64(f"{r}:{key}") % self.w] += 1
    def estimate(self, key):
        return min(self.t[r][h64(f"{r}:{key}") % self.w] for r in range(self.d))

cm = CountMin(eps=0.01, delta=0.01)
stream = ["hot"] * 5_000 + ["warm"] * 500 + [f"cold{i % 20_000}" for i in range(94_500)]
for x in stream: cm.add(x)
print(f"count-min {cm.d}x{cm.w}:", {k: cm.estimate(k) for k in ("hot", "warm", "never")}, "true 5000/500/0")

class HyperLogLog:                            # distinct count in 2^p small registers
    def __init__(self, p):
        self.p, self.m = p, 1 << p
        self.reg = [0] * self.m
    def add(self, key):
        h = h64(key); j = h >> (64 - self.p)                    # first p bits pick a register
        rest = (h << self.p) & M64                              # the remaining bits
        rank = 64 - self.p + 1 if rest == 0 else (64 - rest.bit_length()) + 1
        self.reg[j] = max(self.reg[j], rank)                    # longest run of leading zeros
    def count(self):
        alpha = 0.7213 / (1 + 1.079 / self.m)
        return alpha * self.m ** 2 / sum(2.0 ** -r for r in self.reg)

hll = HyperLogLog(p=12)
for i in range(100_000): hll.add(f"visitor{i % 100_000}"); hll.add(f"visitor{i % 50_000}")
est = hll.count()
print(f"hyperloglog {hll.m} registers: {est:.0f} (true 100000, error {abs(est - 1e5) / 1e3:.2f}%, "
      f"expected ~{104 / math.sqrt(hll.m):.2f}%)")

It prints:

count-min 5x272: hot=5298 warm=812 never=254 (true 5000/500/0)
hyperloglog 4096 registers: 101290 (true 100000, error 1.29%, expected ~1.62%)

1,360 counters stand in for 20,002 keys. "hot" comes out at 5,298 against a true 5,000, which is well inside the ε·N = 1,000 bound. A key never seen gets 254, not 0. So count-min ranks heavy hitters well, but its small counts mean little. Use it for top-K and "is this key over the limit?", not for billing.

Verdict: count-min is for "which keys are big?"; trust its large counts and its order, never its small counts.

6. HyperLogLog — "how many distinct?" in kilobytes

The question it answers: how many unique users, IPs or search terms, without storing them?

A real violation. A dashboard computes daily unique visitors with SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) over the events table, or with a Set per page in memory. Both grow with the number of uniques. The query gets slower every month, and "uniques per page per day" multiplies the cost by the number of pages.

The fix. Hash each item. The first p bits pick one of m = 2^p registers, and the register keeps the longest run of leading zeros seen in the rest of the hash. Long runs are rare, so their length reveals how many distinct items went past. A harmonic mean across the registers gives the estimate, with standard error about 1.04/√m. The code is in §5's listing: 4,096 registers estimated 100,000 distinct visitors (each seen 2–3 times) as 101,290, an error of 1.29% against the expected ~1.6%.

Two properties make it a design tool, not just a trick:

  • Mergeable: the union of two HyperLogLogs is the register-wise maximum. Per-shard or per-hour sketches combine into a daily total without re-reading any events. Count-min sketches merge too, by adding counters.
  • Fixed size: Redis's PFADD and PFCOUNT use at most 12 KB per key, with 0.81% standard error, however many items go in.

Verdict: HyperLogLog turns "count distinct" from a query that grows into a 12 KB value you can merge; use it wherever the exact number is never billed.

7. Where they show up in designs

Design Structure What it saves
LSM stores (Cassandra, RocksDB, HBase) a Bloom filter per SSTable disk reads for keys not in that file. Cassandra's bloom_filter_fp_chance defaults to 0.01 (0.1 under leveled compaction), and 0.01 needs about 3× the memory of 0.1
Web crawler (HLD 82) Bloom filter on seen URLs, plus a content hash re-fetches, in about 10 bits per URL
URL shortener Bloom filter on taken short codes a database read per candidate code
Dedupe / idempotency (HLD 60) Bloom pre-check before the exact key store exact lookups for keys that are new
CDN or cache admission Bloom filter of keys seen once caching one-hit wonders
Rate limiting, top-K trending count-min sketch per window a counter per key during an attack
Analytics uniques HyperLogLog per page per day, merged COUNT(DISTINCT) scans

The read path these protect is in read and write amplification, and the storage-engine choice is in the B-tree or LSM answer.

8. Interview Follow-ups

Q · Mechanism — Why does a Bloom filter never give a false negative? Adding a key sets all k of its bits, and nothing ever clears a bit. A later lookup of that key checks the same k positions and finds them all set. A false positive happens when other keys have set all k bits of an absent key. That is why the rate depends on how full the array is: fill ratio, k and n/m.

Q · Trade-off — Bloom filter or an exact cache of negative results? A negative cache stores each absent key exactly. It's simple and correct, but its memory grows with the number of distinct misses, and an attacker can flood it with random keys. A Bloom filter of the keys that exist uses fixed memory sized from the real key count. It answers for any absent key, even one never asked about. I'd pick the Bloom filter when the existing set is known and large, and a small negative cache with a TTL when misses repeat a lot.

Q · Failure — After a year, the database behind your Bloom filter is busier than at launch, though traffic is flat. Cause: the filter was sized for launch-day keys and never rebuilt. Twice the keys means 1% false positives became about 16%, so more misses reach the database. Confirm it by measuring the filter's real false-positive rate (store lookups that found nothing, divided by lookups the filter let through) and its fill ratio. Fix: rebuild from the store at the new size, alert on fill ratio, or use a scalable filter.

Q · Design — Count unique viewers per video per day for 100 million videos. That is one HyperLogLog per video per day, at under 12 KB each. Sparse encoding in Redis keeps small ones much smaller, and most videos have few viewers. Write with PFADD from the view stream. Read daily numbers directly, and weekly or monthly numbers by merging dailies, with no re-scan. State the ~1% error on the product page, and keep exact counts only where money is paid per view.

Pitfalls

  • "The filter said yes, so the key exists"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a "yes" from the filter looks like an answer, and skipping the store is the whole point.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: only "no" is certain. A "yes" is right except at rate p, so code that treats it as a hit serves wrong data, such as a short code reported as taken that was free.
    ↳ Think instead: "no" skips the store; "maybe" always checks it.
  • Don't size the filter for today's key count.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the formula needs n, and today's n is the number you have.
    ↳ What goes wrong: the rate rises steeply with fill, from 1% to about 16% at twice the size and 68% at four times. Nothing errors; the store just gets busier.
    ↳ Do instead: size for the expected peak, monitor fill ratio and measured false positives, and rebuild or layer before the peak.
  • Not the same: a Bloom filter vs a cuckoo filter
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both answer "maybe present / definitely absent" in a few bits per key.
    ↳ Difference: a cuckoo filter stores short fingerprints, so it can delete, and it is often smaller at low error rates. Its inserts can fail when it is nearly full.
    ↳ Think instead: need deletes or expiry → cuckoo filter; append-only and simple → Bloom filter.
  • Don't use count-min's small counts as facts.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it returns a number for every key, and the number looks like a count.
    ↳ What goes wrong: collisions add up to ε·N to every key. A key never seen above got 254, so thresholds near the noise floor fire on innocent keys.
    ↳ Do instead: use it for top-K and coarse limits well above ε·N; confirm offenders with an exact count.
  • Don't use weak or correlated hashes.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: String.hashCode() or key.hashCode() + i is right there and seems random enough.
    ↳ What goes wrong: clustered or correlated positions raise the real false-positive rate far above the formula, and similar keys (user1, user2) collide in patterns.
    ↳ Do instead: one good 64-bit hash, split into h1 and h2 for double hashing, and measure the rate on real keys.

Connections

  • 28 core system design concepts — caching (§12), indexing (§19) and sharding (§22), the exact structures these sketches stand in front of.
  • Read and write amplification — the LSM read path that per-SSTable Bloom filters cut.
  • URL shortener — a Bloom filter on taken codes before the database check.
  • Flash-sale system — dedupe at the edge under a burst.
  • 155 idempotency and exactly-once — the exact dedupe store a Bloom pre-check sits in front of.
  • HLD interview reference index — items 40, 60 and 82, where these come up in rounds.
