Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The 5 gaps acronym? CBRDL — Config, Build artifact, Runtime, Data, Lifecycle.
Why does Spring Boot fail in container but not local? DevTools off + cache=true + lazy template parse → first real request crashes.
What's the architect's first question on a "works locally" bug? Which of the five gaps is most likely — not "what's the log message".
Why are unit tests insufficient for parity? They run in the same broken environment; you need artifact-level tests (JAR, image).
What's the role of the deployment circuit breaker here? Last line of defense for residual parity failures — not a substitute for closing gaps in CI.

How to use this section: First pass — answer cold, mark misses. Read Sections 1–18. Second pass — re-test only originally-wrong items. Third pass (day before interview) — full re-test.

1. Definition

Dev/prod parity is the principle of minimizing differences between development, staging, and production environments so that code which runs locally also runs in production. Originates from 12-Factor App, factor #10. Failures of parity manifest as the classic "works on my machine" bug.

2. Why It Matters in Production

Every minute a deploy is broken costs customer impact, on-call pages, and engineering opportunity cost. Parity gaps compound:

  • Failed deploys trigger circuit-breaker rollbacks, eat CI minutes, waste engineer time.

  • Late-discovered bugs (production-only) are 10–100× more expensive to fix than build-time bugs.

  • Erodes deploy confidence — teams compensate with slower release cadences and "deploy on Tuesday only" rules. Velocity dies.

  • Hides real bugs — engineers attribute failures to "environment weirdness" instead of root-causing them, so the same class of bug recurs.

For ML/AI systems specifically, parity gaps are worse: a model that scores correctly in a notebook but produces NaN predictions in serving (different pandas version, different feature ordering, different float precision) is impossible to debug without lineage.

3. Algorithm & Math (How the Mechanism Works)

Production failures that don't reproduce locally always come from one of five gaps. This taxonomy structures every interview answer.

The five gaps explained

Gap 1 — Config: Different runtime configuration. Profiles (dev vs prod), application-{profile}.properties, env vars, secrets, beans activated by @Profile / @ConditionalOnProperty. Example: spring.thymeleaf.cache=false (lazy parse) vs =true (parse at first hit).

Gap 2 — Build Artifact: The "binary" running locally is not the binary running in prod. IDE classpath ≠ JAR classloader ≠ Docker image ≠ K8s pod. Each layer adds new failure modes (case-sensitive Linux vs case-insensitive macOS, init containers, sidecars, volume mounts).

Gap 3 — Runtime: Different JVM/Python/Node version, OS, glibc, or CPU architecture. Apple Silicon arm64 image deployed to Fargate amd64 → exec format error. JVM 21 locally, JVM 17 in container → subtle API differences.

Gap 4 — Data: The runtime is identical but the input data is not. Hand-crafted test payloads (no nulls, valid emails) vs real users (empty lists, unicode, 10KB messages, injection attempts).

Gap 5 — Lifecycle: When and how components initialize differs. DevTools (dev only) disables ALL caching. Lazy beans in dev, eager in prod. Health-check probes that trigger code paths only in containers. @PostConstruct hooks that load real models in prod but mocks in dev.

4. Code / Pseudocode Example

The anti-pattern that caused a real ECS rollback — and the fix that closes the gap structurally, not just locally.

// ANTI-PATTERN: Thymeleaf template + dev profile masks the bug

// application-dev.properties
//   spring.thymeleaf.cache=false   ← lazy parse, never triggers in tests
//   spring.profiles.active=dev     ← DevTools active, all caching disabled

// Template fragment (no null guard):
//   <ul>
//     <li th:each="s : ${services}" th:text="${s}"></li>  ← NPE if services=null
//   </ul>

// FIX: close the gap with defensive template + parity test + matched config

// 1. Template with null guard (structural fix)
//   <table th:if="${services != null and !services.isEmpty()}">
//     <tr th:each="s : ${services}"><td th:text="${s}"></td></tr>
//   </table>

// 2. JUnit 5 test that exercises the data gap (runs in CI)
@Test
void rendersWhenServicesIsNull() {
    Context ctx = baseContext();
    ctx.setVariable("services", null);
    String html = assertDoesNotThrow(() -> templateEngine.process(TEMPLATE, ctx));
    assertTrue(html.contains("None specified"));
}

// 3. Match prod's lifecycle locally (close the lifecycle gap)
//   application-dev.properties (updated)
//   spring.thymeleaf.cache=true   ← was false; now matches prod

The fix is structural, not behavioral: don't "be more careful," instead make the test environment indistinguishable from prod so the null case fails in CI, not in production.

5. Concrete Trace (Step-by-Step with Real Data)

Real ECS Fargate incident — Spring Boot service, image :101, contact form with email template.

📥 Input: PR merged with new Thymeleaf email template (no null guards)
    │
    ▼
🔧 [T-1h] Local mvn spring-boot:run → form tested with full payload → ✅
    │   (Gap masked: cache=false + DevTools + hand-crafted services list)
    ▼
📦 [T-30m] Docker build → push to ECR → tag :101
    │
    ▼
🏛️ [T+0s] ECS deploy starts; service updated to revision :101
    │
    ▼
🤖 [T+30s] New task pulls :101, Spring Boot boots successfully
    │   (Template not yet parsed — cache=true means parse-on-first-render)
    ▼
🌐 [T+45s] ALB health check probes /actuator/health → 200 OK
    │
    ▼
📥 [T+60s] Smoke test POSTs to /api/contact with services=null
    │
    ▼
💥 [T+60s] Thymeleaf hits th:each over null → NullPointerException → 500
    │   ← THIS is where the Data Gap fires
    ▼
⚠️ [T+90s] Health checks on business endpoint fail
    │
    ▼
❌ [T+120s] ECS marks task unhealthy → kills it → spawns replacement (also fails)
    │
    ▼
🚨 [T+180s] Deployment circuit breaker trips after 2 failures
    │
    ▼
🔄 [T+210s] Automatic rollback to :100
    │
    ▼
🎯 [T+240s] "Rollback successful" — service healthy on old code

Step 1 (T-1h, local test): Local environment had three gaps stacked invisibly: cache=false (Lifecycle), DevTools active (Lifecycle), and hand-crafted services=[A,B] test payload (Data). All three masked the underlying bug.

Step 2 (T+30s, container boot): Spring Boot boots fine. Cache=true now means template parsing is deferred to first render — which doesn't happen at boot, only on first request to the contact endpoint.

Step 3 (T+60s, the explosion): Smoke test or real user submits form without selecting services. services = null. th:each walks a null collection → NPE. Without null guard in template, no recovery.

Step 4 (T+180s, circuit breaker): ECS deployment circuit breaker is the safety net for unclosed parity gaps. It rolls back automatically before user impact compounds.

Diagnosis time without parity tests: ~30 minutes (CloudWatch logs → NPE → trace to template). With parity tests: zero — the failing test would have blocked the PR.

6. When TO Use This

Apply the parity discipline whenever:

  • Service deploys to a containerized environment (ECS, EKS, GKE, Cloud Run). The container itself introduces gaps you can't catch locally.

  • System has multiple profiles or environment-conditional config. Every @Profile, every application-{env}.properties, every feature flag is a parity surface.

  • ML system crosses runtime boundaries (notebooks → batch → real-time serving). Training/serving skew is a parity gap with its own name.

  • Cost of a failed deploy is non-trivial — i.e., almost always in production. The investment in parity pays back the first time it prevents a rollback.

  • Deploy frequency is high. Manual gates don't scale; parity automation does.

7. When NOT To Use This

Strict parity has real costs. Senior judgment is knowing when to relax it.

  • Throwaway research code / prototype notebooks where reproducibility isn't yet a concern. Investing in parity tooling here is overengineering.

  • One-off scripts where "production" is your laptop. The 12-factor methodology explicitly targets long-running services.

  • Very early-stage products with weekly deploys and no paying customers. Parity discipline matters more as cost-of-failure grows.

  • When parity becomes performance art — running prod-scale staging that costs $50k/month to catch one bug per quarter is bad ROI. Senior engineers maintain a mental list of which gaps have actually bitten the team and prioritize closing those.

  • When divergence is intentional and bounded — smaller scale staging, mocked third-party APIs you don't control, dummy secrets with prod schema. The rule: divergence should be in scale and stubs, never in code paths or configuration logic.

8. Common Misconceptions

Misconception: "Tests passed locally so the deploy is safe."

Reality: Local tests run against IDE classpath, not the JAR, not the Docker image, not the K8s pod. Each layer can introduce new failure modes. You need artifact-level tests, not just unit tests.

Misconception: "Adding more unit tests will catch parity bugs."

Reality: Unit tests run inside the same broken environment. They use the IDE classpath, the dev profile, hand-crafted inputs. Parity bugs live between environments — they require artifact-level tests (docker run the actual image, smoke-test it, replay anonymized prod payloads).

Personal misconception (held before learning): "Spring Boot is the same code everywhere, so running locally is a sufficient check before pushing to ECS."

Reality: I learned the hard way that DevTools + lazy template parsing + hand-crafted test payloads created a permissive local environment that masked the real failure mode. The fix wasn't being more careful — it was making local match prod's lifecycle (cache=true) so the failure surfaces in dev, not in production at 3am.

9. Interview Traps

Trap 1 — Jumping to logs instead of frameworks. When asked "how would you debug a service that works in dev but fails in prod," weak candidates start describing log-reading. Senior candidates lead with the framework: "There are five places environments diverge — Config, Build, Runtime, Data, Lifecycle. Let me walk through which is most likely first." The framework signals systematic thinking.

Trap 2 — Conflating "test the code" with "test the artifact." Candidates describe unit tests when asked how to test a Docker container. The real answer is docker run the actual image in CI, hit it with smoke tests, verify health endpoints, then promote. Anything less is testing the wrong thing.

Trap 3 — Treating staging as "pre-prod scratchpad." Mediocre answer: "a place to test before prod." Senior answer: "Staging exists specifically to close the parity gap that local can't close — same network policies, same IAM, same secrets manager, same DB engine. It's a parity instrument, not a generic test environment."

Trap 4 — "Just redeploy with the fix" after a rollback. Senior answer: capture the failure signal, write a test that reproduces it locally, fix the test first, then deploy. Otherwise you're guessing — and the same gap will fire again.

Trap 5 — Forgetting ML-specific parity gaps. When the topic is ML systems, candidates often miss training/serving skew, feature pipeline parity, and data drift. These are parity gaps with ML-specific names. Mentioning Feast/Tecton as feature stores that exist specifically to close this gap signals depth.

10. Quick Comparison Table

Strategies to close each gap, ordered by maturity.

Gap Cheap Fix Senior Fix Architect Move
Config Document required env vars in README Centralized config service (Parameter Store, Consul) Run prod profile in CI integration tests; fail build on missing config + drift detection
Build Artifact mvn package && java -jar target/*.jar locally Build & smoke-test the actual Docker image in CI Same image artifact promoted across environments — immutable promotion by SHA
Runtime Pin versions in pom.xml / requirements.txt Build matrix in CI across target runtimes Reproducible builds (Bazel/Nix); multi-arch images; hermetic toolchains
Data Add null/edge-case unit tests Property-based testing (Hypothesis, jqwik) Capture prod payloads, anonymize, replay in CI as fixtures
Lifecycle Disable DevTools features in dev Run startup health checks in CI Smoke-test JAR + container in CI before any promotion

11. Key Numbers & Benchmarks

Metric Value Context Source
Cost ratio of prod-found vs build-found bugs 10–100× Industry-standard "shift-left" economics IBM Systems Sciences Institute; Capers Jones research
Healthy deploy success rate target >95% green Below this, teams firefight rather than ship Google DORA / "Accelerate" book benchmarks
Deploy frequency for elite performers Multiple per day Strongly correlated with parity automation DORA State of DevOps 2023
ECS deployment circuit breaker default threshold 10 task failures or 50% failure rate Triggers automatic rollback AWS ECS docs
Time to detect parity failure with CI artifact tests <5 min vs ~30 min via CloudWatch log forensics Internal incident metric
Container cold start vs IDE start 30–60s for Spring Boot Why health-check grace period must be ≥90s Spring Boot reference, Fargate docs

DORA metrics update annually — re-verify the latest "elite performer" thresholds before any interview. The framework is stable but exact numbers shift.

12. Trade-offs & Performance Considerations

Dimension Trade-off
Dev velocity Strict parity (cache=on, no DevTools) slows feedback loops. Counter-balance with hot-reload tooling that doesn't compromise parity (Spring DevTools restart vs full reload, Tilt/Skaffold for K8s).
💰 Cost Running staging at prod-scale is expensive. Compromise: smaller scale but identical configuration and artifacts. Don't trade config parity for cost savings.
Quality Closing gaps catches bugs earlier → fewer rollbacks → higher deploy success rate (target: >95% green). Direct correlation.
Scale At scale, parity becomes harder (multi-region, multi-cluster). Tools like service mesh, GitOps, image promotion pipelines codify parity rather than relying on discipline.
Ops Complexity Each parity-closing tool (artifact registry, config service, feature flag system) adds ops surface. Pick gaps that have caused incidents; close those first. Don't boil the ocean.

13. Real World Usage

Stripe: Identical Docker images across staging and prod, promoted via image SHA. Configuration injected at runtime via env vars and secrets manager. Building a new image for prod is a parity violation by definition.

Netflix: Spinnaker enforces image promotion — the bytes tested in canary are the bytes that ship to prod, never rebuilt. This is the canonical "build once, deploy many" pattern.

Google: Bazel hermetic builds + Borg ensure binary parity across all environments. Configuration delivered via Chubby with per-job overrides. Reproducibility is enforced at the build-system level, not the team-discipline level.

Shopify: Kubernetes namespaces for environment separation, but identical Helm charts with overridden values — parity is the default, divergence requires explicit override and review.

Typical ECS pattern: ArgoCD GitOps with Terraform-managed infra. Same image SHA tagged through dev → test → prod. Drift between environments is a CI failure, not a warning.

14. Interview Explanation (30 Seconds)

"Dev/prod parity means local and production should differ as little as possible. Failures show up as 'works on my machine' bugs, and they always come from one of five gaps: Config, Build artifact, Runtime, Data, or Lifecycle. The fix isn't being more careful — it's structural. Same image promoted across environments, prod profile run in CI, property-based tests for data edge cases. The architect move is treating parity as infrastructure, not developer discipline. The nuance is which gaps to close first — most teams overinvest in build parity and underinvest in data parity, which is where prod actually breaks."

(85 words.)

15. One-Line Memory Hook + Recall Aid

One-Line Hook

Five Gaps: Config, Build, Runtime, Data, Lifecycle — close them or the user closes them for you.

Acronym

CBRDL — pronounced "see-burdle." A burdle is what you carry across the dev/prod gap.

  • Config — profiles, env vars, secrets, feature flags

  • Build artifact — IDE → JAR → Docker → K8s pod (each layer adds failure modes)

  • Runtime — JVM/Python/OS/arch/library versions

  • Data — test payloads vs real user payloads (the most-missed gap)

  • Lifecycle — eager vs lazy init, DevTools vs prod, cache on/off

Memory Story

Imagine deploying as carrying a fragile package (your code) across five rivers. Each river is a gap. You can build a sturdy bridge (close the gap with tooling) or hope the package stays dry (rely on developer discipline). Junior teams hope. Senior teams build bridges. Architects design the bridge-building system so nobody crosses a river without one.

16. Deep Interview Follow-ups (Tiered)

Tier 1 — Clarification

What does "12-factor app" actually mean and which factor is parity?

The 12-Factor methodology (Heroku, 2011) is a set of 12 principles for building cloud-native applications that are portable, scalable, and resilient. Factor 10 is "Dev/Prod Parity" — keep development, staging, and production as similar as possible.

The key insight is that the gap between environments has three dimensions: time gap (how often code goes from dev to prod), personnel gap (different people deploying than coding), and tools gap (different stacks in dev vs prod). The 12-factor answer is to minimize all three by deploying continuously, having the same engineers own dev and prod, and using the same backing services everywhere.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

When is it acceptable to have intentional dev/prod divergence, and where do you draw the line?

Acceptable divergence is bounded and documented: smaller scale, mocked third-party APIs you don't control, local secrets that mirror prod schema but use dummy values, a single-node DB locally vs a multi-AZ replica in prod.

The line is drawn at code paths and configuration logic. Divergence in scale or stubs is fine — divergence in if (env == "dev") { /* different logic */ } is not. The moment your code behaves differently in dev vs prod beyond what configuration explicitly controls, you've created a hidden parity gap that won't surface until production. Senior engineers audit for this pattern in code review and treat env-conditional logic as a code smell that needs justification.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What fails first as your system scales from 1 to 100 services across 3 regions?

Configuration explosion fails first. With 10 services × 3 environments × 50 env vars each = 1500 config values to keep in sync. Manual sync via README docs breaks down around the 5-service mark. Drift detection (CI step that diffs config keys across environments) becomes mandatory. Reference Section 11: elite DORA performers deploy multiple times daily — that's only sustainable if config sync is automated.

Stateful dependencies fail next. You can't replicate prod data volume + distribution in dev cheaply. The architect-level fix is anonymized prod replay (capture prod traffic, scrub PII, replay against staging) plus synthetic load generation. Multi-region adds a third failure: latency, replication, and regional failover behavior differ between single-region staging and multi-region prod, so you also need chaos testing in prod itself — Netflix's Chaos Monkey is the canonical reference.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design (architect-level)

Design a deploy system for a 50-service organization that enforces parity by default. What are your components and what fails first?

The highest-stakes constraint is making divergence expensive and parity cheap. If parity is the default path and divergence requires explicit override-with-justification, the system self-enforces. Inversion is fatal — if every team has to remember to enforce parity, parity fails by entropy.

The components are: an artifact registry (single source of truth for built images, tagged by Git SHA, immutable); a config service (centralized config with environment overlays, drift detection in CI); a promotion pipeline (image SHA flows through dev → staging → prod with automated gates, never rebuilt); a GitOps controller (ArgoCD/FluxCD reconciles desired state from Git); CI artifact tests that smoke-test the actual image, not the IDE classpath; and observability (logs, metrics, traces) wired uniformly across all environments so you can compare behavior.

The first thing I'd monitor is deploy success rate per service — if it drops below 95%, parity has eroded somewhere. The second is config drift between environments as a leading indicator. The third is time-to-detect-parity-failure — if it takes more than 5 minutes to notice that dev and prod diverged on some config key, the detection layer is too coarse. The architect's mental model is: parity is infrastructure, not discipline. Junior engineers say "be careful when deploying"; architects build systems where carelessness can't cause divergence.

17. Connections (Typed Knowledge Graph)

⬆️ Prerequisites (read these first)

  • 12-Factor App Methodology — original framework that names parity as a principle.

  • Docker / Containerization — containers are the most common parity instrument; understanding their guarantees is essential.

  • CI/CD Pipelines — parity is enforced in CI; without a pipeline you have nowhere to enforce it.

⬇️ Builds toward (read these next to deepen)

  • Immutable Infrastructure — extends parity by making every runtime artifact immutable, not just the image.

  • GitOps (ArgoCD / FluxCD) — operationalizes parity as Git-as-source-of-truth across environments.

  • Progressive Deployment (canary, blue/green) — parity-preserving deployment strategies that limit blast radius.

  • Feature Flags & Trunk-Based Development — decouples deploy from release, reducing the surface where parity can drift.

Alternatives / Competing approaches

  • Hermetic Builds (Bazel, Nix) — stronger guarantee than image promotion; rebuilds are bit-identical regardless of host.

  • Reproducible Builds — adjacent guarantee focused on build determinism rather than runtime parity.

  • Branch-per-environment (anti-pattern) — alternative that creates parity gaps; mentioning it as a foil signals you've seen it fail.

Composes with (used together in real systems)

  • Deployment Circuit Breakers (ECS, Argo Rollouts) — last line of defense for residual parity failures; not a substitute for closing gaps.

  • Observability (logs, metrics, traces) — required to detect parity failures; without it, gaps fail silently.

  • Feature Stores (Feast, Tecton) — close the ML-specific parity gap of training/serving skew.

  • Infrastructure as Code (Terraform, Pulumi) — encodes infra parity; without IaC, environments drift by hand.

18. System Design Application

How this concept appears in a system design interview

In any "design a deploy pipeline" or "diagnose this production incident" question, parity is the spine of the answer. Common framings: "Your team deployed and the service crashed in prod but worked in staging — walk me through how you'd design a system that prevents this." Or: "Design a CI/CD pipeline for a 50-service ML platform." Or directly: "How would you architect for high deploy success rate?" The interviewer is testing whether you can name the gaps systematically and design infrastructure that closes them by default.

System context diagram

The critical property: the same :SHA image flows from ECR into all three clusters. Configuration is injected at runtime from a central source with drift detection. The image has no awareness of which environment it's running in.

Capacity / cost back-of-envelope

Scale Constraint Solution
10 services Manual config sync via README breaks; teams forget env vars Centralized config service + CI step that validates required keys per env
50 services Config drift between environments compounds; rebuilds for prod start "creeping in" Image promotion pipeline (build once, promote SHA); drift detection as CI gate
500 services / multi-region Multi-region replication, regional failover behavior diverges from staging GitOps controllers + chaos engineering in prod; ephemeral preview environments per PR
5000+ services / multi-org Cross-org parity (acquisition, federation) impossible to enforce centrally Service mesh + standardized golden-path templates per org

Where this typically breaks at scale

  • At 10x scale: Config drift. New env vars added in prod hotfix, never backported to staging/dev. Detection: CI job that diffs config keys across environments, fails build on missing keys.

  • At 100x scale: Stateful parity. Cannot replicate prod DB volume in staging cheaply. Symptom: queries that work in staging timeout in prod. Mitigation: anonymized prod replay + synthetic load generation.

  • At 1000x scale: Multi-region behavior. Latency, replication lag, and regional failover work differently in single-region staging vs multi-region prod. Only chaos engineering in prod itself catches this class of bug.

  • Operational 3am failure: A config secret rotates in prod but not in dev/staging, smoke tests stop running, parity drift accumulates undetected, next deploy fails for an unrelated reason and you spend the night untangling cascading drift. The wake-up alert is "deploy success rate dropped below 95% over the last 24h".

Monitoring & SLOs

  • Deploy success rate per service — alert if <95% over 24h. Leading indicator of parity erosion.

  • Config drift count between environments — alert if any service has env-specific config keys not present in prod reference set.

  • Time-to-detect parity failure — measured as time from PR merge to first signal of incompatibility. Target: <5 min. If it exceeds 30 min, your CI artifact tests aren't comprehensive enough.

  • Image promotion lag — time between image-built-in-CI and image-running-in-prod. Long lag = parity drift opportunity.

  • Rollback rate — high rollback rate means parity gaps are firing in prod and the circuit breaker is doing the work CI should have done.

The one framing that makes this whole folder click

A microservice architecture converts in-process method calls into network calls. Every pattern here exists to pay for one of the four things you lost in that conversion:

What you lost Patterns that pay for it
Calls always return Timeout, retry, circuit breaker, fallback, bulkhead
Calls are fast Async messaging, caching, backpressure, load shedding
State is consistent Saga, outbox, idempotency, CQRS, eventual-consistency handling
You can debug it Distributed tracing, correlation IDs, structured logs, SLOs

Say this out loud in an interview and the rest of your answers organize themselves.

The 12 you must own

# Pattern File Tier The one-line reason
1 Timeout resilience 🔴 Nothing else works without it; the root cause behind most cascades
2 Retry with backoff + jitter resilience 🔴 Naive retries turn a blip into an outage
3 Circuit breaker resilience 🔴 Stop hammering a dependency that's already down
4 Bulkhead resilience 🔴 One slow dependency must not drain a shared pool
5 Fallback / graceful degradation resilience 🔴 A degraded answer beats an error page
6 Idempotency key data 🔴 The only honest answer to "did that request actually go through?"
7 Saga + compensation data 🔴 Distributed transactions without 2PC
8 Transactional outbox data 🔴 The only correct way to update a DB and publish an event
9 API gateway communication 🔴 Cross-cutting concerns in one place
10 Service discovery + LB communication 🔴 Instances are ephemeral
11 Distributed tracing deployment 🔴 Without it you cannot debug anything
12 Health check / readiness deployment 🔴 The contract that makes rollouts and failover safe

Single points of failure — the checklist you asked for

You named "single point of failure handler." There isn't one pattern; there's an audit. Walk this list against any architecture and you'll find the SPOFs:

Layer The SPOF The standard mitigation
DNS / entry One region, one LB Multi-AZ LB, health-checked DNS failover, anycast
Gateway Single gateway instance N replicas behind an LB, stateless
Service One instance, or all instances in one AZ ≥2 replicas across AZs, anti-affinity
Database Single primary Replicas + automated failover; know your RTO/RPO
Cache One Redis node holding required state Cluster + replicas; and the app must work with a cold cache
Message broker One broker, RF=1 Replication factor ≥3, min.insync.replicas=2
Config / secrets Config server down = nothing boots Cached local copy, fail-open on read
Auth service Every request validates a token remotely Local JWT validation with cached JWKS
Shared library / schema registry Everyone blocked on one artifact Cache, and degrade to last-known-good
A single team or person The org SPOF Runbooks, on-call rotation — architects are expected to name this one

The interview move: don't just list redundancy. For each SPOF ask the three questions — how is it detected, how long does failover take (RTO), and what is lost (RPO)? Redundancy without detection is theatre.

The trap: adding a redundancy mechanism that is itself a SPOF (a single leader-election coordinator, a single sidecar-config source, one shared circuit-breaker state store).

Anti-patterns

  • Distributed monolith. Services that must be deployed together, share a database, or break when one is down. The most common real outcome of a microservices migration.
  • Chatty synchronous chains. A→B→C→D synchronously: availability multiplies (0.99⁴ ≈ 0.96) and latency adds. Break the chain with async or aggregation.
  • Retry without a budget. See #2 — the single most damaging default.
  • Shared database. Kills independent deployability, which was the entire point.
  • Nano-services. More services than engineers. Coordination cost exceeds any benefit.
  • Microservices with no observability. You've made debugging harder and gained nothing.
  • Splitting before you understand the domain. Start modular-monolith, extract along seams that hurt. Saying this is a maturity signal, not a conservative one.

Suggested study order

  1. resilience.md — timeout → retry → circuit breaker → bulkhead → fallback, in that order; they compose in that order too.
  2. data.md — idempotency, saga, outbox. The three that show you've actually operated a distributed system.
  3. communication.md — sync vs async decision, gateway, orchestration vs choreography.
  4. deployment-observability.md — tracing and health checks first.
  5. The SPOF checklist above — run it against one system you've actually worked on and write the answers down. That becomes your best interview story.
  6. Cross-read ../06-ai-systems/AI-Failure-Modes-and-Debugging-Reference-Index.md — every pattern here has a matching incident there.

The composition order (get this right and half the questions answer themselves)

These patterns wrap each other, and the order matters. Resilience4j's default decoration order, outermost to innermost:

Retry ( CircuitBreaker ( RateLimiter ( TimeLimiter ( Bulkhead ( call ) ) ) ) )

Read it as: a bulkhead-limited, time-bounded, rate-limited call, whose failures trip a breaker, and the whole thing may be retried.

The trap: putting Retry inside the CircuitBreaker means each retry counts as a separate failure and trips the breaker 3× faster than intended. Putting the breaker inside the retry (the default above) means the retry sees one breaker decision. Know which you want and say why.

1. Timeout 🔴

  • Problem: a call that never returns holds a thread, a connection, and a caller's patience forever.
  • Rule: every network call has an explicit timeout. Defaults are usually infinite or absurd (some HTTP clients default to no read timeout).
  • Two timeouts, not one: connect timeout (fast, ~1s) and read/response timeout (budget-derived).
  • Budget rule: an inner timeout must be shorter than the outer caller's remaining budget, or the caller gives up first and you've wasted work. Propagate a deadline header if you can.
  • 🧨 Silent variant: timeout set on the HTTP client but not on the DB call, or on the DB call but not on the connection acquisition from the pool.
  • The critical semantic: a timeout means "I don't know," not "it failed." The work may have completed server-side. This is why timeouts force idempotency (→ data.md).
  • Interview line: "Most cascading failures I've seen root-cause to a missing or too-generous timeout."

2. Retry 🔴

Picture: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Retry pattern.

  • Problem: transient failures (a blip, a rebalance, a brief GC pause) shouldn't surface to the user.
  • Non-negotiables:
    • Only retry idempotent operations — or non-idempotent ones carrying an idempotency key.
    • Only retry retryable errors — 503/429/timeouts/connection resets. Never 400, 401, 404, 422. Retrying a validation error is pure waste.
    • Exponential backoff with FULL JITTER. Not fixed delay. Not backoff without jitter — synchronized clients re-converge into a herd.
    • Bounded attempts (typically 2–3) and a retry budget (e.g. retries ≤ 10% of total requests, enforced client-wide).
    • Respect Retry-After when the server sends it.
  • Retry amplification / metastable failure: a 2% error rate plus 3 retries triples load on an already-struggling dependency; the system stays down after the trigger is removed. This is the highest-signal thing in this file — be able to explain it and the fix (budget + jitter + breaker + load shedding).
  • Retry storm math: N callers × 3 retries against a dependency at capacity = a self-inflicted DDoS.
  • Where to retry: at one layer only. Retries at the client, the gateway, the service, and the SDK multiply (3⁴ = 81 calls). Audit for this.

3. Circuit Breaker 🔴

Picture: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Circuit Breaker pattern.

  • Problem: retrying against a dependency that is definitively down wastes resources and delays recovery.
  • States: CLOSED (normal, counting failures) → OPEN (fail fast immediately, no call made) → HALF_OPEN (allow a few probes) → back to CLOSED on success or OPEN on failure.
  • Key config, and what each means:
    • failure-rate threshold (e.g. 50%) over a sliding window (count-based or time-based).
    • minimum-number-of-calls before the rate is even evaluated — without this, 1 failure out of 1 call opens the breaker on a quiet endpoint.
    • wait-duration-in-open-state before probing.
    • permitted-calls-in-half-open.
    • slow-call-rate threshold — trip on latency, not just errors. A dependency that is up but slow is more dangerous than one that's down, because it holds your threads. Most engineers only configure error-rate; configuring slow-call rate is a differentiator.
  • Granularity: one breaker per dependency (ideally per dependency+endpoint), never one global breaker.
  • Pair with: a fallback (#4) — an open breaker without a fallback just fails faster.
  • Trap: breaker state is per-instance by default. 50 pods each learn independently. Shared state is possible but adds a dependency; usually per-instance is correct — but know that you're answering "yes, each pod learns separately" when asked.
  • Half-open thundering herd: all instances probe simultaneously when the wait elapses; jitter the wait duration.

4. Fallback / Graceful Degradation 🔴

  • Problem: an error page is the worst possible response.
  • The fallback ladder, best to worst — being able to rank these is the point:
    1. Cached previous value (stale-while-revalidate) — often indistinguishable from success.
    2. Default / static content — a generic recommendations list, a default config.
    3. Reduced functionality — search without personalization, checkout without loyalty points.
    4. Queue for later — accept the request, process asynchronously, notify.
    5. Honest, specific error — with a retry hint.
  • Design question to ask about every dependency: "Is this required for a degraded answer?" If no, it must be non-blocking with a fallback. If yes, it's a SPOF and needs redundancy (→ README.md SPOF checklist).
  • Trap: a fallback that itself calls a network resource; or a fallback that silently returns empty results, so a total outage looks like "no data found." Always emit a metric when a fallback fires — 🧨 silent fallbacks are how outages go unnoticed for days.
  • Feature flags as manual fallback: the fastest mitigation in an incident is often flipping a flag, not deploying.

5. Bulkhead 🔴

Picture: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Bulkhead pattern.

  • Problem: one slow dependency exhausts a shared resource pool and takes down endpoints that don't even use it.
  • Named after: ship compartments — a breach floods one compartment, not the hull.
  • Two forms:
    • Thread-pool bulkhead — separate pool per dependency; strong isolation, higher overhead, and it moves the blocking off the caller's thread.
    • Semaphore bulkhead — a concurrency cap per dependency; cheap, but the caller's own thread still blocks.
  • Also applies to: DB connection pools (partition by workload — don't let the reporting query starve checkout), HTTP connection pools, and tenant-level quotas (noisy neighbour).
  • Sizing: Little's Law — concurrency = throughput × latency. If a dependency does 100 rps at 200 ms, you need ~20 concurrent slots. Bring this formula; it makes the answer concrete.
  • With virtual threads: thread-pool bulkheads become less necessary for blocking IO, but semaphore bulkheads become more necessary — unbounded virtual threads still exhaust the downstream. Good modern-Java answer (→ Java index #45).

6. Rate Limiting & Throttling 🔴

  • Two directions, don't conflate them:
    • Inbound (protect yourself): per-client/tenant/endpoint limits at the gateway; return 429 with Retry-After.
    • Outbound (respect others): client-side limiter so you never exceed a third-party's quota — mandatory when calling LLM providers with TPM/RPM limits.
  • Algorithms — token bucket (allows bursts; the practical default), leaky bucket (smooths output), fixed window (cheap, boundary-burst flaw), sliding-window log (accurate, memory-heavy), sliding-window counter (the good compromise).
  • Distributed enforcement: Redis + a Lua script for atomicity; or local buckets with periodic sync (approximate but no hot path dependency). Name the accuracy-vs-latency trade-off.
  • In-process implementation lives in ../02-lld; the distributed design lives in ../03-hld.

7. Load Shedding & Backpressure 🔴

Picture: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Queue-Based Load Leveling pattern.

  • Problem: at saturation, accepting more work makes everything slower and fails all of it. Better to serve 80% well than 100% badly.
  • Load shedding: reject early (before doing work), by priority — drop health-check-ish and batch traffic before user-facing; drop free tier before paid.
  • Backpressure: signal upstream to slow down rather than silently buffering. Bounded queues everywhere; a full queue must reject, not grow.
  • The unbounded-queue trap: an unbounded queue converts a throughput problem into a latency problem and then into an OOM. This is the same mistake as an unbounded ThreadPoolExecutor queue (→ Java index #28).
  • Adaptive concurrency limits (Netflix-style, gradient-based) auto-tune the limit from observed latency — a strong name-drop.
  • Queue-depth is your best autoscaling signal, better than CPU.

8. Health Checks & Failure Detection 🔴

  • Liveness (restart me if this fails) vs readiness (stop sending traffic) vs startup (don't judge me yet). Conflating liveness with readiness causes restart loops under load.
  • Deep-health-check cascade: a readiness probe that checks all downstream dependencies means one dependency's blip marks your entire fleet unready — a self-inflicted outage. Keep liveness shallow; check dependencies in a separate diagnostic endpoint.
  • Outlier detection / passive health checking: the LB ejects instances that start erroring, without an explicit probe.
  • Graceful shutdown: deregister → drain in-flight → close pools → exit. Missing this shows up as a burst of 502s on every deploy.

9. Timeout Budget & Deadline Propagation 🟡

  • Pass a remaining-deadline header through the call chain; each hop subtracts its own elapsed time and refuses to start work it cannot finish. Prevents the whole chain doing work for a client that already gave up.
  • gRPC has this built in; with HTTP you carry it yourself.

10. Redundancy & Failover 🔴

  • N+1 / N+2 capacity, multi-AZ by default, multi-region when the RTO justifies the cost.
  • Active-active vs active-passive — active-active exercises the failover path continuously (so it works when needed) but demands conflict handling; active-passive is simpler and its failover path is untested by definition. Untested failover is not failover — say this.
  • RTO/RPO for each stateful component; a design that doesn't state these hasn't been thought through.
  • Fencing tokens to prevent split-brain after failover (→ ../03-hld).

11. Isolation & Cell Architecture 🟡

  • Shuffle sharding: assign each tenant a random subset of instances; a poison tenant affects only its cell, and overlap between any two tenants is tiny. Elegant, and an excellent thing to name.
  • Cell-based architecture: independent full-stack cells, each serving a slice of traffic; blast radius = one cell. The pattern behind most large-scale cloud services.

12. Chaos Engineering 🟢

  • Game days, fault injection, latency injection, dependency kill tests. The point is to verify the patterns above actually work — most fail their first real test.
  • Interview framing: "We had circuit breakers configured for a year; the first game day showed the fallback threw an NPE."

Resilience4j / Spring Boot quick reference

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      paymentService:
        slidingWindowType: TIME_BASED
        slidingWindowSize: 60            # seconds
        minimumNumberOfCalls: 20         # don't judge on tiny samples
        failureRateThreshold: 50         # percent
        slowCallRateThreshold: 50        # percent  <- configure this
        slowCallDurationThreshold: 2s
        waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
        permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 5
  retry:
    instances:
      paymentService:
        maxAttempts: 3
        waitDuration: 200ms
        enableExponentialBackoff: true
        exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2
        enableRandomizedWait: true       # jitter <- non-negotiable
        retryExceptions: [java.io.IOException, java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException]
        ignoreExceptions: [com.acme.BusinessValidationException]
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      paymentService:
        maxConcurrentCalls: 20
        maxWaitDuration: 0               # fail fast rather than queue
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      paymentService:
        timeoutDuration: 3s
        cancelRunningFuture: true

Verify option names against the Resilience4j version you're on — they have shifted across major versions.

The five questions to ask about any dependency

Run this on every arrow in your architecture diagram. It's a complete resilience review.

  1. What's the timeout? (If "none," stop — that's the bug.)
  2. Is it idempotent? (Determines whether you may retry at all.)
  3. Is it required for a degraded response? (Determines fallback vs SPOF.)
  4. What's the blast radius if it's slow — not down, slow? (Determines the bulkhead.)
  5. How would I know it's failing, and how fast? (Determines the alert; without this the other four are decorative.)

docs.html:
Tier: 🔴 CORE · 🟡 SUPPORTING · 🟢 BREADTH · Flags: trap · comparative

1. Synchronous vs Asynchronous 🔴

The first and most consequential decision. Get the framing right:

Synchronous (REST/gRPC) Asynchronous (queue/log)
Coupling Temporal — both must be up Decoupled in time
Availability Multiplies — 0.99⁴ ≈ 0.96 Each hop independent
Latency Adds up the chain Perceived latency drops; end-to-end grows
Consistency Immediate Eventual — must be designed for
Debugging Easy — one trace Harder — needs correlation IDs
Backpressure Implicit (caller blocks) Explicit (queue depth)
  • Rule of thumb: synchronous when the caller genuinely needs the result to respond; asynchronous for everything else — notifications, indexing, analytics, fan-out, anything the user doesn't wait on.
  • Trap: synchronous chains 3+ deep. Availability multiplies and latency adds. Break with async or an aggregation layer.
  • Trap: async chosen for "scalability" where the client blocks on the result anyway — you've added a queue and kept the coupling.

2. Request/Response Protocols 🟡

  • REST — ubiquitous, cacheable, human-debuggable; verbose, over/under-fetching.
  • gRPC — binary, HTTP/2 multiplexed, schema-first, streaming, built-in deadlines; poor browser story, harder to debug.
  • GraphQL — client-shaped queries, solves over-fetching; N+1 resolvers, caching complexity, hard to rate-limit by cost.
  • Decision: gRPC for internal service-to-service at scale, REST at the edge, GraphQL for a BFF serving heterogeneous clients.

3. Messaging Styles 🔴

  • Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ) — competing consumers, message deleted on ack, per-message semantics. Good for work distribution.
  • Log (Kafka, Pulsar) — append-only, offsets, replay, multiple independent consumer groups, per-partition ordering. Good for event streams and rebuilding state.
  • Pub/Sub (SNS, topics) — fan-out to subscribers.
  • Picking wrong here undermines the whole design. The discriminating question: do you need replay and multiple independent readers? Yes → log. No → queue.
  • Kafka mechanics and its failure modes live in ../06-ai-systems/AI-Failure-Modes-and-Debugging-Reference-Index.md §3.

4. API Gateway 🔴

  • Owns: authN/Z, TLS termination, rate limiting, routing, request/response transformation, aggregation, canary traffic splitting, and the public API contract.
  • Trap: business logic creeping into the gateway; it becomes a deployment bottleneck and a shared SPOF.
  • BFF (Backend for Frontend): a gateway per client type (web, mobile, partner) when their needs genuinely diverge — mobile wants fewer, fatter calls.

5. Service Discovery 🔴

  • Client-side (Eureka, Consul + a smart client) — the client picks the instance; more control, more client complexity, per-language libraries.
  • Server-side (k8s Service, ALB) — the client hits a stable name; simpler clients, an extra hop.
  • Modern default: DNS-based via the platform (Kubernetes Services) — say this rather than reciting Eureka, which dates you.
  • Health integration: discovery must remove unhealthy instances quickly, or you route to the dead.

6. Service Mesh vs Library 🟡

  • Library (Resilience4j, Spring Cloud) — in-process, language-specific, versioned with your app, zero extra network hop.
  • Mesh (Istio/Linkerd sidecars) — language-agnostic retries/timeouts/mTLS/tracing, centrally configured; operational complexity and latency overhead.
  • The double-retry trap: mesh retries and library retries both configured = multiplied attempts. Pick one layer per concern and document it.
  • Honest position: mesh pays off with polyglot services at scale; a single-language shop is usually better served by libraries.

7. Saga: Orchestration vs Choreography 🔴

The multi-service workflow question. Both implement the same saga (→ data.md); they differ in who holds the flow.

Orchestration Choreography
Flow lives in A central orchestrator Distributed across event handlers
Visibility Explicit — you can read the workflow Implicit — you reconstruct it from traces
Coupling Orchestrator knows all participants Participants know only events
Adding a step Edit the orchestrator Add a subscriber (no existing edits)
Failure handling Centralized compensation Each service compensates
Risk Orchestrator becomes a god service / SPOF Cyclic event chains nobody understands
  • Practical answer: orchestration for anything with money, compliance, or more than ~4 steps (you need the audit trail and the explicit state); choreography for simple notification-style fan-out.
  • Implementation: a durable workflow engine (Temporal, Step Functions, Camunda) rather than a hand-rolled state machine in a service — this is the answer that sounds like you've done it.

8. Aggregator / Composition 🟡

Picture: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Gateway Aggregation pattern.

  • One service fans out to several and composes the result. Watch for: partial failures (return partial data with a flag, don't fail the whole response), latency = slowest branch, and the fan-out amplification on downstreams.
  • Scatter-gather with a deadline: return what came back within the budget.

9. API Versioning & Contract Evolution 🔴

  • Strategies: URI path (/v2/), header, media type. Path versioning is ugly and wins in practice for public APIs.
  • Expand/contract (parallel change): add the new field → dual-write → migrate consumers → remove the old. Never a breaking change in one deploy.
  • Rules: additive changes only; never repurpose a field; never make an optional field required; tolerant reader (ignore unknown fields).
  • Schema compatibility: backward / forward / full in the schema registry; deploy consumers before producers for backward-compatible changes.
  • Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) — catches breakage in CI instead of production. Strong signal.

10. Correlation & Context Propagation 🔴

  • A trace ID generated at the edge and propagated through every hop and every message header. Without it, distributed debugging is guesswork.
  • Standard: W3C traceparent / OpenTelemetry baggage. Propagate through async boundaries too — messages carry the trace context in headers, which is the part people forget.

11. Anti-Corruption Layer 🟡

  • A translation boundary so an external or legacy model doesn't leak into your domain. Adapter (→ ../02-lld/03-design-patterns/catalogue/structural.md) applied at a bounded-context edge.
  • Where to put vendor SDK types so exactly one class changes when the vendor does.

12. Strangler Fig 🟡

Picture: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Strangler Fig pattern.

  • Incrementally replace a monolith by routing slices of traffic to new services behind a facade, until the old system is unused.
  • The realistic migration answer, and the one interviewers want over "we rewrote it."

1. Database per Service 🔴

  • The rule: a service owns its data; no other service touches its tables. Access is via API or events only.
  • Why: shared databases destroy independent deployability — the thing microservices exist for. A shared schema means a coordinated migration across teams.
  • The cost you must acknowledge: you lose joins, you lose foreign keys across boundaries, and you lose ACID transactions spanning services. Everything else in this file is paying that bill.
  • The distributed monolith: services with separate deployments but a shared database. Worst of both worlds — say this out loud when asked about migration mistakes.
  • Pragmatic middle ground: separate schemas in one physical database, with no cross-schema queries. Cheaper to operate, preserves the boundary discipline, and you can split later. Offering this is a maturity signal.

2. Idempotency 🔴

The single most important concept in this file. A timeout means "I don't know" — idempotency is how you survive not knowing.

  • Mechanism: the client sends an idempotency key (a UUID it generates, stable across retries). The server stores key → result and returns the stored result on a repeat.
  • Storage: a dedupe table or Redis with a TTL longer than the maximum retry window. 🧨 If that TTL expires before a late retry arrives, the retry is processed as new — duplicate charge, duplicate notification. A real, subtle production bug.
  • Natural idempotency: prefer operations that are idempotent by construction — SET status='PAID' over INCREMENT attempts; upsert over insert; absolute values over deltas.
  • At the DB level: a unique constraint is the last line of defense and the one that actually holds under concurrency. UNIQUE(show_id, seat_id), UNIQUE(idempotency_key). Say this in booking/payment designs — it's the answer that lands.
  • Consumer-side: at-least-once delivery means every message consumer needs a dedupe strategy (message ID, or a natural business key).
  • Scope it: keys should be scoped per tenant/user, or one client's key collides with another's.

3. Saga 🔴

  • Problem: a business transaction spanning services, without 2PC.
  • Shape: a sequence of local transactions; each has a compensating transaction that semantically undoes it.
  • Compensation is not rollback. You can't un-send an email or un-ship a package. You send an apology, issue a refund, create a return. Design compensations as business operations. This distinction is what separates people who've read about sagas from people who've built one.
  • Key properties to name:
    • No isolation — intermediate states are visible to other transactions. Mitigations: semantic locks (a PENDING status), commutative updates, pessimistic ordering of steps (do the reversible things first, the irreversible things last).
    • Compensations must themselves be idempotent and retryable, because they can fail too.
    • Some steps are pivot steps — after which you can no longer compensate, only retry forward.
  • Orchestration vs choreography: → communication.md §7.
  • vs 2PC : 2PC gives atomicity but blocks on coordinator failure and doesn't scale; saga gives availability and eventual consistency. Nobody runs 2PC across services in practice — say why.

4. Transactional Outbox 🔴

The pattern that most cleanly signals "I've actually built this."

  • Problem: you must update your database and publish an event. Two systems, no shared transaction. Either order can fail halfway: DB committed but event lost (🧨 silent — downstream never learns), or event published but DB rolled back (a phantom event).
  • Solution: in the same local transaction, write the business row and an outbox row. A separate relay process reads the outbox and publishes, marking rows sent.
  • Relay options: poll the outbox table, or tail the DB log with CDC (Debezium). CDC is lower-latency and doesn't load the DB.
  • Delivery is at-least-once — the relay can crash after publishing, before marking. Hence consumers need idempotency (#2).
  • Inbox pattern: the mirror image on the consumer side — record processed message IDs in the same transaction as the side effect, giving effectively-once processing.
  • Interview line: "There's no way to atomically write to Postgres and Kafka, so I'd use an outbox with CDC." That sentence alone moves the conversation forward.

5. Change Data Capture 🟡

  • Tail the database's replication log and emit changes as events. Zero application code, captures every change including ones made outside your service.
  • Uses: outbox relay, cache invalidation, search-index sync, data-lake replication, RAG corpus freshness (→ ../06-ai-systems).
  • Trap: CDC leaks your internal schema as a public contract. Emit domain events from an outbox rather than raw row changes, unless the consumer is a replica.

6. CQRS 🟡

Picture: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, CQRS pattern.

  • Separate the write model from one or more read models, each shaped for its queries and updated asynchronously.
  • Use when: read and write loads differ by orders of magnitude, or the read shape is genuinely awkward for the write model (search, dashboards, feeds).
  • The cost: eventual consistency becomes user-visible — a user writes and immediately doesn't see it. Design for it explicitly: optimistic UI update, read-your-writes routing, or a "processing…" state.
  • Trap: applying CQRS to plain CRUD. Most systems don't need it, and saying so is the right answer more often than not.

7. Event Sourcing 🟡

Picture: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Event Sourcing pattern.

  • Store the sequence of events as the source of truth; current state is a fold over them.
  • Wins: complete audit trail, temporal queries ("what did this look like on 3 March?"), replay to rebuild any projection, natural fit for regulated domains.
  • Costs to volunteer: schema evolution of old events is permanent, snapshots are required for performance, GDPR erasure conflicts with an append-only store (crypto-shredding is the usual answer), and the mental model is genuinely hard for a team to adopt.
  • Trap: conflating event sourcing with "we publish events." Publishing events ≠ events as the source of truth.
  • Honest position: use it for the one aggregate that needs an audit trail (the ledger), not the whole system.

8. Eventual Consistency, Made Explicit 🔴

  • Name the inconsistency window and what the user sees during it. "Eventually consistent" without that detail is hand-waving.
  • Read-your-own-writes: route a user's reads to the primary (or their write's shard) for N seconds after a write; or return the written value directly.
  • Monotonic reads: sticky routing so a user doesn't see time go backwards across replicas.
  • Reconciliation: a periodic job that compares systems and fixes drift. For anything involving money, reconciliation is not optional — say this whenever a payment design comes up.

9. Distributed Locking 🟡

  • When you actually need it: a single leader for a scheduled job, or exclusive access to an external non-transactional resource.
  • Redlock is contested — under a GC pause or clock skew, a lock holder can believe it still holds a lock it lost. The fix is fencing tokens: a monotonically increasing token passed to the protected resource, which rejects stale tokens.
  • Prefer avoiding it: partition the work by key so each partition has one owner (Kafka does this for free), or use a DB unique constraint / conditional update instead. "The best distributed lock is not needing one" is a good line.

10. Data Consistency Across Services 🟢

  • Shared reference data: replicate read-only copies via events rather than synchronous lookups on the hot path.
  • API composition for cross-service queries (fan out and join in memory) — simple, but N+1 and latency-prone.
  • Materialized view per consumer — each service keeps its own denormalized projection of what it needs from others. The scalable answer, at the cost of storage and staleness.

11. Schema Migration Safety 🔴

  • Expand/contract, always: add nullable column → dual-write → backfill → switch reads → stop writing old → drop. Never a destructive change in one deploy.
  • Never rename or drop a column in the same release that changes the code using it — rollback becomes impossible.
  • Long-running migrations on large tables need online tooling and a lock-timeout, or you take an outage on the DDL itself.

12. Data Retention, Archival & Erasure 🟡

  • Tiering (hot → warm → cold), TTLs, and legal retention windows.
  • GDPR right-to-erasure vs append-only logs, backups, and derived indexes is a genuinely hard architectural problem — crypto-shredding (delete the key, not the data) is the standard mitigation. Increasingly asked at architect level, especially with AI systems that index personal data.

The consistency decision tree

The senior move: the third branch. "If these two operations must be atomic, that's evidence the boundary is wrong" is an answer very few candidates give.

Deployment

1. Deployment strategies 🔴

Strategy How Cost Use when
Rolling Replace instances in batches Cheap; both versions live at once Default for stateless services
Blue-green Two full environments, flip the LB 2× infra; instant rollback Risky releases, DB-compatible changes
Canary 1% → 10% → 50% → 100%, watching metrics Needs good metrics + automation Anything user-facing at scale
Shadow / dark launch Mirror real traffic to the new version, discard responses No user risk; beware side effects Validating a rewrite or a new model
Feature flag Deploy dark, enable by cohort Flag debt Decoupling deploy from release
  • The rolling-deploy constraint: with two versions live simultaneously, every change must be backward-compatible with the previous version — API, message schema, and database schema. This is why expand/contract exists (→ data.md §11).
  • Rollback triggers defined in advance: error rate > X%, p99 > Y ms, a specific business metric dropping. Deciding the trigger during the incident is too late.
  • Deploy ≠ release. Feature flags separate the two; this is the single biggest safety improvement most teams can make.

2. Configuration & secrets 🟡

  • Config external to the artifact; the same image promotes across environments.
  • A config push is a deploy — it deserves canary and rollback too. A surprising share of outages are config changes that skipped the pipeline.
  • Secrets in a manager (Vault, cloud KMS/Secrets Manager) with rotation. 🧨 Credential and certificate expiry is a top cause of "nothing changed" incidents — alert on expiry dates, don't rely on the calendar.

3. Sidecar & Ambassador 🟡

Picture: Microsoft Azure Architecture Center, Sidecar pattern.

  • Sidecar: a helper container beside the app (proxy, log shipper, secret refresher) — language-agnostic cross-cutting concerns.
  • Ambassador: a sidecar that proxies outbound calls, adding retries/mTLS/circuit breaking without touching app code.
  • Cost: resource overhead per pod, an extra network hop, and a second thing that can fail. Note the double-retry trap (→ communication.md §6).

4. Immutable infrastructure & IaC 🟢

  • Never patch a running instance; replace it. Terraform/Pulumi for infra, GitOps for cluster state, so the repo is the source of truth and drift is detectable.

5. Autoscaling 🟡

  • Scale on the right signal: queue depth or consumer lag for workers, RPS or concurrency for services. CPU is a lagging and often misleading signal — especially with IO-bound work or CPU throttling in containers.
  • Account for warm-up time: JVM JIT warm-up and connection-pool priming mean a new pod is slow for its first ~30s. Set a scaling floor for spiky traffic and consider pre-warming.
  • Scale-in is riskier than scale-out — drain gracefully, and use conservative cooldowns to avoid flapping.

6. Multi-environment parity 🟢

  • Staging that differs in data volume, concurrency, or permissions produces "works in staging" incidents. Note: your existing ../03-hld/dev-prod-parity.md covers this — link the two rather than duplicating.

Observability

7. The three pillars + one 🔴

  • Metrics — cheap, aggregated, alertable. RED for services (Rate, Errors, Duration), USE for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors).
  • Logs — structured (JSON), with the trace ID in every line. Unstructured logs at scale are write-only.
  • Traces — the request's path across services; the only way to answer "where did the 900 ms go?"
  • + SLOs and error budgets — the fourth pillar and the one that turns data into decisions: an SLO defines "healthy," and a burned error budget is the objective signal to stop shipping features and fix reliability. Architect-level rounds expect this framing.

8. Alerting philosophy 🔴

  • Alert on symptoms, not causes. "Checkout error rate > 1%" (a user-visible symptom) beats "CPU > 80%" (a cause that may be harmless).
  • Every alert must be actionable and link to a runbook. Alert fatigue is a reliability problem, not a process annoyance — an on-call who ignores pages will ignore the real one.
  • Multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerts on the error budget: page on a fast burn, ticket on a slow burn. Strong, specific thing to name.

9. Distributed tracing 🔴

  • Trace ID at the edge, propagated across every hop including async message headers — the async propagation is the part teams forget, and it's exactly where you most need it.
  • OpenTelemetry as the vendor-neutral standard; sample intelligently (tail-based sampling keeps the slow and failed traces, which are the ones you want).
  • Span attributes carrying tenant, endpoint, and version make traces queryable rather than merely viewable.

10. Golden signals per layer 🟡

Layer Watch
Gateway RPS, 4xx/5xx rate, p50/p95/p99 latency
Service RED metrics, thread-pool saturation, GC pause time
DB QPS, slow queries, connection-pool wait time, replication lag
Cache Hit rate, eviction rate, memory used, hot-key skew
Queue/Kafka Consumer lag (the single best pipeline health metric), DLQ depth, rebalance count
Host/pod CPU throttling (not just usage), memory working set, OOMKills, restarts

11. Cardinality discipline 🟡

  • Metric labels with unbounded values (user ID, request ID, URL with IDs) explode your metrics bill and can take down the metrics backend. Use exemplars/traces for high-cardinality detail; keep metric labels bounded.

12. Health & readiness 🔴

  • Covered in resilience.md §8. The key reminder here: don't check downstream dependencies in your readiness probe — one dependency blip then marks the whole fleet unready and you've created your own outage.

13. Runbooks & on-call 🟡

  • One runbook per alert: what it means, blast radius, first three checks, mitigation, escalation. This is a lead-role deliverable and a concrete thing to point at in an interview.
  • Blameless postmortems with a detection gap section — "why did a customer tell us first?" is often more valuable than the root cause itself.

14. Audit logging 🟢

  • Immutable, append-only, separate from operational logs; who did what to which resource and when. Required in fintech/health, and increasingly for AI systems making consequential decisions.

The observability readiness test

If you can't answer all five from your dashboards in under two minutes, the system isn't observable:

  1. Is it broken right now, and for whom? (SLO burn, error rate by tenant)
  2. When did it start, and what changed then? (deploy/config/flag timeline overlaid on metrics)
  3. Which hop is slow or failing? (trace)
  4. Why is that hop failing? (logs for that trace ID)
  5. Is it getting worse? (queue depth, lag, saturation trend)
